Components.description: A virtual AMM using a constant-product curve with a concentration factor and dynamic spread/peg that programmatically update before filling trades, plus external Backstop AMM Liquidity (BAL). Components.description: The protocol's first backstop for solvency, held in separate per-asset funds (USDC, BTC, ETH, SOL). Faq.answer: Drift is the leading Solana-native perpetual futures DEX. It runs a hybrid liquidity model combining a Just-In-Time (JIT) auction, an on-chain decentralized limit orderbook (DLOB), and a fallback virtual AMM, alongside spot trading routed via Jupiter, borrow-lend markets, and passive strategy vaults.
Faq.question: What is Drift Protocol?

Faq.answer: A taker order first enters a short JIT Dutch auction where market makers compete to fill at or inside the oracle price. Unfilled size then matches against resting limit orders in the DLOB, and any remainder routes to the vAMM, which prices against a Pyth-anchored constant-product curve so every order is guaranteed a fill.
Faq.question: How does Drift's hybrid liquidity model work?

Faq.answer: During the UST/LUNA collapse on 11 May 2022, a design flaw let users withdraw positive PnL and drain the Insurance Fund without socialised-loss or clawback guardrails. About $8.72M net withdrew in 12 hours, depleting the vault to ~$4.94M. Drift paused the protocol, secured $14.5M in external financing, and made users whole by 27 May 2022, then rebuilt as Drift v2.
Faq.question: What happened to Drift v1 in May 2022?

Faq.answer: DRIFT's Token Generation Event and launch airdrop went live on 16 May 2024, distributing 120M tokens (~12% of the 1B supply) to roughly 150,000 eligible wallets including v1/v2 users, Drift Points participants, and Keepers.
Faq.question: When did the DRIFT token launch?

Faq.answer: The Insurance Fund is Drift's primary solvency backstop, kept in separate USDC, BTC, ETH and SOL funds. Anyone can stake the corresponding asset to further collateralise it and earn a proportionate share of the Revenue Pool (fees from liquidations, trading and borrows) every hour.
Faq.question: What is the Insurance Fund and can I stake in it?

Faq.answer: Drift v2 has been audited by Trail of Bits (2022-2023, no high-severity findings) and Neodyme (2024). OtterSec audited the 'Connect by Drift' MetaMask Snap. Zellic has also published a Drift Protocol audit report.

Risks.description: Drift is a complex multi-program Solana protocol (perps engine, vAMM, vaults, insurance fund). Despite audits by Trail of Bits and Neodyme, bugs in the matching engine, margin math or vault programs could cause loss of funds, as the v1 design flaw demonstrated in 2022.

Pricing for the vAMM, JIT auction starting price, funding rates and liquidations is anchored to Pyth oracle feeds. Oracle latency, manipulation or stale prices could trigger mispriced fills, bad liquidations or funding-rate exploits.

The Insurance Fund is Drift's primary solvency backstop and is finite. In extreme volatility (as in May 2022) it can be depleted, forcing socialised losses across all user deposits and positions when losses exceed allotted limits.

The v1 collapse was triggered by the UST/LUNA death spiral: cross-market contagion, mass withdrawals and collateral depegs. As a Solana-native venue, Drift is also exposed to Solana network outages/congestion that can freeze the JIT auction and orderbook keeper network.

The JIT auction and DLOB rely on a network of whitelisted market-maker Keeper bots. If keepers withdraw or fail to fill during stress, order flow falls back to the vAMM at deeper slippage, worsening execution and funding costs for traders.

DRIFT holders control market listings, risk parameters and treasury funds. Concentrated token holdings (large VC/team allocations under the vesting schedule) or low participation could let governance push risk-parameter or treasury changes adverse to smaller users.

Risks.description: The wethDYDX migration bridge and dYdX Chain custom Cosmos modules (x/clob, x/bridge, x/perpetuals, etc.) are complex, novel code. The Informal Systems audit itself surfaced one critical and multiple medium/low issues (since fixed), and any residual bug in matching, liquidation, or the bridge could cause loss of funds.

dYdX v4 is its own sovereign PoS appchain secured by a limited validator set staking DYDX. Its security and liveness depend on that validator set; a small or concentrated validator/stake distribution, or a consensus/liveness failure in CometBFT, would directly halt or compromise trading — unlike an app inheriting Ethereum L1 security.

As a perps DEX, dYdX relies on price feeds for mark prices, funding, and liquidations. Manipulated, stale, or lagging oracle prices — especially for thinly-traded permissionlessly-listed markets — can trigger wrongful liquidations or bad debt in MegaVault.

MegaVault depositors take on market-making risk: yield or loss is distributed pro-rata from PnL on vault positions across many markets. A sharp adverse move, especially in low-liquidity permissionless markets that MegaVault must backstop, can produce losses for LPs rather than yield.

dYdX geoblocks and contractually prohibits US, Canadian, UK and sanctioned-jurisdiction users from the perpetuals software. This concentrates its addressable market outside major regulated venues and exposes the ecosystem to enforcement/regulatory risk around decentralized derivatives and the DYDX token.

Protocol parameters, upgrades (e.g. dYdX Unlimited), trading rewards, and the MegaVault operator are set by DYDX stake-weighted governance. Risks.description: RCA vaults, gvToken contracts and the underwriting mechanism are on-chain smart contracts; a bug or exploit in Ease's own contracts could cause loss of deposited principal that the coverage system itself cannot backstop.

Deposited assets are routed into external DeFi protocols to generate yield, so users take on the failure/exploit risk of those underlying protocols and their yield-bearing tokens in addition to Ease's coverage promise.

The Uninsurance model has no external reserve or premium float; payouts come from depositors' own pooled capital. A large or correlated hack can exhaust available underwriting capacity, and yield-token cover depends on tokens not diverging from underlying value.

Claim validity and payouts are decided by gvEASE DAO vote rather than an independent adjuster. Concentrated or low-turnout voting, or the high 50M-vote threshold, could lead to disputed, delayed, or captured claim decisions.

Because members reciprocally underwrite each other, a systemic DeFi event hitting multiple covered protocols simultaneously could trigger correlated claims across many vaults at once, stressing the whole shared-risk pool.

Faq.answer: Yes. Slashing went live on Ethereum mainnet on April 17, 2025. It lets AVSs burn an operator's restaked funds if the operator fails to meet the AVS's defined conditions, converting service promises into economically enforced commitments.

Risks.description: Restaked ETH and LSTs are held in EigenLayer's core strategy and delegation contracts. A bug in the restaking, delegation, withdrawal or slashing logic could lead to loss or wrongful burning of staked assets across many restakers at once.

Restaking layers new services on the same underlying ETH stake. Correlated slashing or cascading failures across multiple AVSs sharing the same operators/collateral could concentrate losses and, given EigenLayer's dominant share of restaking TVL, stress the broader Ethereum staking economy.

Operator concentration risk: stakers delegate to a limited set of operators who run the off-chain AVS software. A poorly run, malicious or compromised operator can be slashed (funds burned) since April 2025, causing losses for the restakers who delegated to it.

The EIGEN token introduces 'intersubjective forking' — social-consensus resolution of faults that cannot be proven on-chain. This gives token holders / social consensus discretionary power over what counts as misbehavior, and the Eigen Foundation controls emissions/incentives, creating governance and centralization risk.

Restaked collateral (ETH and liquid staking tokens) is exposed to the risk of the underlying LST depegging or the Ethereum consensus-layer slashing that already applies to staked ETH, compounded by the additional AVS-level slashing conditions layered on top.

Risks.description: Tokenized real estate straddles securities and property law. Estate Protocol uses security-token (ST-20) structures and jurisdiction-specific trusts; regulatory treatment of fractional property tokens and Golden-Visa/eligibility claims varies by jurisdiction and is evolving, creating enforcement and marketing-compliance risk.

Ownership depends on off-chain legal trusts that hold property title on behalf of token holders, plus reliance on partners (e.g., SmartCrowd) and the legal team that forms and administers each trust. If a trustee or partner fails to honor obligations, token holders' economic rights could be impaired despite on-chain records.

The tokens are backed by individual physical properties. Property-level risks (vacancy, tenant default, valuation decline, title/custody defects, local market downturns in Dubai/UAE) directly affect rent distributions and token value, and there is little diversification within a single-property offering.

The platform relies on custom ST-20/Polymath-derived and rewards contracts on Arbitrum. No public third-party security audit was found, so undiscovered smart-contract or transfer-manager vulnerabilities could expose funds or ownership records.

The promised secondary marketplace is still 'coming soon'; until compliant on-chain trading is live, tokens may be effectively illiquid, undermining the core liquidity value proposition and leaving holders unable to exit quickly.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#extra-finance.Description: Extra Finance combines a lending market with leveraged LP farming, letting users lever up liquidity positions on Optimism and Base DEXes.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#extra-finance.Differentiator: Tightly integrated lend + leverage-farm design focused on the Optimism/Base (Superchain) DEX ecosystem, with up to ~7x LP leverage.

Faq.question: Who bears bad debt if a leveraged farm position goes underwater?
Faq.answer: The lending pool depositors. Extra Finance's leveraged yield farming design borrows from single asset lending pools to build the LP position, so any shortfall after liquidation falls on the pool ([Introduction to leveraged yield farming](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/leverage-farming/introduction-to-leveraged-yield-farming)). No public loss event was found in this session, and no insurance fund or backstop is documented.

Faq.question: How are lending rates set?
Faq.answer: Extra Finance uses a pseudo fixed interest rate model on its lending pools rather than a purely floating utilisation curve ([Extra Finance docs](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance)). XLend, being an Aave V3 fork, inherits Aave's rate architecture ([XLend audits page](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/security/audits-and-security)).

Faq.question: How much leverage is available?
Faq.answer: The official documentation describes up to 3x and higher depending on the pool ([Extra Finance docs](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance)). Third party writeups have described up to 7x for veEXTRA holders in select pools, so the effective ceiling depends on the pool and the user's lock ([Vesper Finance deep dive](https://medium.com/vesperfinance/extra-finance-deep-dive-9413d2b8f505)). A credit analyst should treat the pool level parameter, not the headline, as the binding constraint.

Faq.question: Is the protocol profitable, and does that flow to token holders?
Faq.answer: DefiLlama shows the leveraged farming sub-protocol with $8.19m cumulative fees and revenue running at roughly $51,415 in Q3 2025, down from $919,432 in Q4 2024, with token holder net income appearing only from Q2 2025 onward ([DefiLlama, Extra Finance leverage farming earnings](https://defillama.com/protocol/extra-finance-leverage-farming?tvl=false&events=false&earnings=true)). Fees are used to buy back EXTRA distributed to veEXTRA lockers each epoch ([EXTRA tokenomics part II](https://medium.com/@ExtraFinance/extra-tokenomics-part-%E2%85%B1-emission-plan-55ca6a9f874f)).

Faq.question: What is the worst case for a lender?
Faq.answer: A fast correlated move in a leveraged LP pair on a chain with thin liquidation liquidity, leaving the lending pool with unrecoverable debt. The structural aggravator is that the team is pseudonymous with no named legal entity, so there is no off chain counterparty to pursue ([Extra Finance FAQ](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/faq)). There is also no bug bounty program to catch vulnerabilities before they are exploited ([Extra Finance audits and security](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/audits-and-security)).

Faq.question: How centralised is governance in practice?
Faq.answer: Proposals require 30,000 veEXTRA and a 50,000 veEXTRA quorum, with discussion in a Discord channel before Snapshot submission ([ve-mechanism and utility V2](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/tokenomics/ve-mechanism-and-utility-v2), [Extra Finance docs governance summary](https://docingest.com/docs/docs.extrafi.io)). Voting power is measured on Optimism mainnet balances, which concentrates governance on the smaller of its two main chains ([Extra Finance docs governance summary](https://docingest.com/docs/docs.extrafi.io)).

Faq.question: What third party risk oversight exists?
Faq.answer: Gauntlet curates the ExtraFi XLend WETH Vault on Morpho on Base, which crossed $20M in deposits in August 2025 ([ExtraFi on X](https://x.com/ExtraFi_io/status/1956322565443449311)). That is curator oversight of a vault that routes into ExtraFi, not a risk mandate over the core protocol.

Risks.description: Leveraged farming positions are collateralized by DEX LP tokens whose value can fall below the debt threshold. If collateral drops, positions are subject to forced liquidation to protect lenders, and higher leverage tiers (up to 7x) sharply narrow the liquidation buffer.

Leveraged LP positions are exposed to impermanent loss on the underlying DEX pools; sharp divergence between paired assets can erode equity independent of price direction and, combined with borrowed leverage, trigger cascading liquidations across correlated positions.

Liquidation and position-health calculations depend on on-chain price feeds. Manipulated or stale prices for thinly-traded farmed assets could mis-trigger or delay liquidations, potentially leaving the lending pools with bad debt.

The protocol runs complex leverage, lending, and (in XLend) smart-account logic across Optimism and Base. Despite PeckShield, BlockSec, and Sherlock audits, undiscovered contract bugs remain a risk; auditors flagged that privileged admin access needed multisig/timelock hardening.

veEXTRA governance controls pool listings, emissions, and parameter changes, and admin keys retain privileged access. Concentrated voting power or compromised privileged roles could push risky pool listings or parameter changes that expose lenders.

Sources.label: Extra Finance Monthly Review: January 2025 (XLend, TVL, PancakeSwap)

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation cascade in volatile LP farms
TypedRisks.description: Farming positions liquidate once Debt Ratio passes an 83.33% LTV threshold, leaving only a 16.67% buffer, and stable pools liquidate at 90.00%. A 3x ETH-USDC position is liquidated if ETH falls more than 36%.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Safe Liquidation 2.0 partial liquidation of typically 30% of the position, 8% fee on the liquidated slice (2.4% effective) instead of 5% on the whole position.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of open positions with Debt Ratio above 75%, and realised liquidation volume per day.

TypedRisks.name: Total equity wipeout in thin liquidity
TypedRisks.description: The protocol explicitly warns of "risk of depleting all assets" where price moves are large and liquidity is insufficient to liquidate at precise execution prices. Equity can fall below debt, leaving nothing for the farmer.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Liquidity thresholds required before a farming pool is listed, plus leverage caps tied to pool TVL and price stability.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: DEX pool depth for each listed farming pair versus outstanding leveraged notional.
linkedAssetsUnmatched: LP pairs in newly listed or low-liquidity pools

TypedRisks.name: Oracle manipulation of the 30-minute TWAP
TypedRisks.description: Liquidation triggers are based on an on-chain 30-minute TWAP. A sustained push on a thin on-chain market can delay or mistime liquidation relative to true market price.
TypedRisks.mitigation: TWAP is aggregated with a Chainlink price feed for pricing, and leverage is capped for low-credibility assets.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Divergence between the on-chain TWAP and the Chainlink reference feed for each listed asset.
linkedAssetsUnmatched: Optimism pair tokens such as VVV

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation bot failure creating bad debt
TypedRisks.description: The docs state directly that if the liquidation bot fails to close a leveraged position in time there would be bad debt. The team initially operates the bot itself for LYF positions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: XLend liquidations are permissionless with a health factor below 1 trigger, which removes single-operator dependency on that product.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Count of positions sitting above the liquidation threshold for more than one block interval.

TypedRisks.name: Realised bad debt from a collateral asset collapse
TypedRisks.description: In February 2025 the protocol suffered bad debt on EXA and the community had to pass an emergency response proposal. Loss size was not disclosed in the monthly review.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Governance emergency response process; asset isolation and per-asset supply, borrow and LTV caps in XLend.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New governance proposals tagged as emergency response, and reserve or bad debt line items per lending pool.

TypedRisks.name: Recursive looping and self-referential liquidity
TypedRisks.description: Leverage supplied by Extra Finance can become a large share of the liquidity in the very pool being farmed, so a forced unwind moves the price against itself. Extra Finance says it may temporarily disable leverage on new positions when its own share of a pool exceeds roughly 30%.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Explicit 30% liquidity proportion trigger that disables new leveraged positions in that pool.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Extra Finance share of total liquidity in each farmed DEX pool.
linkedAssetsUnmatched: Velodrome LP tokens for smaller pairs

TypedRisks.name: Lender withdrawal blocked at high utilization
TypedRisks.description: If the utilization rate of a lending pool is very high, lenders may be unable to withdraw on time until farmers repay. This is a structural feature of the shared lending pool design.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Interest rate curve rises with utilization to draw repayment and new supply.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Utilization rate per lending pool, especially sustained readings above 90%.

TypedRisks.name: Chain concentration on Base and Optimism
TypedRisks.description: Effectively all TVL sits on two OP Stack chains: Base $22.76m and OP Mainnet $1.65m, with only $10.83 on Berachain. A sequencer halt, reorg or bridge failure on Base would freeze the majority of the book, including liquidations.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Deployment across more than one Superchain chain, though both share the OP Stack codebase.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Base and Optimism sequencer uptime and L2 block production; bridge withdrawal queue length.

TypedRisks.name: TVL contraction and franchise decay
TypedRisks.description: TVL fell from $116.79m in August 2024 to $79.78m at end of February 2025 to $24.41m at time of research. Shrinking deposits reduce fee revenue and thin out the liquidity that makes liquidation safe.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Incentive programs including Optimism OP rounds and EXTRA emissions.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Monthly TVL by chain and by product (LYF versus XLend).

TypedRisks.name: Governance token illiquidity
TypedRisks.description: Total EXTRA on-chain liquidity is $713,613, concentrated in Aerodrome V1 at $605,284. Any treasury or incentive sale, or a governance attack requiring token accumulation, interacts with a very shallow market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: EXTRA token owner role has been invalidated so no new mints are possible; 2.25% of protocol fees are burned weekly.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: EXTRA DEX liquidity depth and 2% slippage size.

TypedRisks.name: Lapsed real-time threat monitoring
TypedRisks.description: The Hexagate monitoring partnership was "not yet renewed in 2025, still in review" as of the docs page. Without an active monitoring vendor, detection of an in-progress exploit relies on the team alone.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Immunefi bug bounty with maximum bounty $100,000 remains live; audits by BlockSec, PeckShield and Sherlock.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Public confirmation of a renewed monitoring vendor contract.

TypedRisks.name: Smart contract risk on a large audited surface
TypedRisks.description: The bounty scope covers XAccount factories and a full Aave-style lending market (Pool, PoolConfigurator, ACL_Manager, A_Token, Debt_Token), a wide attack surface for a small team. Oracle manipulation and flash loan attacks are explicitly in scope, meaning they are recognised as live threats.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Three audits (BlockSec, PeckShield, Sherlock December 2024); no admin function to withdraw user funds; multisig-gated configuration.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New critical or high severity bounty payouts, and unaudited contract deployments.

TypedRisks.name: Multisig configuration authority
TypedRisks.description: Protocol configuration is controlled by a multisig, and risk parameters such as leverage caps and liquidation thresholds are set administratively rather than by a slow on-chain vote. Mis-set parameters or key compromise would directly change solvency.
TypedRisks.mitigation: No admin function exists to withdraw user funds; parameter changes are documented as subject to governance procedures.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Multisig signer set changes and parameter change transactions.

TypedRisks.name: Cross-chain token bridge dependency
TypedRisks.description: EXTRA is bridged between chains using a LayerZero OFT implementation. A messaging layer failure would break EXTRA fungibility across the Superchain deployments.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Single canonical OFT implementation rather than multiple wrapped representations.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: LayerZero endpoint incidents and EXTRA supply reconciliation across chains.

TypedRisks.name: Insurance cover reliance
TypedRisks.description: Coverage is offered through third-party providers OpenCover and InsurAce rather than an internal protocol-owned backstop. Payout depends on those providers' own solvency and claims assessment.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Optional external cover available to users; protocol-level reserves not documented.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Available cover capacity and premium pricing on OpenCover and InsurAce for Extra Finance.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#extra-finance.FundingNote: Extra Finance has no disclosed venture funding. DefiLlama lists no raises for the protocol ([DefiLlama API, extra-finance](https://api.llama.fi/protocol/extra-finance)). Instead the protocol has funded growth through ecosystem grants: it was ranked first by the Optimism Grants Council in the Season 7 futarchy grants contest, which awarded 100,000 OP grants to the top five ([Optimism Collective, futarchy grants contest](https://gov.optimism.io/t/experimenting-with-futarchy-for-optimism-grant-allocation-decisions/9678)). A separate 150,000 OP Season 7 grant application was pushed from Cycle 34 to Cycle 35 ([Optimism Cycle 34 Grants Council final report](https://gov.optimism.io/t/cycle-34-grants-council-final-report/9774)), and XLend received an Optimism audit grant in Cycle 35 ([L2BEAT Governance Review #48](https://l2beat.com/publications/governance-review-48)).

bull.claim: Three independent audits from BlockSec, PeckShield and Sherlock, with the XLend money market being an Aave V3 fork that inherits Aave's audit surface (Extra Finance audits and security, XLend audits page).
Ranked first by the Optimism Grants Council among 23 protocols in the Season 7 grants ranking, unlocking a 100,000 OP grant (Optimism Collective).
Real cumulative revenue: $8.19m of cumulative fees on the leveraged farming product alone, with a documented buyback to veEXTRA lockers (DefiLlama earnings view, EXTRA tokenomics part II).
Product diversification is working directionally: XLend went from $135.49K at launch in February 2025 to over $3M by April 2025 (Extra Finance monthly review, February 2025, April 2025).

bear.claim: TVL of $27.04m on 26 July 2026 is roughly 15% of the December 2024 peak of $177.39m (DefiLlama API, extra-finance).
Revenue has collapsed alongside it: $51,415 in Q3 2025 against $919,432 in Q4 2024, a fall of roughly 94% (DefiLlama earnings view).
Fully pseudonymous team, no disclosed legal entity or jurisdiction, and code that is only partially open sourced (Extra Finance FAQ).
No bug bounty program is documented anywhere in the security pages, which is a material gap for a protocol holding tens of millions in leveraged positions (Extra Finance audits and security).

AssetCoverage.assetStrategy: Extra Finance runs two distinct products with two completely different asset surfaces. The older one is **leveraged yield farming (LYF)**, where the "supported asset" is not a single token but an **AMM LP pool** on Velodrome (Optimism) or Aerodrome (Base): the user deposits one or both pool tokens, borrows the pool tokens from Extra's lending reserves, and the protocol mints an LP position that is auto-compounded. Risk is expressed per farming vault as a **Liquidation Threshold stated as a maximum Debt Ratio** plus a **maximum leverage multiple**, not as a per-token LTV, and every farming vault has its own numeric Vault ID ([Extra Finance Pool Info](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/leverage-farming/pool-info)). The second product is **XLend**, an Aave v3 fork on Base and Optimism with conventional per-reserve LTV, liquidation threshold, liquidation bonus, supply cap, borrow cap, E-Mode and isolation-mode debt ceilings ([XLend E-Mode docs](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/e-mode), [XLend Isolation Mode docs](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/isolation-mode)). What distinguishes Extra is the split oracle philosophy between the two: LYF prices positions off the AMM curve itself with a TWAP and a Chainlink deviation guard, while XLend uses Chainlink as primary ([Extra Finance Price Feed](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/leverage-farming/price-feed), [XLend Price Feed](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/price-feed)). The XLend docs "Parameters" page is published but empty, so all XLend numbers below were read directly from the on-chain Aave v3 `Pool.getConfiguration(address)` reserve configuration bitmap on Base pool `0x09b11746dfd1b5a8325e30943f8b3d5000922e03` and Optimism pool `0x345D2827f36621b02B783f7D5004B4a2fec00186` on 2026-07-26, the Optimism pool address being the one published by Extra ([Extra Finance contracts](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/contracts-and-transparency)). Total protocol TVL is roughly $27M, concentrated on Base ([DefiLlama Extra Finance](https://defillama.com/protocol/extra-finance)).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#extra-finance.RiskPosture: Extra Finance is a small and shrinking leveraged farming protocol whose risk is concentrated rather than systemic. The design is conservative in places: partial liquidation at 30% of a position, an 8% fee on only the liquidated slice, per-asset caps in XLend, no admin withdrawal function and a self-imposed rule to disable leverage when its own liquidity share of a farmed pool exceeds about 30%. Against that, the protocol depends on a team-operated liquidation bot for the farming product, on a 30-minute on-chain TWAP that is manipulable in shallow markets, and on two OP Stack chains for essentially all of its book. The February 2025 EXA bad debt event shows the failure mode is real, and the collapse in TVL from roughly $117m in August 2024 to about $24m today means both revenue and the liquidity cushion that keeps liquidations orderly are much thinner than when the parameters were designed.

Competitors.differences: Goldfinch is USD-denominated and focused largely on emerging markets, whereas Florence is euro-denominated and focused on European SME credit; Goldfinch uses a backer/auditor model versus Florence's wholesale-funder model.
Competitors.name: Goldfinch
Competitors.positioning: Decentralized private-credit protocol funding real-world lending to businesses in emerging markets.
Competitors.similarities: Both are on-chain private-credit protocols that channel crypto liquidity to real-world business/SME borrowers via vetted lenders and tokenized exposure.

Competitors.differences: Centrifuge is a broad multi-asset securitization/Tinlake pool infrastructure across asset classes, while Florence is a narrower euro-denominated SME/private-credit lender.
Competitors.name: Centrifuge
Competitors.positioning: RWA tokenization protocol pooling securitized real-world assets (invoices, loans) for on-chain financing.
Competitors.similarities: Both tokenize real-world credit assets and make them composable in DeFi, connecting asset originators to on-chain liquidity.

Competitors.differences: Clearpool centers on institutional borrower credit pools and its own RWA chain (Ozean), whereas Florence is a euro-focused SME lender that plugs into ecosystems like Ozean as an originator.

Components.description: On-chain vaults that hold portfolios of real-world SME loans grouped by a common denominator (originator, geography, or risk/reward). Depositors fund vaults with flrEUR and receive vault tokens representing a claim on the underlying loan portfolio and its interest. Live vaults include Caple (Arbitrum), Junior/SwishFund (Arbitrum) and Avellinia (Base).
Components.name: Loan Vaults

Components.description: Euro-denominated stablecoin-like instrument minted when a new loan is funded and burned when a loan matures and is repaid. It is intended to be 1:1 redeemable for EUR via the protocol Treasury, and is used to deposit into loan vaults. Secondary liquidity is provided via DEX pools (e.g. Camelot/Uniswap).
Components.name: flrEUR (Florin / FLR) token

Components.description: The protocol's native governance and utility token (ERC-20). A portion of real-world interest from loan vaults is used to buy back and burn FFM from the open market. Governance holders are intended to approve collateral and lending terms as the protocol decentralizes.
Components.name: FFM (Florence Finance Medici) token

Components.description: Contract that holds loan repayments and enables 1:1 flrEUR-to-EUR redemption. If the Treasury is empty, participants rely on secondary-market DEX liquidity to exit positions.
Components.name: Treasury

Components.description: External, vetted credit providers (e.g. Caple, SwishFund, Avellinia) that source and manage SME/private-credit exposure. Florence acts as a wholesale funder / re-distributor of their diversified credit rather than originating loans itself, and does not use leverage or fractional reserves.
Components.name: SME lending partners / originators

Faq.answer: Florence Finance is a Euro-denominated RWA (real-world asset) lending protocol that bridges on-chain crypto liquidity to real-world European SME / private-credit lending. Users deposit stablecoins to fund loans made by established SME lending partners and earn a share of the real-world interest on-chain, without the protocol relying on leverage or fractional reserves.
Faq.question: What is Florence Finance?

Faq.answer: The protocol operates on Arbitrum and Base. The FFM governance token is deployed on Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base. Loan vaults are split between Arbitrum (Caple, Junior) and Base (Avellinia), and FFM can be traded on Uniswap; flrEUR liquidity is available via DEX pools such as Camelot.
Faq.question: Which blockchains does Florence Finance run on?

Faq.answer: flrEUR (Florin / FLR) is the euro-denominated funding instrument: it is minted when a loan is funded, burned on repayment, and intended to be 1:1 redeemable for EUR through the Treasury. FFM (Florence Finance Medici) is the separate governance and utility token, whose supply is reduced over time via buyback-and-burn funded by loan interest.
Faq.question: How do the FLR (flrEUR) and FFM tokens differ?

Faq.answer: Users convert stablecoins (e.g. USDC/EURA) into flrEUR and deposit it into a loan vault, receiving vault tokens. They earn a portion of the real-world interest paid by the underlying SME loans, distributed on-chain. Positions can generally be exited via the Treasury (1:1 redemption) or secondary DEX liquidity.
Faq.question: How do users earn yield?

Faq.answer: The primary risk is credit risk from borrower/SME defaults; Florence currently performs the underlying due diligence and plans a default reserve to absorb minor losses. Liquidity risk also applies: if the Treasury is empty, exiting depends on secondary-market liquidity. The current rollout vaults intentionally focus on the riskier junior/subordinated end of the credit spectrum.
Faq.question: What are the main risks?

Faq.answer: Florence states its smart contracts have undergone audits and have run live for over three years with no reported smart-contract losses or credit losses. The protocol is non-custodial: it does not hold users' digital assets but converts stablecoins into credit exposure via lending partners.
Faq.question: Have the smart contracts been audited?

Risks.description: Credit / borrower-default risk is the primary risk: repayment depends on European SMEs and the lending partners (Caple, SwishFund, Avellinia) that originate and manage the loans. Current rollout vaults intentionally target the riskier junior/subordinated/2nd-lien end of the credit spectrum.

flrEUR is intended to redeem 1:1 for EUR via the Treasury, but if the Treasury is empty redemption depends on secondary-market DEX liquidity, which can cause the flrEUR market price to deviate from its EUR peg.

Due diligence, collateral approval and lending-term decisions are currently centralized with the Florence team, with decentralization to FFM governance stated only as a future goal, creating key-person and centralization risk.

Vaults, tokens and Treasury are governed by smart contracts; despite audits and a multi-year live track record, contract bugs or exploits could impair funds. The protocol depends on cross-chain deployments across Arbitrum, Base and Ethereum.

Providing euro-denominated private credit to European SMEs and issuing a EUR-pegged instrument exposes the protocol to evolving EU financial-services, lending, securities and MiCA-style regulation across multiple jurisdictions.

TradFiComparison.differences: Florence tokenizes the exposure (flrEUR + vault tokens) so it is transferable and composable in DeFi, is euro-denominated and permissionlessly accessible, and offers on-chain transparency and secondary liquidity rather than multi-year lock-ups and high minimums of a traditional fund.

TradFiComparison.differences: Florence is a wholesale funder that re-distributes exposure from existing originators on-chain with no leverage or fractional reserves, versus a factoring company that directly buys receivables and warehouses them on its own balance sheet.
TradFiComparison.similarity: Like factoring, several vaults (e.g. Caple) fund short-term working-capital SME loans, providing an alternative funding source to specialist lenders.

Components.description: The core contract at the center of Fluid that custodies all protocol funds. It only interacts with the protocols built on top of it (not end users), consolidating liquidity from every module so newer protocols can automatically tap shared liquidity. It manages automated debt/supply limits, utilization rates, and pluggable interest-rate models.
Components.name: Liquidity Layer

Components.description: Fluid's lending/borrowing protocol. Users supply collateral and borrow against it. The DEX integration introduces Smart Collateral (collateral doubles as AMM liquidity, earning lending interest plus trading fees) and Smart Debt (borrowed debt is deployed as trading liquidity, earning fees that offset borrow APR), pushing capital efficiency well beyond siloed lenders like Aave.
Components.name: Vaults (Smart Collateral & Smart Debt)

Components.description: An AMM built directly on the Liquidity Layer, launched October 2024. It powers Smart Collateral and Smart Debt by turning lending/borrowing positions into productive trading liquidity. Within ~3 months it became the second-largest DEX on Ethereum by volume, and was the fastest DEX to surpass $10B cumulative volume on Ethereum (100 days).

Faq.question: What exactly is the Instadapp relationship?
Faq.answer: Instadapp is the team and the original DeFi aggregator; Fluid is the protocol it built, and the INST governance token was renamed FLUID 1:1 in December 2024 with the same contract address and 100M supply ([Rebranding and Growth Plan](https://gov.fluid.io/t/rebranding-and-growth-plan-for-fluid-protocol/985)). The formal issuer named in the MiCA whitepaper is Interop Labs Ltd. of the BVI ([Instadapp MiCA whitepaper](https://instadapp.io/mica-whitepaper.pdf)). The bug bounty is still listed under the Instadapp program on Immunefi ([Immunefi Instadapp](https://immunefi.com/bug-bounty/instadapp/information/)).

Faq.question: What are Smart Collateral and Smart Debt, in credit terms?
Faq.answer: Smart Collateral means posted collateral simultaneously earns DEX trading fees; Smart Debt means the borrowed position itself provides DEX liquidity, so trading fees reduce net borrowing cost ([Instadapp blog, Fluid DEX](https://blog.instadapp.io/fluid-dex/)). For a lender this raises effective yield per unit of deposit, but it also means the same capital is exposed to lending risk and market making risk at the same time.

Faq.question: Where does bad debt land?
Faq.answer: The Liquidity Layer is shared, so a critical failure in the base contract would compromise Lending, Vaults and DEX simultaneously; this concentration is explicitly identified as the protocol's principal technical risk in a third party assessment ([Envelop audit report, April 2026](https://index.envelop.is/reports/fluid_audit.html)). The mitigating design is the automated per block ceiling system, which throttles abnormal withdrawals or risky loans and buys governance time to intervene ([OAK Research, Fluid](https://oakresearch.io/en/reports/protocols/fluid-new-defi-standard-unify-dex-lending)).

Faq.question: How does liquidation work at 95% LTV?
Faq.answer: Fluid uses a tick based liquidation engine in which traders act as liquidators, allowing penalties as low as 0.1% ([Instadapp blog, Fluid introduction](https://blog.instadapp.io/fluid/)). The tradeoff is that the buffer between a healthy and an insolvent position is very thin, so the system depends on liquidators being present and gas being available in exactly the market conditions where both are scarce.

Faq.question: Do FLUID holders receive protocol revenue?
Faq.answer: Not automatically. Blockworks' token transparency filing states token holders currently have no direct value accrual mechanism, and that any dividends, buybacks or fee distribution would require a governance vote ([Blockworks Token Transparency filing, Fluid](https://blockworks.com/token-transparency/filing/fluid)). The MiCA whitepaper records that a Q4 2025 buyback program was approved by governance ([Instadapp MiCA whitepaper](https://instadapp.io/mica-whitepaper.pdf)), and the December 2024 rebrand proposal set the trigger at $10m annualised revenue ([Rebranding and Growth Plan](https://gov.fluid.io/t/rebranding-and-growth-plan-for-fluid-protocol/985)).

Faq.question: What is the worst case for a lender?
Faq.answer: A critical bug in the shared Liquidity Layer, which functions as a single honeypot across all sub-protocols ([Envelop audit report](https://index.envelop.is/reports/fluid_audit.html)). The MiCA whitepaper is explicit that there is no insurance and no deposit guarantee ([Instadapp MiCA whitepaper](https://instadapp.io/mica-whitepaper.pdf)). A second, slower worst case is governance capture, given a 4M FLUID quorum against a 100M supply and a 1 day timelock ([Yearn Curation, Fluid Lending Protocol](https://curation.yearn.fi/report/fluid/)).

Faq.question: How fast can governance act in an emergency?
Faq.answer: Onchain GovernorBravo has a roughly 1 day voting delay, a roughly 2 day voting period and a 1 day timelock, so a full governance cycle is several days ([Yearn Curation, Fluid Lending Protocol](https://curation.yearn.fi/report/fluid/)). Faster protection comes from the automated ceilings, not from governance ([OAK Research, Fluid](https://oakresearch.io/en/reports/protocols/fluid-new-defi-standard-unify-dex-lending)).

Incidents.description: A compromised Resolv Labs AWS KMS SERVICE_ROLE key was used to mint roughly 80m unbacked USR for about $200,000 of USDC; USR fell from $1.00 to $0.0025 on Curve before recovering to roughly $0.85.
Incidents.amountUsdDisplay: ~$25m extracted from Resolv; ~80m USR minted against ~$200k
Incidents.outcome: USR recovered to ~$0.85. Fluid paused affected markets within about 30 minutes.

Incidents.title: Bad debt
Incidents.description: Fluid held roughly $100m of USR exposure, with about 98% of wstUSR supply looped inside Fluid at up to 6x leverage, so the USR collapse left the protocol with bad debt.
Incidents.outcome: Covered 100% by discretionary off-balance-sheet loans from Lom Lomashuk / Cyber Fund, "weremeow" and the Fluid core team. About $70m of USR-related debt was repaid by 25 March 2026. fToken exchange rates stayed monotonically increasing and Ethereum lenders took no loss.

Incidents.title: Liquidation cascade
Incidents.description: TVL fell from $1.25b to $873m, a 30.3% drop in 24 hours, as looped USR positions unwound and lenders withdrew.
Incidents.outcome: Markets stabilised; a $19.3m settlement was agreed on 12 May 2026, split roughly Resolv $9.7m, Fluid governance treasury $8.2m and Fluid team $1.5m from future revenue.

Incidents.title: Exploit
Incidents.description: Roughly 116,500 rsETH, about 18% of supply, was drained through a LayerZero cross-chain messaging exploit at Kelp DAO.
Incidents.outcome: Fluid froze rsETH markets within hours alongside Aave, SparkLend and Upshift. No bad debt at Fluid. TVL fell from $1.04b to $861m, a 17.5% drop over two days.

Incidents.title: Exploit
Incidents.description: The Ethereum reward distribution system was exploited using compromised operational keys rather than a contract vulnerability; the attacker swapped proceeds to ETH and laundered through Tornado Cash.
Incidents.outcome: Core lending and trading were unaffected.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#fluid.LongDescription: Fluid is a unified liquidity protocol built by the Instadapp team, in which a single Liquidity Layer sits underneath a lending market, vaults and a native DEX, so the same dollar of deposits backs multiple functions at once ([Instadapp blog, Fluid introduction, 10 Oct 2023](https://blog.instadapp.io/fluid/)). Its two signature primitives are Smart Collateral, where collateral is simultaneously deployed as DEX liquidity earning trading fees, and Smart Debt, where the borrowed position itself acts as DEX liquidity so trading fees offset borrowing cost ([Instadapp blog, Fluid DEX, 19 Jun 2024](https://blog.instadapp.io/fluid-dex/)). The Liquidity Layer is deliberately minimal, a contract that stores assets and validates supply, borrow, repay and withdraw with automated per block debt and collateral ceilings, while rate logic and risk management live in modules on top ([OAK Research, Fluid](https://oakresearch.io/en/reports/protocols/fluid-new-defi-standard-unify-dex-lending)). That architecture supports LTVs up to 95% with liquidation penalties as low as 0.1% via a tick based liquidation engine where traders act as liquidators ([Instadapp blog, Fluid introduction](https://blog.instadapp.io/fluid/)). The Instadapp governance token INST was renamed FLUID at a 1:1 ratio in December 2024, keeping the same token address and 100M supply ([Rebranding and Growth Plan for Fluid Protocol](https://gov.fluid.io/t/rebranding-and-growth-plan-for-fluid-protocol/985)).

Risks.description: Fluid concentrates all funds in a single shared Liquidity Layer contract, so a bug there would be systemic across lending, vaults, and DEX. Auditors (MixBytes) noted the code is optimized for maximum gas efficiency at the expense of clarity, which complicates review and raises the risk of subtle undiscovered bugs.

Vault liquidations depend on price oracles to value collateral and debt. Manipulated or stale oracle prices could trigger unfair liquidations or allow under-collateralized borrowing, a risk amplified because Smart Collateral/Smart Debt positions are also live AMM liquidity.

The unified design means DEX, lending, and borrowing share the same liquidity pool. A sharp DEX volume/price shock or a mass withdrawal can simultaneously stress collateral valuation, borrow availability, and liquidation capacity across all modules rather than being isolated to one product.

Because collateral and debt double as trading liquidity, positions are exposed to impermanent-loss-style rebalancing and volatile-asset price swings on top of normal borrow risk, which can accelerate a position toward its liquidation threshold.

FLUID holders control fee structures, integration priorities, risk parameters, and treasury actions (e.g., the DAO transferred 12M FLUID to the Labs team wallet in Dec 2024). Concentrated voting power or a malicious/erroneous parameter change could adversely affect users.

TypedRisks.name: Looping concentration in yield-bearing stablecoin wrappers
TypedRisks.description: Roughly 98% of wstUSR supply sat inside Fluid leverage loops at up to 6x when USR broke, giving ~$100m exposure to a single wrapper that was 18.9% of all-chain lending TVL. The current book repeats the shape: SUSDAI 19.9%, WSTETH 16.8%, WEETH 12.9%, REUSD 12.7%, WBTC 6.8%, top five 69.0%.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Isolated vault design with per-vault parameters; May 2026 oracle upgrades added token classification and legal agreements with asset issuers.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of a wrapper's total supply held inside Fluid vaults, and top-five collateral concentration as a percentage of lending TVL.

TypedRisks.name: Collateral issuer key compromise leading to bad debt
TypedRisks.description: On 22 March 2026 a compromised Resolv Labs AWS KMS SERVICE_ROLE key allowed ~80m unbacked USR to be minted for ~$200k of USDC, and USR fell from $1.00 to $0.0025 on Curve. Fluid absorbed roughly $10m to $21m of bad debt as a result.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Bad debt was covered 100% by discretionary off-balance-sheet loans, and a $19.3m settlement was agreed in May 2026 split across Resolv, the Fluid treasury and the Fluid team.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Issuer operational security disclosures, and any unexplained expansion in a collateral token's supply relative to attested reserves.

TypedRisks.name: Bridged LRT collateral exploit
TypedRisks.description: On 18 April 2026 about 116,500 rsETH, roughly 18% of supply and ~$292m, was drained through a LayerZero cross-chain messaging exploit at Kelp DAO. Fluid TVL fell from $1.04b to $861m, a 17.5% drop over two days.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Fluid froze rsETH markets within hours, alongside Aave, SparkLend and Upshift; no bad debt resulted.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Supply reconciliation for bridged LRTs across chains, and LayerZero endpoint incident feeds.

TypedRisks.name: Bank run risk from shared liquidity layer
TypedRisks.description: All products draw on one Liquidity Layer, so a shock in one collateral drains liquidity available to every other market. The Resolv event produced ~$300m of net outflows in a single day and a 30.3% TVL fall in 24 hours.
TypedRisks.mitigation: fToken exchange rates are monotonically increasing so lenders did not realise losses on Ethereum; utilization-linked rate curve (USDC kink1 85% at 5.40%, kink2 93% at 7.50%, max 40%).
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Single-day net outflow as a percentage of TVL, and Liquidity Layer free liquidity.

TypedRisks.name: Sustained very high utilization blocking withdrawals
TypedRisks.description: Several markets run near their ceiling: BNB USDT 96.7%, Polygon USDT0 92.1%, Plasma USDT0 90.9%, Arbitrum USDC 90.3%, Ethereum GHO 86.7% and ETH 84.9%. At these levels lenders cannot exit at scale without a rate spike forcing repayment.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Two-kink rate model with a 40% maximum rate on USDC to force deleveraging past kink2 at 93%.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Utilization by asset and chain, and time spent above kink2.

TypedRisks.name: Thin liquidation buffers on high-LTV correlated pairs
TypedRisks.description: LTVs run from 80% to 95% and the liquidation penalty can be as low as 0.1% for correlated pairs such as wstETH/ETH. A 0.1% penalty gives liquidators almost no margin for gas and slippage in a fast market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Tick-based liquidation engine designed for high throughput at low penalty; per-vault parameterisation.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Realised liquidation shortfall versus penalty collected, and liquidator participation count per event.

TypedRisks.name: Modular oracle configuration error
TypedRisks.description: Oracles are configured per vault and mix Chainlink, Uniswap V3 TWAP, Redstone and custom center-price oracles. Heterogeneous per-vault wiring means a single misconfigured feed can mispricing an entire market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: May 2026 oracle upgrade added per-key pricing, multi-source feeds and deviation checks.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Per-vault oracle deviation alerts and feed staleness.

TypedRisks.name: One-day governance timelock
TypedRisks.description: The GovernorBravo timelock at 0x2386DC45AdDed673317eF068992F19421B481F4c enforces only an 86,400 second delay, with a 4,000,000 FLUID quorum and 1,000,000 FLUID proposal threshold. A single day gives lenders almost no time to exit ahead of a hostile or mistaken parameter change.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Guardian Avocado multisig 0x4F6F977aCDD1177DCD81aB83074855EcB9C2D49e operating 7-of-14 can pause but cannot increase risk.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Queued proposals in the timelock and FLUID voting-power concentration.

TypedRisks.name: Discretionary treasury and multisig action outside governance
TypedRisks.description: A team multisig drew roughly $8m of USDC and USDT from the shared liquidity layer via a pre-approved credit line before the governance vote on the bad debt, and the proposal to move fGHO and iETHv2 from treasury to a team multisig drew public criticism including from Curve founder Michael Egorov. Critics argued it altered the risk exposure of USDC and USDT depositors.
TypedRisks.mitigation: The action was subsequently put to governance and disclosed publicly; a formal settlement was agreed in May 2026.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pre-approved credit line draws by non-governance multisigs, and treasury asset transfers.

TypedRisks.name: Operational key compromise on peripheral systems
TypedRisks.description: On 1 June 2026 the Ethereum reward distribution system was exploited for about $215,000 through compromised operational keys rather than a contract flaw, with proceeds swapped to ETH and laundered through Tornado Cash. Core lending and trading were unaffected.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Incident was contained to the rewards subsystem.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Unexpected reward distribution transactions and operational key rotation cadence.

TypedRisks.name: Unaudited upgrade coverage gap
TypedRisks.description: Fluid has eight audits from four firms (PeckShield, StateMind, MixBytes, Cantina) but no formal verification, and no 2026-dated audit covering the 31 March 2026 module upgrade executed as proposal #126 at block 24779519. Upgrades shipping ahead of audit coverage is a recurring pattern.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Immunefi bug bounty under the Instadapp name paying up to $500,000 for smart contract critical and $100,000 for high.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Ratio of executed upgrade proposals to published audit reports covering them.

TypedRisks.name: Licensed deployment dependency via Jupiter Lend
TypedRisks.description: Jupiter Lend on Solana is a lending and borrowing protocol "powered by Fluid's modular Liquidity Layer", running up to 90% to 95% LTV with liquidation penalties as low as 0.1%. A failure of Fluid's engine propagates to a Solana venue Fluid does not itself operate, and reputational damage runs both ways. Exact licensing and revenue terms were not confirmed in sources fetched here.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Jupiter Lend markets are fully isolated with their own assets, risk parameters and curator, including a Bitwise x Ethena co-curated market.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Jupiter Lend market health and any Fluid engine incident that would apply to Solana deployments.
linkedAssetsUnmatched: Ethena assets in the Bitwise market

TypedRisks.name: DEX rebalancing turning impermanent loss permanent
TypedRisks.description: Fluid DEX automatically rebalances smart collateral and smart debt positions, which converts impermanent loss into realised permanent loss, an effect the team associates with LVR. DEX v2 is built to address this but launch has been held back pending market conditions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Design works best on stablecoin and correlated pairs; DEX v2 pending, Solana DEX in final audit.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Realised loss versus fees earned on smart collateral and smart debt positions.

TypedRisks.name: Franchise contraction after consecutive incidents
TypedRisks.description: Lending TVL fell from $1.28b in February 2026 to $750.8m by 27 April 2026, a 41% decline, against a peak of $2.37b on 9 October 2025. Buybacks were paused after roughly 1.3% of supply was repurchased and FLUID emissions were cut.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Foundation forgoing $250,000 per month from March to June 2026; aWETH Redemption Protocol launched April 2026 with $10b initial capacity, processing over $440m of withdrawals.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Monthly lending TVL by chain, FLUID emissions schedule, and buyback resumption.

TypedRisks.name: Multi-chain expansion outpacing risk tooling
TypedRisks.description: Fluid runs on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Plasma, Base, Polygon and BNB Chain, and is extending to Solana, a Venus Flux deployment co-engineered on Fluid, and the Sui Hashi Bitcoin lending testnet. Each venue adds an oracle set, a bridge and a sequencer that the core team must monitor.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Per-chain isolated liquidity layers and per-vault parameters.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Number of live chains versus incident response times; per-chain TVL (Ethereum $527.7m, Arbitrum $131.2m, Plasma $107.6m, Base $32.4m, Polygon $4.7m as of 11 May 2026).

Scale is real and institutionally validated: $796.5m TVL with $755.2m borrowed as of 26 July 2026, and the Aave DAO bought $4M of the token at a $350m FDV (DefiLlama API, fluid, Aave governance, ARFC Fluid alignment).

Strongest security posture of the four entities: four audit firms across Liquidity Layer, Vault and DEX, a $500,000 maximum Immunefi bounty and an additional $80,000 audit competition (Fluid audits and security, Immunefi Instadapp, Immunefi IOP Fluid Protocol).

Best disclosure of the four: a named BVI issuer, a published MiCA whitepaper, onchain-verified governance parameters and a third party token transparency filing (Instadapp MiCA whitepaper, Yearn Curation, Blockworks Token Transparency filing).

bear.claim: TVL has fallen from a peak of $2.684bn on 9 October 2025 to $796.5m, a decline of roughly 70% in under a year (DefiLlama API, fluid).

The shared Liquidity Layer is a single point of catastrophic failure across Lending, Vaults and DEX, and cumulative earnings are historically negative at about minus $192.3M due to past incentive distributions (Envelop audit report, April 2026).
Token concentration is high, with roughly 94% of supply in the top 100 wallets, against a governance quorum of only 4M FLUID out of 100M (Envelop audit report, Yearn Curation).

AssetCoverage.assetStrategy:
Fluid's core innovation is that a **vault is the unit of listing, not a token**, and both sides of a vault can be a **DEX position rather than a plain ERC-20**. In classic Fluid vaults the collateral token and the debt token are ordinary assets, but in **smart collateral** vaults the deposit is an LP share of a Fluid DEX pool, and in **smart debt** vaults the borrowing itself is a DEX position so the borrower earns trading fees on the debt leg while paying borrow interest. Vault 44 on Ethereum, wstETH-ETH collateral against wstETH-ETH debt, is smart collateral plus smart debt at once, and vault 51, WBTC-cbBTC against WBTC-cbBTC, is the BTC analogue. This means "supported asset" for Fluid has to be read as an ordered pair plus a mode, and the same underlying token can appear with materially different collateral factors depending on the pairing. Fluid also runs a **dual-oracle design** where the price used to permit an operation can differ from the price used to permit a liquidation, and vault upgrades are shipped by deploying new vault versions and winding down the old ones over months rather than by mutating parameters in place ([Fluid governance, Deploy Fluid upgrades to Vault protocol](https://gov.fluid.io/t/deploy-fluid-upgrades-to-vault-protocol/764), [MixBytes analysis of the Fluid vault](https://mixbytes.io/blog/modern-defi-lending-protocols-how-its-made-fluid-vault)). Every parameter row below was read live on 2026-07-26 from the Fluid public vault API for each chain, for example [api.fluid.instadapp.io/v2/1/vaults](https://api.fluid.instadapp.io/v2/1/vaults). Protocol TVL is roughly $797M ([DefiLlama Fluid](https://defillama.com/protocol/fluid)).

Column mapping for Fluid: "Max LTV %" is the vault `collateralFactor`, "Liq. threshold %" is `liquidationThreshold`, "Liq. bonus %" is `liquidationPenalty`, "Supply cap" is the liquidity layer `baseWithdrawalLimit` in collateral-token units, and "Borrow cap" is `maxBorrowLimit` in debt-token units. Fluid additionally publishes a `liquidationMaxLimit` (LML), the hard ceiling above which a position can be fully liquidated, which is reported in Notes.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#fluid.RiskPosture: Fluid is the most technically sophisticated protocol in this set and also the one with the most recent damage. Its shared Liquidity Layer and tick-based liquidation engine allow 80% to 95% LTVs with penalties as low as 0.1%, which is genuinely best in class, and Yearn's curation team scored it 1.4 out of 5.0, "Minimal Risk". The problem is not the engine, it is what gets plugged into it: Fluid repeatedly ends up holding almost the entire float of a third-party yield-bearing wrapper inside 6x loops, so an issuer failure at Resolv in March 2026 turned into $10m to $21m of Fluid bad debt and a 30% TVL fall in a day. Bad debt was made whole, but by discretionary loans and a team multisig drawing a credit line before the governance vote, which is a governance answer rather than a structural one, and the one-day timelock leaves lenders little room to act on such decisions. Today's book still shows top-five collateral at 69% and several markets above 90% utilization, so the same shape is in place, and the Jupiter Lend and Venus deployments extend that shape to venues Fluid does not run.

Components.description: A U.S.-registered money market mutual fund managed by Franklin Templeton, registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 and overseen by the SEC. It invests substantially all assets in U.S. government securities, cash and repurchase agreements, targeting a stable $1.00 net asset value per share under Rule 2a-7. It was the first U.S.-registered mutual fund to use a public blockchain as its official system of record for share ownership.

Components.description: Franklin Templeton's proprietary, institutional-grade tokenization platform that processes transactions, records share ownership on-chain, and administers token-based investments. Faq.answer: BENJI is the on-chain token representing a share of the Franklin OnChain U.S. Government Money Fund (FOBXX). One BENJI token equals one fund share. FOBXX is a U.S.-registered money market mutual fund investing in U.S. government securities, cash and repos, targeting a stable $1.00 NAV.
Faq.question: What is BENJI and how does it relate to FOBXX?

Faq.answer: BENJI originally launched on Stellar in 2021 and has since expanded to multiple public chains including Polygon, Avalanche, Base, Arbitrum, Aptos, Solana, Ethereum and BNB Chain. Stellar remains the fund's primary network. Each chain hosts a separate BENJI contract, with the transfer agent acting as the authoritative record across deployments.
Faq.question: Which blockchains does BENJI run on?

Faq.answer: Yield is distributed daily through share-count rebasing: new BENJI tokens are minted directly into holder wallets each business day rather than the token price rising. Distributions for weekends and holidays accrue and post on the next business day. Franklin Templeton publishes a daily 7-day effective yield on the fund's product page.
Faq.question: How is yield paid to BENJI holders?

Faq.answer: Investors must complete Franklin Templeton's KYC and AML onboarding, after which their wallet is allowlisted to receive BENJI; non-approved wallets cannot hold the token. Retail access is available through the Benji Investments app in select U.S. states, and institutions access via authorized channels, subject to the same suitability standards as traditional U.S. money market funds.
Faq.question: Who can buy BENJI and what are the requirements?

Faq.answer: Redemptions are processed off-chain through the Benji Investments app or institutional channels and settled in U.S. dollars. The transfer agent reconciles on-chain balances daily with the official shareholder register.

The fund targets a stable $1.00 NAV but is not guaranteed; under stress (e.g., rate shocks or a run on repos/government securities) the share value could deviate from $1.00, as with any money market fund, potentially causing BENJI to trade away from par.

BENJI is issued as tokens via smart contracts deployed on multiple chains; bugs, vulnerabilities or errors in these contracts or the Benji platform could impair token minting, rebasing distributions, transfers or reconciliation with the official register.

The fund relies on public blockchains (Stellar and others) as its system of record; outages, congestion, chain reorganizations or consensus failures on any supported network could disrupt on-chain transactions and settlement, requiring reliance on off-chain records.

Franklin Templeton retains centralized control over the allowlist, wallet authorization, cross-chain movement and the primary shareholder register; holders depend on the firm's operational decisions and continued support of each deployment rather than decentralized governance.

Risks.description: The gToken vaults (gDAI, gUSDC, etc.) are the direct counterparty to every trade. During sustained periods where traders' net PnL outpaces collected fees, the vault's backing can be drawn down, exposing LPs to losses and impairing the gToken exchange rate.

Execution prices depend on gTrade's custom Chainlink DON, which fetches median spot prices from a set of exchange APIs. Oracle latency, feed manipulation, or thin off-chain liquidity on a given asset could allow mispriced fills or be exploited, which is especially sensitive given leverage up to 150x.

gTrade uses an upgradeable Diamond (EIP-2535) architecture across multiple chains and vault contracts. Bugs in the diamond facets, vault accounting, or the oracle aggregator could cause loss of user or vault funds despite audits and timelocks.

A June 2022 CertiK audit flagged a centralization / privileged-role concern (acknowledged), and governance can alter core parameters — e.g. the 'Make Gains Great Again' vote paused buyback-and-burn in 2026. Concentrated control over upgrades and reward policy is a governance risk to token holders and LPs.

As a synthetic leveraged venue, gTrade is exposed to correlated, cross-market stress: simultaneous large adverse moves across crypto/forex/equities positions, cascading liquidations, or a stablecoin depeg of the collateral (DAI/USDC) could stress vault solvency at once.

Risks.description: Hypervisor vaults, UniProxy deposit-proxy contracts, and newer hooks are complex smart contracts holding pooled funds. Gamma was exploited on January 4, 2024 (~$3.4M-$4.5M+) when an overly permissive price-change threshold let an attacker flash-loan-manipulate deposit values and mint excess LP tokens; its predecessor Visor Finance lost ~$8.2M to an infinite-mint bug in December 2021.

Active rebalancing of concentrated-liquidity ranges exposes LPs to impermanent loss and rebalancing risk: repositioning ranges around volatile pairs can realize losses if price moves sharply, and vault performance depends heavily on strategy parameterization and external incentive programs rather than fee income alone.

Vault deposit/rebalance logic relies on price references and price-change thresholds. Mis-set thresholds or manipulable pool prices (as in the January 2024 incident) can allow attackers to distort deposit valuations and mint disproportionate LP tokens.

Gamma's vaults are layered on top of third-party CLMM DEXes (Uniswap V3/V4, Algebra-based DEXes) across many chains. Bugs, exploits, or liquidity failures in an underlying DEX or host chain, or changes to their fee/AMM mechanics, propagate directly into Gamma vault performance and safety.

Auditors flagged that the system is heavily parameterized by contract owners (e.g., thresholds, strategy settings). Reliance on privileged multisig/governance control over these parameters is itself a risk vector; mis-configuration was a contributing factor in the January 2024 exploit.

Components.description: Isolated smart-contract accounts that hold a borrower's collateral and debt together and can interact with integrated DeFi protocols. Users effectively get a 'leveraged wallet' via account abstraction, borrowing pool liquidity to trade or farm with up to ~10x leverage while collateral and positions stay ring-fenced per account.
Components.name: Credit Accounts

Components.description: Single-asset liquidity pools where passive lenders deposit and earn APY funded by borrower interest and fees. Depositors receive Diesel Tokens (dTokens; ERC-4626 vault shares in V3) that accrue interest proportional to their share. V3 introduced quotas, collateral/exposure limits and risk-segmented pools.
Components.name: Passive lending pools

Components.description: Governance token of the Gearbox DAO with a 10 billion total supply. GEAR is used to vote on supported assets, integrations and parameters; V3 tokenomics add staking and gauge/quota voting that influences borrowing fees per asset and revenue distribution.

Components.description: Whitelisted adapter contracts that let Credit Accounts route leveraged capital into external DeFi protocols (e.g. Uniswap, Curve, Convex, Balancer, Pendle, Lido/staking). Adapters are what make Gearbox leverage 'composable': the same borrowed liquidity can be deployed across many integrated strategies.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#gearbox.Description: Gearbox is a generalized leverage protocol: users open Credit Accounts to borrow against collateral and deploy leveraged positions into integrated DeFi strategies (Curve, Convex, Lido, Yearn).
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#gearbox.Differentiator: Credit Accounts compose leverage across protocols rather than a single isolated farm: up to ~10x with a unified margin position.

Faq.question: Where does bad debt land if a Credit Account goes underwater?
Faq.answer: Liquidation is meant to close the account before equity is exhausted. If a shortfall still occurs, the protocol first absorbs it from unclaimed protocol fees, and any remainder is socialised across pool depositors through a reduction in the Diesel (LP) token exchange rate ([Gearbox liquidation dynamics](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/liquidation-dynamics)). Passive lenders are therefore the residual bearer of loss, not the DAO treasury.

Faq.question: Who sets the interest rate a lender earns?
Faq.answer: Base rates come from a two kink utilisation curve configured per pool with parameters U1, U2, base rate and three slopes ([Gearbox markets and rates](https://docs.gearbox.finance/developers/gm-markets-rates)). On top of that, quota rates are set either by GEAR stakers voting in gauges or by a market curator, and that extra fee is split between passive lenders and the DAO ([GEAR utility and staking](https://docs.gearbox.finance/gear-token/utility-and-staking)).

Faq.question: How does liquidation actually work?
Faq.answer: Health factor is total weighted value divided by total debt, checked after every call a Credit Account makes; falling below the threshold allows liquidation, which can be partial or full ([Gearbox dev docs](https://github.com/Gearbox-protocol/dev-docs/blob/main/pages/v2/architecture/overview.md), [Gearbox liquidation dynamics](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/liquidation-dynamics)). Liquidators take a premium of roughly 3% to 4% and the protocol takes 1% to 1.5% ([Gearbox protocol fees](https://docs.gearbox.finance/overview/protocol-fees)).

Faq.question: What is the worst case for a passive lender?
Faq.answer: The worst case is a correlated collateral shock or an oracle failure that leaves accounts insolvent faster than liquidators can act, at which point losses hit the Diesel exchange rate directly ([Gearbox liquidation dynamics](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/liquidation-dynamics)). The historical average leverage across Credit Accounts has been high, around 5.57x with a weighted average health factor of 1.105 in one 2023 monthly report, which is a thin buffer ([Gearbox April protocol update](https://medium.com/gearbox-protocol/gearbox-april-protocol-update-9c4d309d5b2f)).

Faq.question: Can the DAO seize or reprice a live market?
Faq.answer: No. Documentation states explicitly that the DAO cannot change risk parameters of a live curator managed market and cannot seize or reallocate deposits; it governs versions, chain activation and the fee split ([Gearbox docs, Protocol DAO](https://docs.gearbox.finance/about-gearbox/governance-and-operations/protocol-dao)). That is a credit positive for market isolation and a credit negative for the DAO's ability to intervene in a crisis.

Faq.question: Has Gearbox ever had a loss event?
Faq.answer: Public claims of zero security incidents and zero bad debt over five years come from the co-founder in a July 2026 conference talk, not from an independent audit of the record ([Mikhail Lazarev talk summary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HcD37L1mVxI)). Treat it as a management assertion. No third party incident post mortem for Gearbox was found in this session.

Faq.question: How fast can the protocol respond to an emergency?
Faq.answer: A 4 of 12 veto and unpause multisig exists for rapid response, deliberately limited so it can only block, never propose ([V3.0 operational multisigs](https://docs.gearbox.finance/about-gearbox/governance-and-operations/v3.0-operational-multisigs)). Technical changes otherwise sit behind a 2 day timelock ([V3.0 operational multisigs](https://docs.gearbox.finance/about-gearbox/governance-and-operations/v3.0-operational-multisigs)).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#gearbox.LongDescription: Gearbox is a two sided credit protocol: passive lenders deposit into ERC-4626 pools, and active users open Credit Accounts, isolated smart contract wallets that hold both the user collateral and the borrowed funds and can only call whitelisted adapters and hold whitelisted tokens ([Gearbox dev docs, V2 architecture overview](https://github.com/Gearbox-protocol/dev-docs/blob/main/pages/v2/architecture/overview.md)). Because the borrowed capital never leaves the account, Gearbox can extend leverage well above what a normal overcollateralised loan allows while still enforcing a health factor check after every single call ([Gearbox dev docs](https://github.com/Gearbox-protocol/dev-docs/blob/main/pages/v2/architecture/overview.md)). The original design was published as a tech paper in April 2021 by Mikhail Lazarev and Ilgiz Gimaltdinov, framing Credit Accounts as a new DeFi primitive for margin trading, leveraged farming and leveraged CDPs ([Gearbox tech paper](https://static.gearbox.finance/docs/Gearbox.pdf)). V3 added quotas and gauges, so GEAR stakers vote on the extra rate borrowers pay per collateral asset, and moved the protocol toward a permissionless, curator operated market model where the DAO builds rails and Market Curators set risk parameters ([Gearbox docs, Protocol DAO](https://docs.gearbox.finance/about-gearbox/governance-and-operations/protocol-dao)). Current documentation frames Credit Accounts as user owned smart contract wallets with solvency checks behind every action, targeted at both retail and institutional flows ([Gearbox docs, Powered by Credit Accounts](https://docs.gearbox.finance/introduction/powered-by-credit-accounts)).

Risks.description: Borrowers run leveraged positions (up to ~10x) inside Credit Accounts. A sharp adverse move in collateral value can push a Credit Account below its liquidation threshold; if liquidations lag or fail in volatile/illiquid conditions, the lending pool can accrue bad debt that impairs passive lenders.

Composability risk: Credit Accounts deploy borrowed liquidity into external protocols (Curve, Convex, Pendle, Lido, etc.) via adapters. A failure, exploit or depeg in any integrated protocol propagates into Gearbox positions and can cascade into the shared lending pools.

Credit Account health factors and liquidations depend on price oracles for collateral and integrated assets. Oracle latency, manipulation or misconfiguration on medium/long-tail or L2 assets (which V3 explicitly supports) could allow undercollateralized borrowing or unfair liquidations.

The protocol relies on complex Credit Manager, pool and adapter contracts across V1/V2/V3 and multiple chains. Despite extensive audits, undiscovered bugs in adapters or the account-abstraction layer could lead to loss of pool or user funds.

Which assets, protocols and risk parameters (collateral limits, quotas, borrow fees) are allowed is set by GEAR-based DAO governance and executed via a treasury multisig that originally held ~51% of supply. Concentrated voting power or a malicious/erroneous parameter change could raise systemic risk for lenders.
