TypedRisks.name: Curator sets unsafe risk parameters
TypedRisks.description: Curators act as Administrator over a Market Configurator and control every risk parameter including liquidation thresholds, quotas and the interest rate model. Wrong liquidation thresholds on allowed assets can make LP pools insolvent, and ChainSecurity notes the Configurator role is fully trusted and can configure most system parameters.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Administrator changes are subject to a 24-hour minimum timelock; curators must bear first loss via staking under the GIP-264 model; revenue split default 50% curator, 50% DAO.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pending Market Configurator transactions in the 24-hour timelock, and curator stake size versus pool TVL.

TypedRisks.name: Emergency Admin bypasses the timelock
TypedRisks.description: The Emergency Admin role bypasses the 24-hour timelock and can pause a market, set debt limits to zero and forbid adapters or tokens. It cannot increase risk, but it can freeze a user's ability to manage a leveraged position at the worst moment.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Role is constrained to risk-reducing actions only; a whitelisted Emergency Liquidator can still liquidate when a market is paused.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Emergency Admin transactions and market pause events.

TypedRisks.name: Oracle failure causing cascading liquidations
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox's own risk page states a rogue oracle can cause cascading liquidations and bad debt, and the protocol relies on Chainlink, Redstone and composite smart contract oracles. Composite oracles that derive an exchange rate from another contract inherit that contract's failure modes.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Dual-oracle design pairs a Main Feed for liquidation with a Reserve Feed acting as a guardrail against incorrect or outdated valuations; Price Feed Store whitelisting is required to create a market.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Main Feed versus Reserve Feed deviation per asset, and feed staleness on Redstone push feeds.

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation cascade on LRT depeg
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox explicitly cites the April 2024 ezETH cascade as the motivating case for its Loss Policy, when rapid price falls outran liquidators. Leverage of up to 40x on a credit account means small collateral moves are enough to breach a health factor of 1.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Loss Policy blocks a liquidation that would create bad debt if the position is healthy under an aliased fundamental price; partial liquidation via a Deleverage Bot triggers at a configured minHF such as 1.05 with a reduced premium.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Count of accounts with health factor below 1.05, and frequency of Loss Policy blocked liquidations.

TypedRisks.name: Bad debt socialised onto LPs
TypedRisks.description: If a Credit Account is liquidated with Total Value below Total Debt, unclaimed protocol fees are burned first and any remaining loss is socialised by reducing the Diesel LP token exchange rate. Lenders, not borrowers, take the residual.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Fee buffer absorbs first; Loss Policy avoids realising losses at distressed prices; Gearbox reports no bad debt since inception in 2021.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Diesel token exchange rate; any non-monotonic move is a realised LP loss.

TypedRisks.name: Loss Policy pausing liquidations during a real repricing
TypedRisks.description: The aliased bad debt policy halts liquidation when a position is healthy at fundamental price even though it is underwater at market price. If the market price is correct and the peg never returns, the deferred loss is larger when it is finally realised.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Aliased pricing is configurable per market, so curators choose the fundamental reference; the fundamental check still permits liquidation when the asset is genuinely insolvent.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Duration and notional of positions sitting in Loss Policy blocked state, and market versus aliased price gap.

TypedRisks.name: Liquidator dependency and MEV
TypedRisks.description: Liquidations depend on third-party liquidators who Gearbox acknowledges may malfunction, and the risks page also flags sandwich and MEV extraction against protocol operations. In small accounts the liquidation premium may not cover gas, which historically left core contributors liquidating at their own expense.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Token-backed backstops, a Reserve Fund and the recruitment of more professional liquidators; partial liquidation is executed by a specialised Deleverage Bot.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Time from health factor below 1 to liquidation, and liquidator address diversity.

TypedRisks.name: Adapter and integration surface risk
TypedRisks.description: Credit Accounts reach into external protocols through adapters, and Gearbox says credit accounts can connect to assets that are not on DEXes or not even tokenised. Each adapter imports the security assumptions of the target protocol.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Strict adapter allowlists (kpk's handbook specifies allowlists plus utilisation caps and quota limits); Emergency Admin can forbid an adapter immediately; Bytecode Repository verification ensures only audited bytecode is deployed.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New adapter deployments per market, and the number of distinct external protocols reachable from a single credit account.

TypedRisks.name: Concentration in a small set of curators
TypedRisks.description: Five curators including Invariant Group, Re7 and Maven11 manage over $1.5b, with Re7 alone running more than $700m to $800m across 100+ pools on 14 chains. Correlated curator behaviour or a single curator's operational failure affects a large share of the system.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Curators hold no custody and perform no active allocation, only parameter management; markets are isolated so a failure is contained within the affected pool.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Curator TVL share, and overlap of the same collateral assets across different curators' markets.

TypedRisks.name: Depeg of base or collateral assets
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox lists depeg of base assets as a named risk, and its curated markets accept synthetic dollars and tokenised treasuries such as Ethena sUSDe and USDe, Sky sUSDS, Midas mTBILL and mBASIS. Isolated lending contains the loss within the affected LP pool rather than the whole protocol.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Isolated pool architecture; per-asset quotas cap how much debt any one collateral can secure; Chaos Labs LT and LB methodology includes a circuit breaker for persistent deviations.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Secondary market price versus redemption value for each synthetic or tokenised asset.

TypedRisks.name: Lender exit blocked at full utilization
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox states plainly that an LP cannot withdraw if the pool is fully utilised. Under the Two-Kink interest rate model, curators can also set isBorrowingMoreU2Forbidden to cap borrowing past U2.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Utilization-dependent interest rate curve with a slope 3 penalty above U2 to force repayment; Tumbler rate keeper adjusts quota rates by epoch.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pool utilization versus U1 and U2, and days spent above U2.

TypedRisks.name: Extreme chain sprawl
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox says it is deployed on 27 blockchains, "the most of any lending protocol", having added five chains and more than 25 markets under Permissionless. Every additional chain adds a sequencer, an oracle network and a liquidator set that must all work during a stress event.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Markets are isolated per chain and per curator; the team forks networks eight times a day to test against black swan events.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Per-chain TVL versus liquidator coverage, and chain-level incident history.

TypedRisks.name: Documentation and audit link integrity
TypedRisks.description: The security page lists audits by ChainSecurity, Consensys Diligence, Sigma Prime and ABDK but carries the note that "Links above are placeholders", so the published evidence trail is incomplete. Verifiable audit coverage is the main external check on a permissionless curator system.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Immunefi bug bounty paying up to $1,000,000 for critical; formal verification of critical math components; Bytecode Repository restricts deployment to audited bytecode.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Publication of resolved audit links and new audit reports for each V3.1 release.

TypedRisks.name: Regulatory and legal uncertainty
TypedRisks.description: Gearbox's own terms flag legal and regulatory uncertainty, and its curated markets increasingly hold tokenised treasury products such as mTBILL and mBASIS that sit closest to securities regulation. Curators are identifiable commercial entities rather than anonymous parties.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Isolated markets mean a regulated asset can be removed without touching other pools; Emergency Admin can forbid a token immediately.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Regulatory actions against tokenised treasury issuers or against curator entities.

TypedRisks.name: Governance transition and DAO abandonment of pools
TypedRisks.description: GIP-264 in August 2025 fully abandoned DAO-governed pools in favour of the Permissionless model, migrating to curators including kpk and Maven11. Users who chose Gearbox for DAO oversight now depend on commercial curator diligence instead.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Curators must bear first loss via staking; the DAO retains the Veto Admin rapid-response multisig and the 50% revenue share.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of TVL in DAO pools versus curator pools, and curator stake at risk.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#gearbox.TradFiAnalogue: a prime brokerage margin account funded by a syndicated revolving credit facility. The lender side resembles a senior secured revolver; the borrower side resembs a prime broker margin account where the broker holds the client assets in a segregated account and can liquidate them.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#gearbox.OrgIntro: Gearbox publishes no CEO or executive team. Named individuals are visible mainly through the multisig signer lists.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#gearbox.FundingNote: A June 2023 Wintermute strategic investment is listed by one exchange data page but the amount is undisclosed and that same page carries an "$8.5m seed, 26 April 2022" line that conflicts with both DefiLlama and the protocol's own supply docs, so it is not treated as confirmed here ([HTX GEAR token page](https://www.htx.com/tokens/gear/)).

bull.claim: Credit Accounts monetise better than plain money markets: Messari estimated return on assets nearly seven times higher than traditional lending protocols and modelled 70% TVL growth to roughly $230m (Messari, Lending Renaissance, 12 March 2024).
Governance and execution are genuinely separated: any user can execute a queued, non vetoed transaction after timelock, removing multisig dependency (Updated governance flow).

The permissionless curator model lets third parties launch markets without a DAO vote while the DAO keeps the bytecode registry, which scales the protocol without scaling governance load (Gearbox docs, Protocol DAO).
Deep audit coverage across V2 and V3 from ChainSecurity, ABDK, Consensys Diligence and Decurity, plus a live Immunefi program with $427.4k paid to date (Gearbox audits, Immunefi Gearbox).

bear.claim: TVL of $18.42m on 26 July 2026 is about 4.4% of the April 2024 peak of $419.3m, so the lender base that funds the whole model has largely left (DefiLlama API, gearbox).
Total capital raised is only about $8.04m across three rounds, which is thin funding for a protocol maintaining eleven chain deployments (DefiLlama Gearbox, DefiLlama API, gearbox).

AssetCoverage.assetStrategy:
Gearbox is the protocol where "supported asset" is least meaningful as a flat list. Liquidity providers deposit into an **underlying-asset pool**, for example a WETH, wstETH, USDC, USDT, DAI, GHO, crvUSD, WBTC, tBTC or DOLA pool, each pool owned by a named **curator**. A borrower opens a **credit account**, a smart contract wallet that holds borrowed funds plus their own collateral, and each pool is served by one or more **credit managers** that define, per credit manager, the exact list of tokens that may sit in the account and the **liquidation threshold** applied to each. On top of that, a credit account can only interact with the outside world through **adapters**, whitelisted contracts that translate a call into an allowed action against a specific integrated protocol such as Curve, Convex, Pendle, Balancer, Uniswap, Lido, Mellow or a specific ERC-4626 vault. The asset surface is therefore the cross product of collateral tokens with per-manager liquidation thresholds, quota limits set in the PoolQuotaKeeper which act as a per-collateral borrow cap, and the adapter whitelist. Gearbox documents its price layer as "Chainlink Price Feeds, Redstone Price Feeds as well as some composite smart contract oracles", and it documents that "the current version of Gearbox has isolated lending only, in which case the risk is contained within LP pools" ([Gearbox risks and T&C](https://docs.gearbox.finance/developers/risks-and-t-c-2), [Gearbox adapters and integrations](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/adapters-integrations)). The interest rate model is a two-kink curve with an `isBorrowingMoreU2Forbidden` switch that hard-blocks borrowing past the second kink ([Gearbox interest rate model](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/interest-rate-model)). All numeric values below were read live on 2026-07-26 from mainnet: 21 pools, 89 credit managers, 227 collateral tokens with liquidation thresholds, and 888 adapters, via the CreditAccountCompressor at 0x4115708Fc8fe6bB392De2e0C21c2C81dA2222394 and the pool and quota-keeper contracts. Gearbox TVL is roughly $18.4M ([DefiLlama Gearbox](https://defillama.com/protocol/gearbox)).

Column mapping for Gearbox: "Max LTV %" is not a Gearbox concept, so it is reported as n.a.; "Liq. threshold %" is the per-credit-manager liquidation threshold, reported as the observed range across credit managers where a token appears in more than one; "Borrow cap" is the PoolQuotaKeeper quota limit for that collateral in the named pool; there is no supply cap primitive.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#gearbox.RiskPosture: Gearbox has the strongest loss record of the four, with no bad debt since 2021 including through the April 2024 ezETH cascade where it was the single most affected venue with $33m liquidated and still turned a profit. Its protections are unusually concrete: a dual-oracle Main and Reserve feed, a Loss Policy that halts liquidation when a position is only underwater at a dislocated market price, partial liquidation via a Deleverage Bot at a reduced premium, per-asset quotas that cap how much debt any collateral can secure, formal verification of the math libraries and a $1,000,000 Immunefi bounty. The risk has instead moved to the counterparty layer. Since GIP-264, risk parameters are set by commercial curators such as K3 Capital, Re7 Labs, kpk and Chaos Labs, and Gearbox's own auditor notes the Configurator role is fully trusted; a 24-hour timelock is the only structural brake, and an Emergency Admin can bypass even that. Combine that with credit accounts reaching up to 40x across adapters into Mellow, Pendle, Ethena and Sky, and 27 chains to police, and the plausible failure mode is not a contract bug but one curator parameterising one exotic collateral badly.

Faq.answer: GMX is a decentralized perpetual and spot exchange on Arbitrum and Avalanche. Rather than matching a taker against a maker on an order book, traders trade against a pool of liquidity providers — the shared GLP pool in V1 and isolated GM pools in V2. LPs collectively take the opposite side of trader profit and loss and earn trading and swap fees in return.
Faq.question: What is GMX and who is the counterparty to trades?

Faq.answer: GMX uses external oracle prices (Chainlink, plus GMX's own low-latency feeds in V2) instead of an internal AMM curve. In V1 this meant zero price impact at the oracle price; V2 added price impact, borrowing and funding fees to make the model more robust against manipulation and imbalance.
Faq.question: How does GMX price trades?

Faq.answer: V1 uses one shared multi-asset pool (GLP) that backs every market. V2, launched in August 2023, splits liquidity into isolated per-market GM pools with their own parameters, adds funding rates and price impact, and expands the list of tradeable assets. V2 isolates risk so a problem in one market does not drain liquidity backing others.
Faq.question: What is the difference between GMX V1 and V2?

Faq.answer: No. GMX had a fair launch with no venture-capital round or private token sale. The token supply came largely from migrating the earlier Gambit/XVIX tokens, plus Uniswap liquidity, esGMX vesting reserves, a floor-price fund, marketing/community and a small (~1.9%) team allocation.
Faq.question: Did GMX raise money from VCs?

Faq.answer: GMX suffered two notable incidents. In September 2022 a trader manipulated the AVAX/USD oracle price to extract roughly $565K from GLP on Avalanche, exploiting V1's zero-price-impact design. In July 2025 an attacker drained about $40M+ from GMX V1 on Arbitrum via a re-entrancy/accounting flaw; after GMX offered a 10% white-hat bounty, the exploiter returned the bulk of the funds.
Faq.question: Has GMX been hacked?

Risks.description: GMX prices trades from external oracle feeds with historically zero price impact on V1. If the referenced spot price is manipulated (as in the Sept 2022 AVAX incident), traders can extract value from LPs at the manipulated oracle price.

GLP and GM liquidity providers are the direct counterparty to all traders. When traders are net profitable, LPs bear those losses, so LP returns depend on aggregate trader performance rather than being purely fee-driven.

GMX's contracts hold large pooled liquidity. The July 2025 V1 exploit (~$40M+) abused a re-entrancy / GLP accounting desynchronization, demonstrating that complex pool-accounting logic remains an attack surface despite multiple audits.

GLP concentrates multiple assets in one pool (V1) and GM pools hold specific collateral tokens (V2). Sharp moves or depeg in an underlying pool asset directly impair LP value and the backing behind open positions.

Protocol parameters, treasury and emergency actions (e.g. halting V1 trading after the 2025 hack) are controlled by the core team and a multisig / DAO. Concentrated control over pausing and upgrades is a trust and centralization risk.

Faq.answer: Goldfinch is a decentralized credit protocol launched in January 2021 that brings real-world private-credit lending onchain. Its original model provided uncollateralized USDC loans to emerging-market lenders through Borrower Pools, with credit risk assessed off-chain by Backers rather than secured by crypto collateral.
Faq.question: What is Goldfinch?

Faq.answer: Instead of on-chain collateral, Goldfinch relied on off-chain credit underwriting by Backers, real-world legal recourse against borrowers, and a tranched structure where junior (Backer) capital absorbs first losses before the diversified Senior Pool.
Faq.question: How did Goldfinch make loans without crypto collateral?

Faq.answer: Goldfinch Prime, launched February 2025, is a pivot toward institutional-grade private credit. It gives non-U.S. investors onchain exposure to funds from managers such as Apollo, Ares and Golub that collectively manage over $1 trillion, targeting 9-12% net returns via GPRIME pool tokens.
Faq.question: What is Goldfinch Prime?

Faq.answer: Yes. The protocol suffered three notable defaults totaling roughly $18 million: a ~$5M loan to Kenyan motorbike financier Tugende, a ~$7M writedown on a $20M Stratos facility, and a Lend East default in April 2024 where only ~$4.25M of a ~$10.2M loan was repaid.
Faq.question: Has Goldfinch had loan defaults?

Faq.answer: Goldfinch was founded in 2020-2021 by former Coinbase engineers Mike Sall and Blake West. Warbler Labs, spun out in 2022 with Sall as CEO and West as CTO, is the core development company supporting the protocol; the Goldfinch Foundation supports the DAO/governance.
Faq.question: Who built Goldfinch and what is Warbler Labs?

Faq.answer: The native token is GFI, used for governance and incentives. Figures on price and market cap should be checked against a live source, as GFI declined sharply following the protocol's defaults.
Faq.question: What token does Goldfinch use?

Risks.description: Off-chain borrower default risk is the protocol's dominant realized risk. Goldfinch suffered ~$18M in defaults: Tugende (~$5M, funds diverted to a struggling parent in breach of terms), a $20M Stratos facility (~$7M written down to $0, backstopped by Warbler Labs), and Lend East (April 2024, only ~$4.25M of ~$10.2M repaid).

The original model was uncollateralized/undercollateralized: loans relied on off-chain credit assessment and legal recourse rather than on-chain collateral, so recovery on default depends on slow, uncertain legal processes across foreign jurisdictions.

Real-world private-credit lending and tokenized fund exposure face securities and cross-border regulatory scrutiny; Goldfinch Prime is explicitly restricted to non-U.S. persons, and the model depends on off-chain legal enforceability that varies by jurisdiction.

Credit underwriting and recovery decisions are concentrated in Backers and Warbler Labs rather than fully decentralized; Goldfinch also cut ties with a third-party risk adviser, raising questions about independence of risk oversight.
As an Ethereum protocol handling pooled USDC across tranched Borrower Pools, Goldfinch carries smart-contract risk, mitigated by multiple Certik and Trail of Bits audits but not eliminated.

Faq.answer: Hidden Hand is a governance-incentives (bribe) marketplace built by Redacted. Protocols deposit incentives to attract votes in vote-escrow (ve) gauge and emissions systems, and vote-escrow token holders who delegate or vote earn those incentives. It generalized the earlier Votemak/Tokemak model to serve many DeFi protocols.
Faq.question: What is Hidden Hand?

Faq.answer: Hidden Hand takes a 4% fee on incentive (bribe) revenue, so voters/delegators receive 96%. The 4% protocol fee has been distributed roughly 35% to the treasury, 50% to rlBTRFLY lockers, and 15% to the DAO Reserve. There is no cost for voters to use the platform.

Faq.answer: Hidden Hand runs separate incentive markets across multiple vote-escrow ecosystems, including Balancer, Aura, and Frax, and historically served protocols such as Tokemak and Ribbon. It acts as an aggregator that consolidates ve-token voting power and routes it toward the highest incentives.
Faq.question: Which ecosystems does Hidden Hand support?

Risks.description: Hidden Hand's entire value proposition is monetizing governance influence. By auctioning vote direction to the highest incentive, it can misalign gauge/emissions outcomes from protocol fundamentals and concentrate influence in whoever pays most, a form of governance capture in the host ecosystems (Balancer, Aura, Frax).

Incentive deposits, vote accounting, and reward claims run through Hidden Hand smart contracts (v1 and v2, plus the Marionette/adapter contracts). Bugs or exploits in these contracts, or in the off-chain reward-computation architecture, could lead to loss or misallocation of deposited incentives.

Rewards depend on an off-chain process that computes vote-weighted distributions and posts claimable merkle data; users rely on Redacted's operational integrity and continued service. This dependency is sharpened by the wind-down, after which the platform stops operating and unclaimed rewards may be forfeited once the claims window closes.

Hidden Hand is tightly coupled to the ve-token 'Curve wars' incentive economy (Convex/Votium, Balancer/Aura, Frax). Declining bribe demand, ve-token depreciation, or contraction of that meta-governance economy directly reduces Hidden Hand volume and fee revenue, a dynamic the team cited when announcing the shutdown.

Explicit vote-buying ('bribe') marketplaces occupy an uncertain legal/regulatory position; incentivized-governance and vote-payment models could attract scrutiny that affects the marketplace or its users.

Faq.answer: Hyperliquid is a purpose-built Layer-1 blockchain whose core application is a fully on-chain central limit order book (CLOB) for perpetual futures and spot trading. It aims to deliver a centralized-exchange-like experience — deep liquidity, sub-second finality, high throughput — while keeping the order book, matching, and liquidations fully on-chain. It is one of the dominant on-chain perpetuals venues.
Faq.question: What is Hyperliquid?

Faq.answer: No. Founder Jeff Yan has said the team rejected all venture capital and self-funded development using profits from the founders' trading operation. In early 2024 they reportedly turned down a VC offer valuing the project at $1 billion in order to keep the platform 'credibly neutral' with no privileged insiders. There is no on-record equity or token raise.
Faq.question: Did Hyperliquid raise money from VCs?

Faq.answer: At the November 29, 2024 genesis event, roughly 310 million HYPE — 31% of the fixed 1 billion supply — was distributed to eligible early users based on accumulated points, fully unlocked at launch. Tokens were pushed to wallets rather than manually claimed. No allocation went to private investors, and reporting cited over 90,000 recipients.
Faq.question: What was the HYPE airdrop?

Faq.answer: HLP (Hyperliquidity Provider) is a community-owned protocol vault that provides market-making quotes across perps, absorbs backstop liquidations, and accrues a share of trading fees. Depositors share the vault's profit and loss directly with no performance fee. Because it can end up holding the losing side of a crowded book, its returns are event-driven rather than a steady yield, and it can experience drawdowns during fast directional moves.
Faq.question: What is the HLP vault?

Faq.answer: On March 26, 2025, a trader exploited the low-liquidity JELLYJELLY memecoin: a large short was forced onto the HLP vault via the liquidation engine while the token's spot price was pumped ~400% in an hour, driving HLP's unrealized loss to roughly $12M. The validator set convened and voted to delist JELLY perps, settling positions at a price favorable to the vault. HLP ended the day in profit, but the episode drew heavy criticism of Hyperliquid's decentralization given how quickly a small validator set intervened.
Faq.question: What happened in the JELLY incident?

Risks.description: The active validator set is small and top-heavy, with a large share of stake historically held by Hyper Foundation validators. The March 2025 JELLY response — validators convening to delist a perp and set a settlement price within minutes — showed that a quorum can override normal market outcomes, raising real questions about decentralization and discretionary intervention.

Value entering and leaving Hyperliquid depends on an Arbitrum-based bridge contract audited by Zellic. Bridge and node software are a concentrated attack surface; any bug in the bridge, node binaries, or HyperEVM precompiles could put user funds or chain integrity at risk.

The HLP vault backstops liquidations across all listed perps and can inherit the losing side of a crowded or manipulated book. A large, illiquid, or manipulated market (as with JELLY) can push HLP into sharp drawdowns, and losses in the shared vault propagate to all depositors simultaneously.

Perp mark prices, funding, and liquidations rely on price inputs that can be manipulated for thinly traded or newly listed assets. Attackers have pumped low-liquidity spot markets to distort on-venue pricing and force adverse liquidations onto the protocol.

As a purpose-built L1 with a custom HyperBFT consensus and a relatively small validator set, Hyperliquid depends on the liveness and correctness of that set. Consensus stalls, validator collusion, or client bugs would halt trading and settlement across both HyperCore and HyperEVM.

Hyperliquid offers high-leverage perpetual derivatives to a global user base without traditional KYC gating at the protocol level. Perpetual futures face increasing regulatory scrutiny across jurisdictions, and enforcement actions or access restrictions could materially affect volumes and the HYPE fee/buyback economics.

Faq.answer: InsurAce is a decentralized, multi-chain DeFi insurance (cover) protocol launched on Ethereum mainnet in April 2021. It lets users buy cover against smart-contract exploits, stablecoin de-pegs, and custodian (CEX) failures, and lets capital providers underwrite that risk in exchange for INSUR rewards. Its distinguishing feature was cross-chain, portfolio-based covers and a two-arm design where an investment arm generates yield to subsidize low premiums.
Faq.question: What is InsurAce?

Faq.answer: Yes. After UST de-pegged in May 2022, InsurAce ran a fast-tracked claims process and its community Claims Assessors approved 155 UST de-peg claims (rejecting 18), paying out roughly $11.7 million against only about $94,000 in premiums collected on those covers. It remains one of the largest real payouts by a DeFi cover protocol.
Faq.question: Did InsurAce actually pay claims after the Terra/UST collapse?

Faq.answer: InsurAce appears to be effectively wound down or dormant as of 2026. The primary insurace.io domain now resolves to a domain-for-sale parking page, the public GitHub org shows almost no activity after 2023-2024, HTX delisted the INSUR token in February 2025 for insufficient volume, and third-party tracker OpenCover paused data collection on InsurAce in May 2025. Treat the protocol as inactive; independently verify before relying on any cover.
Faq.question: Is InsurAce still operating?

Faq.answer: It uses an actuary-based pricing model plus a two-arm structure: idle capital in the cover pools is deployed by an investment arm into yield strategies, and that yield is returned to insurers/insurees. It also pioneered portfolio-based covers, bundling multiple protocols/assets into one cover to cut per-item premium and gas costs.
Faq.question: How does InsurAce keep premiums low?

Faq.answer: InsurAce was audited by SlowMist (early 2021, ahead of its April 2021 mainnet launch) and by PeckShield (concluded July 12, 2021, rated 'Low Risk'). SlowMist's review flagged higher-severity issues, including a reordering-attack risk and a missing permission check on an owner-adding function, which the team reported fixing before launch.
Faq.question: How were InsurAce's smart contracts audited?

Risks.description: As a cover/insurance protocol, InsurAce is itself the counterparty on every policy. Its ability to pay depends on the size and solvency of its capital pools; the UST event showed payouts (~$11.7M) can vastly exceed premiums collected (~$94k), stressing reserves.

InsurAce underwrites stablecoin de-peg cover, concentrating de-peg risk on its own balance sheet. A large correlated de-peg event (as with UST in 2022) can trigger many simultaneous claims that draw down reserves faster than premiums replenish them.

Cover, staking, claims and cross-chain contracts are exploitable. SlowMist's 2021 audit found higher-severity issues (a reordering-attack risk and a missing permission check on an owner-adding function) that had to be fixed pre-launch; multi-chain deployment widens the attack surface.

Claims are approved or rejected by INSUR-staking Claims Assessors. This makes payout decisions dependent on token-weighted voting, which can be swayed by concentrated holders or low participation and creates a conflict between claimants and capital providers.

Protocol viability depends on ongoing premium demand, capital-provider incentives and token value. Declining activity (HTX delisting for sub-$50k daily volume, parked domain, dormant repos) indicates a wind-down where cover may effectively be unavailable or unenforceable despite historic branding.

jGLP takes leveraged exposure to GMX's GLP basket. Adverse moves in GLP's underlying assets, or a fall in the jGLP position value relative to borrowed USDC debt, can trigger deleveraging/liquidation and losses for depositors.

The protocol is deeply dependent on external protocols it builds on - GMX/GLP for jGLP-jUSDC, Dopex for options vaults and Metavaults, and Aura/Balancer for jAURA. A failure, exploit, or economic change in any of these underlying protocols directly impairs Jones vaults.

The audited GLP contracts retain 'centralized aspects,' meaning privileged roles can influence vault behavior; concentrated governance/admin control creates the risk of adverse parameter changes or misuse.

Protocol activity has collapsed from its 2022-2023 peak (JONES ~99.7% off ATH, sub-$1M market cap, thin liquidity). Low TVL and liquidity raise the risk of degraded vault performance, wind-down, or difficulty exiting positions at fair value.

Leverage and rebalancing rely on accurate pricing of GLP and underlying assets; oracle mispricing or manipulation on the underlying platforms could cause incorrect leverage calculations, mistimed rebalances, or unfair liquidations.

Faq.answer: JustLend DAO is the largest lending / money-market protocol on the TRON blockchain and was TRON's first official lending platform, launched December 7, 2020. It is built on the Compound V2 architecture and is part of the JUST ecosystem associated with TRON founder Justin Sun. Users lend and borrow TRON-based assets such as TRX, USDT and USDD.
Faq.question: What is JustLend DAO and what chain is it on?

Faq.answer: You supply TRX or TRC-20 tokens into a market and receive jTokens, which accrue interest algorithmically based on pool supply and demand. To borrow, you must over-collateralize with supplied assets. If your collateral value falls below the required threshold relative to your debt, your position can be liquidated. Interest rates float automatically with utilization.
Faq.question: How does lending and borrowing work?

Faq.answer: JST is the TRC-20 governance token of the JUST / JustLend DAO ecosystem, with a maximum supply of 9.9 billion. Holders vote on protocol parameters and proposals via GovernorBravo + Timelock. Since October 2025 the DAO runs a revenue-funded JST buyback-and-burn program, making JST deflationary; the first round burned 560 million JST (about 5.66% of supply).
Faq.question: What is the JST token used for?

Faq.answer: sTRX is JustLend DAO's one-click TRX liquid-staking product launched in April 2023 under TRON Stake 2.0. You stake TRX, receive the sTRX token, and JustLend automatically handles Super Representative voting and rents out the resulting TRON Energy to earn yield. The Energy Rental market lets users rent Energy for transactions at roughly 50-80% below the cost of burning TRX.
Faq.question: What is Staked TRX (sTRX) and Energy Rental?

Faq.answer: In June 2026 JustLend DAO launched Supply and Borrow Market V2, moving from a single shared pool to an isolated-collateral model with a dual-layer structure of Vaults (where depositors supply) and Markets (where borrowers pledge collateral), plus an Adaptive Curve interest-rate model. Each market has its own loan-to-value settings so a price crash or liquidation in one market stays contained instead of threatening the whole protocol.
Faq.question: What changed in the SBM V2 (isolated lending) upgrade?

Faq.answer: Yes. CertiK published a security assessment dated April 8, 2022, and SlowMist audited the sTRX / Staked TRX contracts. JustLend DAO also runs a bug-bounty program on Immunefi with rewards up to $50,000 for critical smart-contract vulnerabilities. Audits reduce but do not eliminate smart-contract risk.
Faq.question: Has JustLend been audited?

Risks.description: JustLend runs exclusively on TRON, a chain widely criticized for its high degree of centralization (a small, foundation-influenced set of Super Representatives). Chain-level halts, censorship or governance capture would directly impair the protocol, and the sTRX product is tightly coupled to TRON's Super Representative voting and Energy/Stake 2.0 mechanics.

The protocol sits inside the JUST ecosystem broadly associated with Justin Sun, who and whose entities (TRON, related token issuers) have faced SEC litigation and regulatory scrutiny. Adverse action against the founder/ecosystem, or against the USDD stablecoin heavily used as collateral/borrow asset, presents an outsized regulatory overhang versus jurisdiction-neutral peers.

CertiK's audit specifically flagged oracle design as a risk area. Collateral valuation and liquidation depend on price feeds configured by protocol admins; a manipulated, stale or misconfigured feed could cause bad-debt-inducing under-liquidation or unfair liquidations, especially on thinner TRON-native markets.

The CertiK audit and SlowMist review highlighted centralization of admin/reserve controls: admins can set fee parameters (minFee, feeRatio) without hard min/max bounds, and permissions had to be migrated to governance/Timelock contracts. Concentrated JST holdings within the JUST ecosystem mean on-chain governance could in practice be steered by a small group.

A large share of activity is in USDT and especially USDD, an ecosystem stablecoin. USDD has previously traded below its $1 peg; a USDD depeg would impair collateral values, strand borrowers, and could generate protocol bad debt given USDD's prominence as both a supplied and borrowed asset.

The protocol is a large Compound V2 fork extended with custom sTRX, Energy-rental and, since June 2026, isolated-market (SBM V2) contracts. Despite CertiK/SlowMist audits and a $50k Immunefi bounty, forked and newly rewritten lending code carries residual exploit risk, and the SBM V2 rewrite is comparatively new and less battle-tested.

Faq.answer: Kamino is a Solana-native DeFi protocol that combines a lending/borrowing money market (Kamino Lend), automated concentrated-liquidity vaults, and one-click leverage/Multiply products. It grew out of Hubble Protocol, launched its liquidity product in August 2022 and its lend/borrow product in November 2023, and is the largest lending protocol on Solana.
Faq.question: What is Kamino Finance?

Faq.answer: Users deposit supported assets (including yield-bearing tokens like staked SOL) as collateral and borrow other assets against them in an over-collateralized position. Interest rates are set algorithmically by utilization. If a position's loan-to-value exceeds the liquidation threshold, it can be liquidated. Kamino Lend V2 also supports isolated modular markets and fixed-rate borrowing.
Faq.question: How does borrowing on Kamino work?

Faq.answer: KMNO is Kamino's governance and rewards token, launched 30 April 2024 with a 10 billion max supply. Holders can govern protocol parameters, incentive programs and revenue, and KMNO is distributed via seasonal reward campaigns to active users.

Faq.answer: Kamino is Solana-native. All of its smart contracts (klend, kfarms, scope oracle, vaults, LIMO limit orders) run on the Solana blockchain, so users benefit from Solana's low fees and fast finality but are also exposed to Solana network risk.
Faq.question: Which chain does Kamino run on?

Faq.answer: Yes. Kamino states it has completed roughly 20 external security reviews across its components, with audits from OtterSec, Sec3, Offside Labs, Certora, Ackee Blockchain and RX Security. All audit reports are public in the Kamino-Finance/audits GitHub repository, and the team reports zero critical vulnerabilities to date.
Faq.question: Is Kamino audited?

Faq.answer: In 2025 Kamino began integrating tokenized RWAs, starting with ACRED, a tokenized feeder into Apollo Global's private credit fund issued via Securitize. Through Kamino's Multiply product users can loop ACRED for yield and borrow against tokenized exposure to real-world credit.

Risks.description: Kamino is entirely Solana-native. A Solana network outage, congestion or halt (Solana has experienced multiple downtime incidents) can prevent liquidations, oracle updates, deposits and withdrawals, potentially leaving positions unmanageable or under-collateralized during volatility.

K-Lend relies on Kamino's Scope oracle aggregation layer and underlying price feeds (e.g. Pyth/Switchboard). Stale, manipulated or mispriced feeds, especially for thinner Solana collateral or LP/liquid-staking tokens, could cause faulty liquidations or allow bad debt to accrue.

Kamino accepts yield-bearing and less-liquid Solana collateral (liquid-staked SOL, LP tokens, and tokenized RWAs like ACRED). Depegs, liquidity crunches or redemption gating on such collateral can outpace liquidations and create protocol bad debt.

Despite ~20 audits and no critical findings to date, Kamino's klend, vault, farms, scope and LIMO programs are complex Solana smart contracts; a bug or exploit in any component, or in the automated leverage/Multiply logic, could lead to loss of user funds.

The KMNO token controls incentive programs, risk parameters and revenue disbursement. Concentrated token holdings or governance capture could push through risk-parameter or market-listing changes that favor insiders or introduce unsafe collateral.

Faq.answer: K2 is a risk-management L2 built on top of Karak. It acts as a sandbox where DSSs can develop, test, and launch upgrades before deploying to L1, since running everything directly on L1 can be prohibitively expensive.

Faq.answer: Karak introduces multi-asset restaking, letting restakers secure a DSS with a basket of assets rather than only ETH. This is intended to prevent a single asset's failure from compromising a DSS.

Faq.answer: Karak is built by Andalusia Labs, which also builds the Subsea risk-management marketplace and the Watchtower institutional security platform. Andalusia Labs raised a $48M Series A in December 2023 at a valuation north of $1 billion.

Risks.description: Karak's restaking, slashing, and withdrawal logic is complex; the July 2024 Code4rena audit found 4 High and 5 Medium severity issues, including a slashing bug that could permanently lock user ETH when all vault shares were burned during withdrawal.
The protocol's slashing mechanism allows a privileged owner/controller to penalize stakers by reducing staked assets, concentrating power that could be misused or misconfigured.
Restaking rehypothecates the same capital across multiple DSSs (leverage is possible), so a correlated slashing event or cascade across DSSs could compound losses across the shared security pool.

Karak accepts a broad basket of multi-asset collateral (ETH, LSTs, LRTs, stablecoins). Volatility, depeg, or failure of any accepted asset backing a DSS can reduce the effective economic security provided.
Stakers must delegate to operators who choose which DSSs to secure and can be slashed; a malfunctioning, malicious, or under-provisioned operator exposes delegated stakers to loss.

Risks.description: rsETH relies on complex deposit, oracle and withdrawal contracts plus off-chain (AWS Lambda) automation for undelegation. Audits found no criticals but issues required fixes, and LlamaRisk flagged the absence of an active bug bounty at review time and limited public GitHub visibility.

The LRTOracle hardcodes stETH at 1:1 with ETH; if stETH (or ETHx) depegs, an arbitrageur could deposit the cheap asset and withdraw unaffected collateral, and the basket design socializes one asset's depeg across all rsETH holders. rsETH itself traded at roughly -1.5% discount during April 2024 market stress.

Exchange-rate integrity depends on the internal LRTOracle and permissioned price updates (ETHx rate sourced from Stader's contract; secondary Chainlink feed with 24h heartbeat). Faulty, stale or manipulated feeds could misprice mints and withdrawals.

Restaking runs through EigenLayer and a small set of professional node operators (e.g. Kiln, Allnodes, Luganodes) delegating to multiple AVS. Failure, downtime or (once live) slashing at EigenLayer/AVS/operator level flows through to rsETH.

At the LlamaRisk review no DAO existed; the protocol was controlled by a 6/8 admin multisig and a 2/5 manager multisig plus a 10-day timelock, with upgrade, oracle and operator powers concentrated in the team — a centralization and key-management risk.

Accepted collateral is concentrated in a few LSTs (stETH, ETHx) subject to deposit caps; ETHx is issued by the founders' own Stader platform, creating correlated exposure between the collateral issuer and the protocol operator.

Risks.description: stETH is not hard-pegged and can trade below ETH on secondary markets during stress. In June 2022, cascading selling by Celsius and Three Arrows Capital plus the Terra collapse pushed stETH to a multi-percent discount to ETH in the Curve pool before native withdrawals existed.

Lido's very large share of Ethereum staking concentrates influence in LDO governance and its operator set, raising concerns about single-protocol control of validation. The Dual Governance system (live June 2025) was introduced specifically so stETH holders can veto or rage-quit DAO decisions they view as harmful.

Because Lido delegates to a set of professional node operators and DVT clusters, validator slashing or extended downtime is passed through to stETH holders. Lido reports negligible historical slashing, but a large correlated slashing or client-bug event across operators would directly reduce stETH's backing.

stETH rebases and the withdrawal accounting depend on the Lido oracle reporting beacon-chain balances. A compromised, buggy, or manipulated oracle report could misstate rewards or the stETH:ETH exchange rate, which is why the oracle has been repeatedly re-audited (e.g., Oracle v7.1 in 2026).

The protocol comprises complex, upgradeable contracts (Staking Router, withdrawal queue, Dual Governance, stVaults). Despite 90+ audits, high-severity findings have surfaced in reviews (e.g., critical/high issues flagged and fixed during Lido V3 audits in late 2025), so residual smart-contract risk remains.

mETH is a reward-bearing claim on staked ETH whose secondary-market price can trade below its intrinsic ETH exchange rate during stress or thin liquidity; cmETH adds a second wrapping layer that can decouple from mETH.

cmETH routes principal into third-party restaking protocols (EigenLayer, Symbiotic, Karak) and their AVSs, exposing holders to those external protocols' operator, slashing and contract failures beyond Mantle's control.

Underlying yield depends on Ethereum PoS validator performance; validator downtime or slashing reduces mETH's exchange rate, and unstaking is subject to Ethereum's exit queue plus protocol withdrawal delays.

mETH Protocol is governed by Mantle with COOK as its governance token and a large treasury/contributor allocation; concentrated voting power and treasury control could steer parameters against some stakeholders.
The mETH exchange rate relies on an oracle (separately audited); faulty or manipulated oracle updates could misprice mETH for mint/redeem and downstream DeFi integrations.

Faq.question: What actually happened with Orthogonal Trading?
Faq.answer: Orthogonal Trading defaulted on $36 million of loans, reported on 5 December 2022. Roughly $31m of that sat in the M11 USDC pool, hitting remaining LPs by about 80 percent, and $5m in the M11 WETH pool, a 17 percent hit; at least $2.5m of recovery was expected and M11 Credit considered legal action ([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/192097/maple-finance-default-orthogonal-trading)). The DeFi Education Fund's explainer ties the outcome to Maple's pool-underwriter discretionary model, which differs from the algorithmic overcollateralisation used by Aave or Compound ([DeFi Education Fund](https://www.defieducationfund.org/maple-finance-what-happened/)).

Faq.question: Has Maple changed its model since then?
Faq.answer: Yes, materially. The current syrup products provide "fixed-rate, overcollateralized loans to institutional borrowers" with automatic margin calls and a dynamic instant liquidity buffer, rather than the earlier undercollateralised permissioned pools ([Maple docs, syrup FAQ](https://docs.maple.finance/syrupusdc-usdt-usdg-for-lenders/faq), [Maple, built for scale](https://maple.finance/insights/syrupusdc-and-syrupusdt-built-for-scale)). OAK Research reports collateral ratios above 150 percent and zero losses since 2023 ([OAK Research overview](https://oakresearch.io/en/reports/protocols/maple-finance-complete-overview-hub-on-chain-institutional-lending)).

Faq.question: Is syrupUSDC a stablecoin?
Faq.answer: No. Maple states directly that syrupUSDC is not backed by USDC, that its value derives from the loan pool and that there is no affiliation with Circle ([Maple docs, syrup FAQ](https://docs.maple.finance/syrupusdc-usdt-usdg-for-lenders/faq)). It is a yield bearing claim on a credit book, and the risk documentation lists Smart Contract Risk, Default Risk and Risk of Loss ([Maple docs, syrup risks](https://docs.maple.finance/legal/syrupusdc-and-syrupusdt-risks)).

Faq.question: How did Maple handle the April 2026 rsETH exploit?
Faq.answer: It was named among affected protocols in the $292m LayerZero bridge attack of 20 April 2026 ([ChainUp Eye](https://www.chainupeye.com/en/s-articles/article425)). Maple's own account is that rsETH was never approved by its Risk Committee, that indirect exposure via Aave V3 mainnet and a Mantle isolated market was unwound within 24 hours, that it met over $800 million of redemptions in 72 hours and that it ended the episode with "no active lending positions across DeFi" ([Maple, Where Maple Stands](https://maple.finance/insights/where-maple-stands-where-defi-goes)).

Faq.question: What is Maple's regulatory posture?
Faq.answer: Mixed and deliberate. The Cash Management product is offered to US accredited investors under a Reg D exemption, invests in T-bills and reverse repos via StoneX, carries Relm Insurance cover and targets the 1-month T-bill rate less 0.5 percent ([Maple, Cash Management](https://maple.finance/insights/maple-cash-management-opens-to-us-investors)). No incorporation jurisdiction for the operating entity is disclosed in any fetched source, and administrative control over the protocol sits with "The Maple DAO" ([Maple docs, syrup risks](https://docs.maple.finance/legal/syrupusdc-and-syrupusdt-risks)).

Faq.question: How does governance work?
Faq.answer: stSYRUP is the sole governance token under MIP-012, and voting requires connecting a wallet with sufficient stSYRUP balance to Snapshot, with a 7-day voting window ([MIP-012](https://community.maple.finance/t/mip-012-stsyrup-as-the-sole-governance-token-of-the-maple-finance-ecosystem/348), [Syrup docs, governance and voting](https://syrup.gitbook.io/syrup/syrup-token/governance-and-voting)). The Snapshot space is snapshot.org/#/maple.eth with a quorum of 5 percent of circulating supply, and Discourse at community.maple.finance carries proposals ([Maple DAO governance process](https://maple.finance/insights/maple-dao-governance-process)).

Faq.question: How big is Maple and does it earn real money?
Faq.answer: DefiLlama shows $2.108b of TVL on Ethereum as of 26 July 2026, annualised fees of $102.25m and annualised revenue of $12.64m, with $3.54m of that flowing to holders ([DefiLlama Maple](https://defillama.com/protocol/maple-finance)). Maple's own About page claims $4.43 billion of AUM and $23.96 billion of loans originated ([Maple About](https://maple.finance/about)).

Faq.question: Who accepts Maple paper as collateral?
Faq.answer: Aave onboarded syrupUSDC to the V3 Core instance on 27 June 2025 with a 150,000,000 supply cap, 73 percent LTV, 78 percent liquidation threshold and E-Mode parameters of 90/92/4 ([Aave ARFC](https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-onboard-syrupusdc-to-aave-v3-core-instance/22456)). Maple also lists Circle, Sky, Spark, Aave, Chainlink, Bitwise, Fireblocks, Anchorage Digital, Morpho, Pendle, ether.fi and Uniswap among ecosystem partners ([Maple About](https://maple.finance/about)).

Incidents.description: A 10 million USDC loan to Babel Finance in the Orthogonal Trading pool on Maple was liquidated. A Notice of Default had been issued on 1 July 2022 for violating a representation in the Master Loan Agreement, and the smart contracts recognised default on 9 July.
Incidents.outcome: Pool Cover including an extra 1 million USD deposited on the day was liquidated, but liquidation value is capped at a third of the USDC in the Balancer pool. The remaining 7,852,146 USD was absorbed evenly by lenders in a pool of 244,000,237.40 USD, a 3.2% loss to all lenders.

Incidents.title: Default
Incidents.description: Auros Global missed the principal payment on a 2,400 wETH loan worth about 3 million USD from an M11 Credit pool, citing a short term liquidity issue caused by the FTX insolvency. Total Auros exposure to the M11 wETH pool was 8,400 wETH, about 10.7 million USD, plus a 7.5 million USDC loan from a second M11 pool.
Incidents.outcome: Restructuring rather than write off. M11 Credit recovered an initial 60% in February 2023 and secured full repayment of 7.5 million USDC and 8,400 wETH including interest on 8 November 2023.

Incidents.title: Default
Incidents.description: Orthogonal Trading defaulted on about 36 million USD of loans on Maple, made up of about 31 million USDC across four loans plus roughly 5 million USD in wETH. Maple stated Orthogonal had been operating while effectively insolvent and had misrepresented its financial position, with the losses tied to funds trapped on FTX.
Incidents.outcome: Maple severed ties with Orthogonal, M11 Credit issued the default notice, and the loss fell on lenders in the affected pools.

Incidents.title: Wind-down
Incidents.description: Following the 2022 defaults, Maple wound down its undercollateralised lending model. Deposits that had approached 1 billion USD in May 2022 fell to 21 million USD of TVL in March 2023.
Incidents.outcome: All pools launched in 2023 were overcollateralised and only about 10% of outstanding loans remained undercollateralised by September 2023. Maple brought underwriting in house under Maple Direct.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#maple.LongDescription: Maple runs institutional onchain credit, originating loans to institutional borrowers and packaging the resulting cashflows for lenders. Its current flagship products, syrupUSDC and syrupUSDT, provide access to "fixed-rate, overcollateralized loans to institutional borrowers", with automatic margin calls and a dynamic instant liquidity buffer ([Maple docs, syrup FAQ](https://docs.maple.finance/syrupusdc-usdt-usdg-for-lenders/faq), [Maple, built for scale](https://maple.finance/insights/syrupusdc-and-syrupusdt-built-for-scale)). Loans are governed by Master Lending Agreements with collateral posted against each one, and Maple is explicit that "each loan is subject to the risk of default and could lead to potential losses for Lenders" ([Maple docs, syrup risks](https://docs.maple.finance/legal/syrupusdc-and-syrupusdt-risks)). This is the only entity in this set with genuine counterparty credit risk, and it has already realised one: the December 2022 Orthogonal Trading default on $36m of permissioned pool loans ([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/192097/maple-finance-default-orthogonal-trading)). Maple also runs a US-facing Cash Management product under a Reg D exemption for accredited investors, investing in T-bills and reverse repos via StoneX ([Maple, Cash Management](https://maple.finance/insights/maple-cash-management-opens-to-us-investors)).

Risks.description: Maple's core model is credit to a curated set of crypto-native institutions. Even with overcollateralization, borrower default is the central risk: in December 2022 Orthogonal Trading defaulted on ~$36M after misrepresenting its FTX exposure, causing an ~80% loss to lenders in the affected M11 USDC pool. Loan performance depends on the quality of Maple Direct's underwriting and borrower disclosure.

Overcollateralized loans are backed by volatile crypto (BTC, ETH, SOL) at roughly 105-130% collateral ratios held in custody contracts. A sharp price drop can erode the collateral buffer, and liquidating large positions in stressed markets may not fully cover the loan, especially given short 30-180 day tenors.

Lender funds sit in Maple's pool, loan and withdrawal-manager contracts. Pre-mainnet audits found high-severity bugs (e.g. Three Sigma's V2 findings allowing bogus fee managers, arbitrary origination fees, or a malicious withdrawal-manager to drain pools), which were fixed; residual contract risk remains inherent to the protocol.

Maple operates a KYC-gated institutional credit business and, via Maple Direct, issues real secured loans to legal entities. This exposes lenders and the protocol to securities, lending-license and cross-border regulatory risk, particularly as it expands into APAC/LATAM and tokenized Treasury-style products.

syrupUSDC yield ultimately depends on USDC/USDT lent to borrowers. A depeg or freeze of the underlying stablecoin, or of syrupUSDC relative to its net asset value during a rush of withdrawals, could impair redemptions since loans are locked for fixed tenors and cannot be recalled instantly.

TypedRisks.name: Institutional borrower default
TypedRisks.description: Loans are originated to institutional counterparties and each loan is subject to the risk that the borrower does not repay. Maple documentation states lenders can lose the entire value of their deposit.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Overcollateralised structure with margin call and liquidation thresholds, Master Lending Agreements with Maple Foundation acting as Security Agent, collateral liquidation on default
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Count and notional of loans marked impaired or defaulted in the pool loan book

TypedRisks.name: Offchain credit underwriting is unverifiable onchain
TypedRisks.description: Borrower selection, credit limits and covenant monitoring are performed offchain by Maple Direct and are not observable by depositors. The Yearn Curation report identifies this offchain credit process as a core dependency of the product.
TypedRisks.mitigation: In-house underwriting team, published collateral composition and collateral ratio, third party curation reviews
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Divergence between published collateral ratio and pool NAV, delay in publishing loan book updates

TypedRisks.name: Collateral concentration in BTC and XRP
TypedRisks.description: Verified onchain collateral was 53.92% BTC at about 667 million USD and 25.38% XRP at about 314 million USD out of about 1.24 billion USD total. A correlated drawdown across these two assets would hit most of the book at once.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Collateral ratio of about 168.96%, margin call at 85% LTV and liquidation at 90% LTV for BTC, asset level LTV caps
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Rolling 30 day correlation and drawdown of BTC and XRP against posted collateral value

TypedRisks.name: Tokenised treasury collateral dependency on Superstate USTB
TypedRisks.description: 16.16% of collateral, about 200 million USD, is Superstate USTB, a permissioned tokenised treasury fund. Redemption of that collateral depends on Superstate's offchain fund operations rather than an onchain market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Overcollateralisation, low volatility of the underlying treasury exposure
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Superstate USTB redemption queue length and any suspension of subscriptions or redemptions

TypedRisks.name: Custodian dependency for collateral held offchain
TypedRisks.description: Collateral supporting Maple's institutional loans sits with a small set of regulated custodians. Failure, freeze or operational error at a custodian would delay or prevent liquidation of collateral.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Use of multiple regulated custodians rather than a single provider, tri party arrangements on institutional financing deals
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Custodian attestation cadence, any withdrawal suspension announcement from a named custodian

TypedRisks.name: Hardcoded 1 USD price for USDC in internal liquidation logic
TypedRisks.description: The Yearn Curation report flags that Maple's internal liquidation path values USDC at a hardcoded 1 USD. A sustained USDC depeg during a liquidation would misprice recoveries in favour of the borrower.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Chainlink oracles used elsewhere in the system, emergency pause via multisig
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: USDC secondary market price versus 1.00, especially during liquidation windows

TypedRisks.name: Pool Delegate is an externally owned account
TypedRisks.description: The Pool Delegate role, which controls loan origination and impairment for the pool, is held by an externally owned account rather than a multisig. Compromise of that key would give an attacker control over pool level credit actions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Timelocked governor contracts elsewhere in the stack, Tenderly invariant checks every block with PagerDuty alerting, emergency multisig pause
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Unexpected transactions from the Pool Delegate address, unscheduled impairment events

TypedRisks.name: Impairment mechanism can unilaterally reduce pool value
TypedRisks.description: Maple's impairment mechanism allows the delegate to write down the recorded value of a loan, which immediately reduces the pool's net asset value for all depositors. Depositors have no vote on whether or when an impairment is applied.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Published impairment policy in Maple documentation, disclosure obligations, third party curation monitoring
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any impairment event recorded against the pool, step changes in syrupUSDC exchange rate

TypedRisks.name: Withdrawal queue and secondary market liquidity mismatch
TypedRisks.description: Withdrawals run through a FIFO queue that normally clears in minutes to two days but can take up to 30 days. The Uniswap V4 secondary pool held about 20.1 million USD with about 726 thousand USD daily volume and about 5.4% slippage on a 1 million USD exit, and could not fill a 10 million USD order.
TypedRisks.mitigation: FIFO withdrawal queue with published maximum, liquid buffer held in the pool, Aave and Sky integrations for liquidity
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Queue clearing time, secondary market depth and realised slippage on syrupUSDC exits

TypedRisks.name: No tranching, no insurance fund, losses socialised
TypedRisks.description: There is no junior tranche or insurance reserve absorbing first loss. A credit loss is shared pro rata across all pool depositors, exactly as happened in the 2022 Babel liquidation on Maple V1.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Overcollateralisation on current loans, conservative LTV bands
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pool NAV per share falling below its prior high water mark
linkedPartnersUnmatched: Maple International Operations SPC as loan counterparty

TypedRisks.name: Securities law exposure on yield bearing deposit products
TypedRisks.description: Maple opened its tokenised treasury pool to US accredited investors in August 2023 only after securing a Rule 506(c) Regulation D exemption from the SEC, and even then US investors could deposit USDC but not USDT. The Syrup product remains closed to persons in the United States, Australia and about 30 other jurisdictions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Reg D 506(c) exemption for the US cash management pool, PoolPermissionManager enforcing permissioned deposits, geographic restrictions
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Changes to the restricted jurisdiction list, any SEC or foreign regulator action against tokenised credit products
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: CoinDesk on Maple's Reg D exemption

TypedRisks.name: Offshore legal entity structure and enforceability of recovery
TypedRisks.description: The lending counterparty is Maple International Operations SPC, a Cayman segregated portfolio company, with Maple Labs Pty Ltd in Australia and Syrup Ltd offshore. Recovery against a defaulted borrower depends on enforcing Master Lending Agreements across multiple offshore jurisdictions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Segregated portfolios limiting cross contamination, Maple Foundation acting as Security Agent under the Master Lending Agreements
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Time to recovery in any new default, any litigation filings involving Maple entities

TypedRisks.name: Smart contract and upgradeability risk
TypedRisks.description: Maple contracts are upgradeable by the Maple DAO and admin controls exist over the pools. Maple documentation states that a smart contract failure can result in loss of deposited funds.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Audits by Trail of Bits, Spearbit, Three Sigma, 0xMacro, Sherlock, Dedaub and Sigma Prime across releases, governor timelocks, Immunefi bug bounty of 500 thousand USD, no smart contract exploit to date
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New unaudited contract deployments, timelock queue contents, Immunefi disclosures

TypedRisks.name: Oracle and cross chain messaging dependency
TypedRisks.description: Collateral valuation depends on Chainlink price feeds and oracle wrappers, and cross chain distribution of syrupUSDC depends on Chainlink CCIP. Chainlink is identified as a critical external dependency.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Chainlink feeds with wrappers, CCIP receiver audited by Dedaub in November 2025 and Sigma Prime in January 2026, block level invariant monitoring
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Oracle staleness or deviation alerts, CCIP message failures or halts

TypedRisks.name: Concentration in a single institutional financing programme
TypedRisks.description: Maple was an inaugural borrower in Cantor Fitzgerald's bitcoin financing business, whose initial phase is sized up to 2 billion USD. A single large bilateral programme concentrates both funding and counterparty exposure.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Multiple lending venues, overcollateralised bitcoin backed structure, Anchorage Digital as custodian on the transaction
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Size of the Cantor facility relative to total Maple loan book

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#maple.TradFiAnalogue: a private credit fund with a secured institutional loan book, wrapped in a transferable share (syrupUSDC), plus a money market fund for the Cash Management product.

bull.claim: Real, audited scale: $2.108b of TVL as of 26 July 2026 with $102.25m of annualised fees and $12.64m of annualised revenue, the largest revenue base of any entity in this set (DefiLlama Maple).

The post-pivot loan book has performed: over $15 billion of overcollateralised loans and more than $100 million of interest with zero losses, including through the April 2026 stress when it met over $800 million of redemptions in 72 hours (Maple, Where Maple Stands).

Institutional acceptance is documented, not aspirational: Aave onboarded syrupUSDC to V3 Core on 27 June 2025 at a 150,000,000 supply cap and 73 percent LTV after joint ACI, LlamaRisk and Chaos Labs review (Aave ARFC).
Token value accrual is live, with 25 percent of protocol revenue buying back SYRUP from November 2025 under MIP-019 and $3.54m of annualised holders revenue (DefiLlama Maple).

bear.claim: Maple has already lost lender money once. The December 2022 Orthogonal Trading default on $36m produced roughly an 80 percent hit to remaining LPs in the M11 USDC pool and a 17 percent hit in the M11 WETH pool (The Block).

The structural criticism from that event has not gone away: Maple's discretionary pool-underwriter model concentrates judgement in a small group, unlike the algorithmic overcollateralisation of Aave or Compound (DeFi Education Fund).

Redemption is buffer-dependent, not guaranteed. syrupUSDC is explicitly not backed by USDC and relies on a "dynamic instant liquidity buffer", which is exactly the mechanism that would be tested in a correlated run (Maple docs, syrup FAQ, Maple, built for scale).

Regulatory surface is real and only partly addressed: the Cash Management product depends on a Reg D exemption limited to US accredited investors, while no incorporation jurisdiction is disclosed for the operating entity and administrative control rests with "The Maple DAO" (Maple, Cash Management, Maple docs, syrup risks).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#maple.RiskPosture: Maple is the most credit heavy protocol in this set, and its risk is fundamentally about who is borrowing rather than about code. It has never suffered a smart contract exploit, but it has suffered real credit losses: lenders took a 3.2% haircut on the Babel liquidation in July 2022 and a roughly 36 million USD default from Orthogonal Trading in December 2022, both traceable to a borrower misstating its position. Maple's answer since then has been to move underwriting in house, require overcollateralisation, and lean on regulated custodians and a Reg D exemption to serve institutional and accredited money, which is a genuine improvement but shifts the exposure rather than removing it. What remains is a concentrated book, more than three quarters of collateral in BTC and XRP, a single externally owned Pool Delegate key, an impairment switch that can cut depositor value without a vote, and secondary liquidity too thin to absorb a large exit. Depositors should treat syrupUSDC as a credit fund with a token wrapper, not as a money market position.

Risks.description: Maverick's automated liquidity-shifting logic and Programmable Pool 'accessor' contracts are complex. Dedaub's audit of the PoolPosition contracts flagged a critical LP-share minting issue and a medium-severity reentrancy risk (since addressed), underscoring the contract-risk surface of the dynamic-distribution machinery.

Modes that follow price in one direction (Right/Left) or shift with price (Both) can convert an LP's position heavily into the depreciating asset and expose it to impermanent-loss / directional-loss dynamics; a wrong directional bet or a sharp reversal can realize losses relative to simply holding.

veMAV concentrates governance and incentive-direction (emissions/gauge) power in the hands of the largest lockers. This can bias emissions toward pools that benefit large holders and create vote-buying / bribe dynamics around incentive allocation.

Long-tail and permissionlessly listed pairs on Maverick v2 can be thin. Low-liquidity pools are more exposed to price manipulation, high slippage and the amplified impermanent loss that auto-shifting concentration can produce in volatile, illiquid markets.

Faq.question: Has Morpho taken bad debt?
Faq.answer: Yes, at the vault level. After the Stream Finance deUSD collapse on 8 November 2025, Morpho delisted the Elixir sdeUSD/USDC market and the affected MEV Capital vault carried roughly 3.6% bad debt, with deUSD falling from $1 to $0.11 and about $500M of market cap evaporating across Euler, Morpho and Silo ([Binance Square](https://www.binance.com/en/square/post/32330428064082)). Analysts subsequently mapped roughly $285M of potential exposure across DeFi from the same event ([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/377491/analysts-map-285m-in-potential-exposure-across-defi-after-stream-finances-93m-loss)). The protocol itself has no shared pool to socialise those losses, which is the design intent.

Faq.question: Who sets rates and risk parameters?
Faq.answer: Nobody centrally. Each market's IRM and LLTV are chosen at creation from governance-approved sets and are immutable thereafter, with AdaptiveCurveIRM the only approved model and nine approved LLTV values ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/concepts/market/)). Governance can whitelist new LLTVs and IRMs and flip a fee switch capped at 25% of borrower interest, but cannot change a live market ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/governance/organization/)). Effective risk selection is made by vault curators.

Faq.question: Who is actually the credit underwriter I am relying on?
Faq.answer: The vault curator. At launch these were Steakhouse Financial, Block Analitica and B.Protocol ([Morpho LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/morpho-labs_movetomorpho-activity-7150863577116012545-n8Yy)), and by April 2026 the set included the Ethereum Foundation, Gauntlet and Steakhouse ([Real World Tokenspace](https://www.realworldtokenspace.com/research/2026-04-24-morpho-vaults-ethereum-foundation-gauntlet-steakhouse-curators)). Morpho's own documentation includes explicit curator security considerations and a bad-debt handling guide ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/curate/concepts/security-considerations/), [Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/curate/tutorials-v1/bad-debt/)).

Faq.question: How does liquidation work?
Faq.answer: If a borrower's position exceeds the market LLTV, anyone can liquidate it by repaying a portion of the debt in exchange for a discounted portion of the collateral ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/concepts/market/)). The liquidation incentive factor formula is not stated on that page, so `n.a.` for the exact discount schedule.

Faq.question: What is the worst case for a lender?
Faq.answer: A curator allocating into a market whose collateral asset breaks and whose oracle keeps pricing it, which is exactly the Stream Finance pattern: the loss lands entirely inside that vault ([Binance Square](https://www.binance.com/en/square/post/32330428064082)). Contract risk is mitigated by audits from Spearbit, OpenZeppelin, ChainSecurity, Certora, Zellic and Blackthorn ([Morpho audits](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/resources/audits/)) and a $2.5M Cantina bounty ([Cantina](https://cantina.xyz/bounties/35a5f0a1-2ffd-432c-8f3b-77d169add8c3)), but curator risk cannot be audited away.

Faq.question: What is Midnight and how is it different from Blue?
Faq.answer: Midnight is Morpho's fixed-rate, fixed-term protocol, live on Base mainnet from July 2026 with cbBTC and USDC across multiple maturity dates. It is offer-driven: lenders and borrowers propose their own rates, maturities and terms rather than relying on a protocol-defined utilisation curve, and it externalises loan risk, rate and duration to market participants rather than replacing Blue ([Binance Square](https://www.binance.com/en/square/post/347128040805697)).

Faq.question: Who owns Morpho and where does value accrue?
Faq.answer: The Morpho Association, a shareholder-free French nonprofit, owns Morpho Labs SAS as a wholly owned subsidiary, so the MORPHO token is the only asset ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/governance/organization/), [DL News](https://www.dlnews.com/articles/defi/morpho-nonprofit-to-absorb-development-team/)). The June 2026 $175M raise was structured as a token purchase agreement with proceeds to the Association at roughly a $2B valuation ([Lex Substack](https://lex.substack.com/p/defi-the-175mm-bet-on-morpho)).

Incidents.title: Exploit

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#morpho.LongDescription: Morpho unbundles lending into an immutable primitive plus an external curation layer. A Morpho variable-rate market (Morpho Blue) pairs exactly one collateral asset with one loan asset and fixes four parameters at creation, the oracle, the interest rate model, the LLTV and the two assets, after which they persist in perpetuity; market creation is permissionless and requires no governance vote, though the LLTV and IRM must be drawn from governance-approved sets ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/concepts/market/)). Governance-approved LLTVs are 0, 38.5, 62.5, 77.0, 86.0, 91.5, 94.5, 96.5 and 98.0 percent, and the only approved IRM is AdaptiveCurveIRM ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/concepts/market/)). Because each market is isolated and immutable, risk selection moves to vault curators: MetaMorpho and Vaults V2 allocate depositor funds across markets, so the depositor is really buying a curator's credit judgment. In 2026 Morpho added a fixed-rate, fixed-term protocol, Midnight, launched on Base in July 2026, in which lenders and borrowers propose their own rates and maturities instead of relying on a utilisation curve ([Binance Square](https://www.binance.com/en/square/post/347128040805697)).
