CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#radiant.TradFiAnalogue: a failed non-bank lender in members' voluntary liquidation, where the operating business is closed, the loan book is being run off, and a claims administrator distributes recoveries in tranches.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#radiant.FundingNote: No venture funding round is documented in the fetched sources. Radiant's capital came from its RDNT token and protocol revenue rather than an identified equity raise, and the remediation multisig is funded from protocol revenue, DAO treasury, adjusted emissions, reserves, new investments and new partner contributions ([Radiant docs](https://docs.radiant.capital/radiant/remediation/remediation-plan)).

bull.claim: Contracts remain immutable and accessible and the remediation portal is available indefinitely, so users retain the ability to withdraw, repay, close positions, claim rewards and unlock dLP tokens (Binance Square).

The wind-down is orderly and governance-ratified rather than abandoned: a community council administers the plan, zeroShadow remains engaged within available resources and any recovered funds pass to affected investors (Binance Square, Radiant docs).

The Convenience Class actually delivered for the large majority of claimants: $10 to $1,000 claims at a 30% haircut covering 95% (28K) of affected users, distribution beginning Q4 2025 (Radiant docs).

The post mortem is unusually candid and technically detailed, naming compromised addresses, devices and multisig thresholds, which makes it a usable operational-security reference for other protocols (Radiant post mortem).

bear.claim: The protocol is dead as a going concern: lending disabled everywhere since 1 June 2026, emissions ceased, the DAO in a maintenance state with no viable path forward (Binance Square, The Block).
Capital destruction was near-total: $386.8M peak TVL in December 2023 down to $613,179 on 26 July 2026 (Crypto.news, DefiLlama).
Recovery is essentially off the table: CertiK observed 2,834 ETH, roughly $10.8M, moved through Tornado Cash by October 2025, and the attacker is a DPRK-nexus group (The Defiant).
Remediation is explicitly unguaranteed and one claim class was excluded entirely: unlimited-allowance wallet drains are not eligible after a proposal failed quorum (Radiant docs).

Radiant is in wind down and should not be read as a live venue. The DAO began winding down on 1 June 2026, having never recovered from the October 2024 DPRK linked exploit that drained about $50M; TVL across all four chains was about $2.21M on 1 June 2026, split roughly Arbitrum $939k, Ethereum $468k, Base $458k and BNB Chain $343k, and RDNT had already been delisted by OKX, Crypto.com and finally Binance, per [The Defiant](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/radiant-capital-winds-down-2m-husk-dprk-50m-heist). The [protocol sunset technical reference](https://docs.radiant.capital/radiant/protocol-sunset/technical-reference) states that the lending pool borrow parameter has been set to 1, which effectively disables borrowing, that RDNT emissions have ended, and that deposits, withdrawals, repayments and liquidations still function, with Chainlink adapters continuing to read live feeds. That is exactly what the contracts show: on both the Arbitrum and Ethereum pools every borrowable reserve reads a borrow cap of 1. Historical loan to value and liquidation threshold values are still stored on chain, and they are reported below as stored values, not as an invitation to use the protocol. Radiant's asset strategy when live was Arbitrum first, with GMX ecosystem collateral (GM and GLV tokens) that no other protocol in this set lists, plus a RIZ isolated market layer.

Arbitrum core pool `0xE23B4AE3624fB6f7cDEF29bC8EAD912f1Ede6886`, Ethereum core pool `0xA950974f64aA33f27F6C5e017eEE93BF7588ED07`, both listed in the [Radiant contracts documentation](https://docs.radiant.capital/radiant/contracts-and-security/arbitrum-contracts) and [Ethereum contracts documentation](https://docs.radiant.capital/radiant/contracts-and-security/ethereum-contracts). All liquidation bonuses read 15 percent.

Other Ethereum reserves read the same way and are omitted for space: USDT 75/78, WBTC 73/78, sDAI 77/80, rETH 75/80, weETH 72.5/75, LINK 65/70, USDS 77/80, tBTC 70/75, UNI 65/70, cbBTC 73/78, cbETH 75/80, PYUSD 72/75, LBTC 73/78, PAXG 60/68 and AAVE 65/70, all with a 15 percent liquidation bonus, all read from [the Ethereum pool](https://etherscan.io/address/0xA950974f64aA33f27F6C5e017eEE93BF7588ED07#readProxyContract).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#radiant.RiskPosture: Radiant is no longer a going concern and its risk profile should be read as exit risk, not lending risk. Two exploits inside ten months, a roughly 720 ETH shortfall from a flash loan against an empty new market in January 2024 ([Radiant post-mortem](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/post-mortem-report-radiant-capital-aea46cb985ae)) and about 50 million USD from a device-malware multisig compromise in October 2024 ([Radiant post-mortem](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/radiant-post-mortem-fecd6cd38081)), destroyed the protocol's capital base and its trust. Neither loss was recovered, and after eighteen months with no external investment and no grants the DAO began an orderly wind-down on 1 June 2026 ([WuBlockchain](https://www.wublockchain.xyz/news/radiant-capital-wind-down-after-50m-exploit-failure-19380)). The dominant risks now are operational rather than financial: borrowing is disabled with caps at 1, RDNT emissions have stopped, support is best-effort, the front-end only survives through end of year, and the DAO explicitly warns that no further upgrades, patches or interventions should be assumed ([Sunsetting Radiant Capital DAO](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/sunsetting-radiant-capital-dao-entering-recovery-phase-and-lessons-for-the-future-of-defi-c47837ffa499)). Some RIZ vault losses were declared permanently irrecoverable ([RIZ post-mortem](https://community.radiant.capital/t/post-mortem-october-16-2024-exploit-impact-on-riz-vaults/2220)). Net posture: critical, terminal, and the only rational user action is capital withdrawal, which is exactly what the DAO itself advises.

Risks.description: Complex vault logic involving flash loans, Aave positions and cross-protocol composability creates a broad attack surface; a bug in the delta-neutral or omnichain contracts could cause loss of deposits despite the Sherlock audit.

The strategy is fully dependent on external protocols (GMX/GLP for yield, Aave for the hedge borrow, Balancer/Uniswap for execution, LayerZero/Stargate for messaging and bridging); failure, insolvency, or parameter changes at any of these breaks the strategy.

GLP valuation and the BTC/ETH hedge sizing rely on accurate price feeds; oracle manipulation or staleness could misprice the hedge, leaving the vault directionally exposed or subject to bad liquidations.

The hedge can drift from true delta-neutrality (basis/funding divergence, rebalancing lag, or Aave borrow-rate spikes), so the vault may retain residual market exposure and underperform or incur losses during sharp moves.
Omnichain design depends on LayerZero and Stargate bridging; cross-chain message failures, bridge exploits, or Arbitrum sequencer downtime could delay rebalancing/hedging and strand PnL in transit.
As a wound-down protocol, ongoing/tail risk exists around final distributions, unclaimed vault deposits, and reliance on source-protocol interfaces for legacy positions after the app was shut down.

Risks.description: Each property's title is held by a RealT-affiliated LLC (or Inc.), not by token holders directly; holders own LLC membership interests and rely entirely on RealT's custody, management, and honest recordkeeping. Reporting found some homes were sold as tokens while the deeds still listed the prior owner because the purchase never closed, meaning token holders may not own what they paid for.

RealTokens are unregistered securities sold under Reg D Rule 506(c) (U.S. accredited investors only) and Reg S (offshore). RealToken Inc. is not a registered broker-dealer or investment advisor, exposing investors to Howey/securities-law enforcement risk and, as seen in Detroit, municipal nuisance-abatement litigation and personal-liability claims against founders.

The underlying assets are concentrated, low-cost single-family homes subject to vacancy, deterioration, unpaid property taxes, blight tickets, and code violations. Portfolio-wide vacancy and mismanagement have caused rental income to collapse and left some tokens effectively worthless.

RealTokens are highly illiquid: secondary sales are gated by per-property whitelisting on the YAM P2P market and thin DEX liquidity, so holders may be unable to exit at or near fair value, especially during stress or reputational crises.

Custom ERC-20 transfer-restriction logic, the YAM peer-to-peer exchange, and the RMM (an Aave fork) carry smart-contract risk. Public repositories indicate reliance on in-house development and static analysis (Slither) rather than a clearly published, named third-party audit for the token/YAM contracts.

Risks.description: Vault strategies depend on complex smart contracts (vault logic, Opyn oToken minting, auction settlement). Bugs or upgrade flaws could freeze or lose funds; OpenZeppelin's V2 audit flagged a critical instant-withdrawal issue among others.

Covered-call vaults cap upside and remain exposed to sharp downside moves in the underlying (ETH/WBTC). In a rapid market move, deposited collateral can lose value faster than premiums compensate, and options can be assigned against depositors.

Options are sold to external market makers via auction. Reliance on a limited set of institutional counterparties for bidding and settlement concentrates dependence and can degrade pricing or liquidity in stressed conditions.

Concentrated token-holder governance was demonstrated by RGP-33 passing with only 133 RBN holders voting, enabling a full protocol wind-down and token conversion — a small quorum controlling material outcomes for all holders.
Strike selection, settlement pricing, and option valuation rely on external price feeds; manipulated or delayed oracle data could produce mispriced strikes or incorrect settlement.

Risks.description: rETH minting/burning, the deposit pool, and minipool/megapool contracts hold and route large amounts of ETH. A bug in the newer Saturn megapool contracts or the rETH exchange-rate accounting could impair redemptions or lock funds despite audits.

The rETH:ETH exchange rate and network balances are set by oDAO members submitting data via threshold consensus (default 51%). Collusion, compromise, or a stale/incorrect oracle submission by oDAO members could mis-price rETH.

Node operators post an ETH bond plus (historically) RPL as insurance collateral. If a validator is slashed or penalized beyond the operator's bond, or if RPL's value falls sharply relative to the ETH being insured, the buffer protecting rETH holders can be eroded.

rETH is backed by validators run by independent, permissionless node operators. Operator downtime, poor performance, or failure to exit validators on request can drag on rETH yield and complicate redemptions, and rETH holders rely on those operators honoring the protocol's economics.

Control is split between the on-chain pDAO (RPL holders) and the permissioned oDAO. Concentrated RPL voting power, low participation, or the trusted oDAO set can push through parameter or upgrade changes (e.g., the Saturn revenue-split levers) that materially alter operator and rETH-holder economics.

Risks.description: Securitize's entire model depends on maintaining SEC transfer-agent, broker-dealer/ATS and exempt-reporting-adviser registrations across multiple jurisdictions. Changes in securities law, enforcement posture or the classification of tokenized funds could restrict issuance, distribution or secondary trading.

Value in tokenized products depends on off-chain counterparties — asset managers (BlackRock, Apollo), fund administrators, custodians and banks that hold the underlying assets. Investors rely on Securitize and these partners honoring redemption and administration obligations; a partner default or operational failure would impair token value.

The DS Protocol / DSToken contracts enforce compliance, minting, burning and transfers on-chain. Bugs such as the totalIssued burn-logic cap-lock flagged in the September 2025 Halborn audit could freeze issuance or break transfers; upgradeable proxy patterns also introduce admin-key and upgrade risk.

Tokenized funds like BUIDL (money-market/Treasury backed) and ACRED (private credit) are only as sound as their underlying collateral. Private credit exposure in ACRED carries default, illiquidity and valuation risk, and interval-fund redemption limits can restrict investor exits regardless of on-chain liquidity.

Products span many chains (Ethereum, Aptos, Avalanche, Polygon, Solana, BNB Chain and others) with cross-chain movement relying on Wormhole. Chain outages, reorgs or a bridge exploit could disrupt transfers or compromise assets bridged between networks.

Components.description: Core Sense v1 contract that takes any yield-bearing asset (a 'Target', e.g. stETH or cUSDC) via an adapter and splits it into two fixed-term ERC-20 tokens for a given maturity: a Principal Token (PT, 'sP' prefix) that redeems 1-for-1 for the underlying at maturity, and a Yield Token (YT, 'sY' prefix) that claims the yield accrued until maturity. Combining PT+YT reconstitutes the Target.
Components.name: Sense Divider (yield stripping)

Components.description: A custom fixed-rate automated market maker (a YieldSpace implementation) where PTs and YTs trade. Its key innovation is that LPs deposit the yield-bearing Target itself as the quote asset rather than the underlying; accrued Target yield is excluded from the YieldSpace invariant and reserved for LPs, so LP capital keeps earning even when no trading occurs. Space is deployed on Balancer V2 vault infrastructure and includes a TWAP oracle.
Components.name: Sense Space AMM

Components.description: Permissionless connector contracts that onboard a specific yield-bearing asset into Sense (e.g. Lido stETH, Compound cUSDC). Adapters define how a Target's scale/underlying is read, enabling anyone to add new fixed-income markets without core-team approval.
Components.name: Adapters

Components.description: A Roller Liquidity Vault that automatically rolls liquidity from an expiring PT/YT series into the next maturity, letting LPs maintain continuous fixed-income exposure without manually migrating at each rollover. Audited separately by Sherlock and Fixed Point Solutions in late 2022.
Components.name: Roller / Auto-Roller (RLV)

Faq.question: Is Sense still running?
Faq.answer: No. The protocol was sunset on 26 October 2023 after 18 months of operation, the UI was open sourced, the core team ceased contributions and users were told to withdraw by 1 December 2023 ([Sunsetting Sense](https://medium.com/sensefinance/sunsetting-sense-and-releasing-it-into-the-ether-cd8c8e1731ad)). DefiLlama shows $42,168 of stranded residual TVL as of 26 July 2026 ([DefiLlama Sense](https://defillama.com/protocol/sense)).

Faq.question: Why did it shut down?
Faq.answer: Demand, not a hack. The team's stated reason was that "the current DeFi market landscape lacks the consistent demand for fixed rates" ([Sunsetting Sense](https://medium.com/sensefinance/sunsetting-sense-and-releasing-it-into-the-ether-cd8c8e1731ad)). No exploit or bad debt event is recorded in any fetched source.

Faq.question: What made Sense technically distinctive?
Faq.answer: Sense Space, its AMM. It was "an application of the Yieldspace Invariant pool model, that has been further adapted to allow both of the underlying assets to be yield-bearing", which the team called "the fundamental technical innovation behind Sense Core" ([Why Sense](https://medium.com/sensefinance/why-sense-1c78f21d12b3)). It was also a debtless stripping protocol supporting early redemption ([Introducing Sense Space](https://medium.com/sensefinance/introducing-sense-space-85a949087209)).

Faq.question: How did the tokens work?
Faq.answer: Each Series had a Target asset and a Maturity. PT and YT were prefixed sP and sY, PT plus YT equalled the underlying, PT redeemed 1:1 at maturity and YT became worthless after it ([Sense docs, core concepts](https://docs.sense.finance/docs/core-concepts/), [Sense docs, FAQ](https://docs.sense.finance/docs/faq/)).

Faq.question: Was Sense well audited?
Faq.answer: Yes, unusually so for its size: eight reviews across Peckshield, ABDK twice, Fixed Point Solutions (Kurt Barry) three times, Spearbit and Sherlock, spanning Sense v1, Space v1 and the Rolling Liquidity Vault between November 2021 and November 2022 ([Sense docs, security](https://docs.sense.finance/developers/security/)). The shutdown was a commercial decision, not a security failure.

Faq.question: Did Sense have a token or a DAO?
Faq.answer: No governance token or governance venue is documented in any fetched source, so both are `n.a.` The Terms of Service names Sense Finance, Inc. as the operating company ([Sense Terms of Service](https://sense.finance/tos), [Sense docs, FAQ](https://docs.sense.finance/docs/faq/)).

Faq.question: Can the code still be used?
Faq.answer: Yes. The UI was open sourced at the sunset, and the contracts remain published under the sense-finance GitHub organisation with 14 repositories, including the deployed Divider at 0x86bA3E96Be68563E41c2f5769F1AF9fAf758e6E0 ([Sunsetting Sense](https://medium.com/sensefinance/sunsetting-sense-and-releasing-it-into-the-ether-cd8c8e1731ad), [GitHub Sense Finance](https://github.com/sense-finance), [sense-v1 README](https://github.com/sense-finance/sense-v1/blob/dev/README.md)).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#sense.LongDescription: Sense was a yield stripping protocol on Ethereum that split a yield bearing Target asset into Principal Tokens and Yield Tokens for a defined Series with a Maturity, where PT plus YT always equals the underlying and PT redeems 1:1 at maturity while YT becomes worthless after it ([Sense docs, core concepts](https://docs.sense.finance/docs/core-concepts/)). Sense described the mapping in explicitly bond terms: "PTs are like zero-coupon bonds, delivering a single cash flow at maturity" and "YTs are like floating rate bonds" ([Sense, Designing Yield Tokens](https://medium.com/sensefinance/designing-yield-tokens-d20c34d96f56)). It traded through Sense Space, a custom fixed-rate AMM adapting the YieldSpace invariant so that both pool assets could be yield bearing, and used Rolling Liquidity Vaults to automate maturity rolls ([Sense, Introducing Sense Space](https://medium.com/sensefinance/introducing-sense-space-85a949087209), [Sense docs, RLV](https://docs.sense.finance/docs/rolling-liquidity-vaults/), [Why Sense](https://medium.com/sensefinance/why-sense-1c78f21d12b3)). This protocol is sunset. On 26 October 2023 the team wrote that "After 18 months of operation, we've made the decision to sunset the Sense Protocol and open-source the UI", telling users to withdraw by 1 December 2023 ([Sunsetting Sense](https://medium.com/sensefinance/sunsetting-sense-and-releasing-it-into-the-ether-cd8c8e1731ad)).

Remaining PTs/YTs and Space LP positions rely on immutable, unmaintained contracts with no team support, no active UI, and effectively no liquidity; any residual value must be interacted with directly on-chain.

Sense is a complex yield-stripping system (Divider, adapters, Space AMM built on Balancer V2, and the Auto-Roller vault). Despite multiple audits, unmaintained immutable contracts cannot be patched, so any latent bug in the Divider, adapters, or Space math is permanent and unmitigable now that the team has stepped away.

Each fixed-income market depended on the specific yield-bearing Target it wrapped (e.g. Lido stETH, Compound cUSDC). Adapters were permissionless, so a poorly-chosen or compromised Target could impair the PT/YT of that series; PT redemption value is only as sound as the underlying Target and its adapter's scale accounting.

Space integrated a TWAP oracle and adapters read a Target's 'scale' to value redemptions and yield accrual. Manipulation or mispricing of the Target scale or the Space TWAP could distort PT/YT valuations and enable mispriced trades or unfair redemptions.

Because Targets were assets like stETH, a depeg of the underlying yield-bearing asset (e.g. stETH trading below ETH) would directly reduce the redemption value of the corresponding Principal Tokens, transmitting the underlying's peg risk to Sense fixed-income holders.

TypedRisks.name: Protocol sunset and abandonment of core development
TypedRisks.description: On 26 October 2023 the Sense team announced it would sunset the protocol after 18 months and cease core contributions, citing that the DeFi market lacked consistent demand for fixed rates. The UI was open sourced for community use.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Advance notice, open sourcing of the interface, published withdrawal instructions
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any commit activity or governance action after the sunset date

TypedRisks.name: Loss of hosted interface after 1 December 2023
TypedRisks.description: Users were directed to withdraw through app.sense.finance by 1 December 2023, after which Sense relinquished hosting of the interface. Any remaining position must be recovered by interacting with contracts directly.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Open sourced UI that anyone can self host, contracts remain onchain and noncustodial
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Availability of the hosted app, existence of a community maintained frontend

TypedRisks.name: Unmaintained contracts with live admin powers
TypedRisks.description: Admin privileges over the protocol include adjusting guarded launch caps, toggling permissionless mode, verifying adapters, onboarding adapter factories, backfilling Scale, pausing the Divider and pausing adapters, and updating the Periphery. These powers sit with a 2 of 3 multisig on Ethereum mainnet that no longer has an active core team behind it.
TypedRisks.mitigation: 2 of 3 multisig at 0xDd76360C26Eaf63AFCF3a8d2c0121F13AE864D57, guarded launch restricting the Divider to Verified Adapters
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any transaction from the admin multisig, changes to the multisig signer set

TypedRisks.name: Backfill Scale admin power over yield accounting
TypedRisks.description: The admin can Backfill Scale, the abstract metric the Divider uses to decide how Target is split between PT and YT holders. Whoever holds that power can effectively set the payout split of a series.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Multisig control rather than a single key, documented as an explicit admin privilege
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Backfill Scale transactions, unexpected changes in redemption values at settlement

TypedRisks.name: Adapter verification is a trusted centralised gate
TypedRisks.description: Sense distinguishes Verified Adapters, checked by the Sense team, from Unverified Adapters which the documentation says are unverified or deemed unsafe and could be controlled by malicious actors. With the team gone, no new verification happens.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Guarded launch means the Divider interfaces only with Verified Adapters until permissionless mode is enabled
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Whether Divider.addAdapter permissionless mode has been enabled, adapters onboarded after October 2023
linkedAssetsUnmatched: All Target assets exposed through adapters

TypedRisks.name: Adapter discretion over the scale value
TypedRisks.description: Sense documentation states the adapter has full discretion in how and when it determines the scale value, and the Divider queries the adapter for scales on collects and redemptions. A faulty or hostile adapter can therefore misallocate Target between PT and YT holders.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Adapter verification, required overrides of scale, getUnderlyingPrice, wrapUnderlying and unwrapTarget on BaseAdapter
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Scale values reported by each adapter versus the observable Target to Underlying exchange rate

TypedRisks.name: Third party conversion risk between Target and Underlying
TypedRisks.description: Sense only holds the Target asset, so all users are exposed to the risk that the Target cannot be converted back into the Underlying. Sense gives the example that Compound cDAI or Aave aDAI may not be convertible to DAI when a user wants to exit.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Position can be held in Target terms rather than exiting to underlying, documented and disclosed
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Utilisation and liquidity of the underlying lending market, any withdrawal freeze at Compound or Aave

TypedRisks.name: Balancer V2 dependency through the Space AMM
TypedRisks.description: The Space AMM is built on Balancer V2, so every liquidity provider is exposed to Balancer V2 smart contract risk in addition to Sense's own. Sense states that LPs holding to maturity are exposed to Sense and Balancer V2 smart contract risk.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Space implements the Yieldspace invariant and exposes a manipulation resistant LP share price and TWAR
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Balancer V2 security disclosures, Space pool balances

TypedRisks.name: Sense Fuse Pool solvency risk
TypedRisks.description: Sense identifies Fuse Pool solvency risk as a distinct risk affecting only users of the Sense Fuse Pool, alongside market risk for borrowers and lenders in that pool. Fuse pools are isolated lending markets whose bad debt is not backstopped by the wider protocol.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Isolation of the Fuse Pool so the risk does not extend to other Sense users
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Collateralisation and utilisation of the Sense Fuse Pool, presence of undercollateralised positions

TypedRisks.name: Liquidity and price risk when exiting before maturity
TypedRisks.description: LPs who remove liquidity before maturity and convert to Target terms are exposed to liquidity and price risk in Space pools, because returning to Target requires selling excess PTs or YTs into the pool and incurring slippage. With the protocol sunset, that liquidity is thinner than ever.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Holding LP shares to maturity removes the exposure, keeping YTs while providing liquidity reduces it
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Space pool depth per series, realised slippage on exits

TypedRisks.name: Duration risk causing LP underperformance
TypedRisks.description: Sense documents cases where an LP underperforms the underlying at maturity, for example if implied rate and target rate both fall to zero early in the pool's lifecycle so duration risk creates a loss the variable rate exposure fails to recover.
TypedRisks.mitigation: YT retention acting as an effective hedge on duration risk, fixed maturity structure
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Implied rate versus target rate path over the life of a series

TypedRisks.name: Residual smart contract risk with no active bounty stewardship
TypedRisks.description: Sense was audited eight times between 2021 and 2022 by Peckshield, ABDK, Fixed Point Solutions, Spearbit and Sherlock, and ran an Immunefi bounty of up to 50 thousand USD. Sense nonetheless advises users to only risk funds they are willing to lose, and with the team gone there is no one to triage a new disclosure.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Eight completed audits, Immunefi programme up to 50 thousand USD, noncustodial design where users retain their private keys
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any new vulnerability disclosure against Sense contracts, whether the bounty is still funded

bull.claim: The intellectual contribution stands: Sense articulated the cleanest TradFi mapping in the sector, that "PTs are like zero-coupon bonds, delivering a single cash flow at maturity" and "YTs are like floating rate bonds" (Designing Yield Tokens).
Sense Space was a genuine primitive, a YieldSpace invariant adapted so both pool assets could be yield bearing, which the team identified as the core innovation behind Sense Core (Why Sense).

The code carries eight independent audits between November 2021 and November 2022, including Spearbit and Sherlock, and was open sourced at sunset, so it is a usable reference implementation (Sense docs, security, Sunsetting Sense).
It was backed at $5.2m by Dragonfly Capital, Bain Capital Crypto and Robot Ventures, so the design was validated by specialist capital before the market turned (CoinDesk).

bear.claim: **Sense is sunset and is not a live protocol.** The 26 October 2023 announcement ended core team contributions after 18 months of operation and set a 1 December 2023 withdrawal deadline (Sunsetting Sense).
What remains is $42,168 of stranded TVL on Ethereum as of 26 July 2026, across a single tracked pool (DefiLlama Sense).
The stated failure mode is the category risk for every entity in this sector: "the current DeFi market landscape lacks the consistent demand for fixed rates" (Sunsetting Sense).
There is no token, no DAO and no treasury to restart from; total capital raised was a single $5.2m round in August 2021 (DefiLlama Sense, CoinDesk).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#sense.RiskPosture: Sense is a discontinued protocol, and that is the dominant fact about its risk profile. It never suffered a documented exploit, it was audited eight times by credible firms including Spearbit and Sherlock, and it was noncustodial throughout, so the technical foundation was sound. What killed it was demand: the team concluded in October 2023 that DeFi simply did not want fixed rates consistently enough to sustain the product, wound it down, and open sourced the interface. Anyone still holding a Sense position is now dealing with unmaintained contracts, a hosted frontend that was switched off on 1 December 2023, and a 2 of 3 multisig that retains real powers including pausing the Divider and backfilling the Scale value that determines how much Target each PT and YT holder receives. Layered on top are the dependencies Sense always had, on Balancer V2 for the Space AMM and on Compound or Aave for converting Target back to Underlying. The residual risk is not that Sense will be hacked, it is that no one is left to respond if something goes wrong.

Risks.description: The entire coverage product is exposed to smart-contract exploit risk: valid claims (e.g. the $4.5M Euler payout) draw directly from the USDC staking pool, and the underwriting contracts themselves are attack surface.

The coverage pool was severely undercapitalized relative to outstanding exposure: reserves fell ~90% to ~$2.9M while $16.5M of cover was live, meaning a single large claim could exhaust reserves and leave cover unpaid.

Sherlock deposited staker USDC into external yield venues (Maple Finance) and lost ~$4M when borrower Orthogonal Trading defaulted after FTX exposure, showing coverage capital was exposed to third-party credit/counterparty default.

Claim outcomes depend on the Sherlock Protocol Claims Committee (core team + advisors) with escalation only to UMA's Optimistic Oracle; claimants face discretionary, centralized first-pass decisions and a fee to escalate.

Coverage mispricing (protocols charged far less than the loss frequency warranted) plus stakers rushing to withdraw during the 2023 crisis created a run-risk that threatened the viability of the whole coverage model, ultimately forcing a pivot away from staker-funded cover.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#sky.LongDescription: Sky, formerly MakerDAO, is the largest decentralized stablecoin issuer, managing USDS and legacy DAI alongside the sUSDS savings token and SKY governance token. Its credit-sector relevance comes from how it deploys its balance sheet: the protocol-set Sky Savings Rate, collateralized vault borrowing, and allocations of USDS liquidity into lending markets through Stars such as Spark. The Endgame restructuring splits the ecosystem into semi-autonomous SubDAOs, with Sky Core setting monetary policy. Sky is listed here for its lending-adjacent liquidity role while remaining primarily a stablecoin protocol.

Faq.question: Has SparkLend ever taken bad debt?
Faq.answer: No bad-debt event appears in the fetched sources, and the closest live test went the other way. When Kelp DAO's bridge was compromised on 18 April 2026 and 116,500 unbacked rsETH were minted, Aave V3 and V4 faced roughly $195M of potential bad debt while SparkLend was left with $37,300 of frozen residual rsETH, worth 15.32 rsETH, because PhoenixLabs had filed an exit proposal on 16 January 2026 and halted new rsETH supply by spell on 29 January 2026 ([KuCoin](https://www.kucoin.com/news/flash/sparklend-exits-rseth-on-same-day-aave-expands-exposure)). Spark's own framing is that its risk pillars are designed to stack so that a failure in any single component, oracle, issuer, liquidator or market liquidity, does not cascade into bad debt ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). Spark co-founder Sam MacPherson nonetheless cautioned on 19 April 2026 that protocols claiming no rsETH exposure may still carry indirect exposure through user collateral ([KuCoin](https://www.kucoin.com/news/flash/sparklend-exits-rseth-on-same-day-aave-expands-exposure)).

Faq.question: Who sets the interest rates?
Faq.answer: Not the utilisation curve alone. SparkLend rates respond to supply and demand, but transparent rates act as a fixed rate in the short term and change based on Sky Governance, and the Spark Liquidity Layer automatically moves USDS, USDC and USDT into and out of SparkLend based on target borrow rates, utilisation and available inventory at other venues ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). In practice Sky Governance sets the target and the SLL enforces it by supplying or withdrawing inventory, which is closer to a central-bank standing facility than to a pure market-clearing curve. Per-market supply and borrow caps are also configured by Sky Governance ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)).

Faq.question: What happens at liquidation?
Faq.answer: If a position's health factor drops below 1 but stays above 0.95, up to 50% of the position's debt can be covered in a liquidation call; at or below 0.95, up to 100% can be covered, with the collateral transferred depending on debt covered, oracle prices and the applicable liquidation bonus ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). Governance has a softer tool as well: the borrowing power of any asset can be reduced to 0% without impacting existing borrowers, which lets it phase out a collateral type without forcing liquidations as the first response ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). Forced liquidation is still used when required, as with the remaining BTC e-mode positions on 8 June 2026 ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)).

Faq.question: What is the worst case for a lender?
Faq.answer: Spark and Sky publish an explicit six-layer loss waterfall: internal junior risk capital at the Prime level, then Prime-external junior risk capital, then external senior risk capital via srUSDS (planned, not yet deployed), then the Sky Surplus Buffer, then Sky's Aggregate Surplus Buffer, then a SKY token backstop where Sky mints SKY to recapitalise ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings)). Only if all of that is exhausted are residual losses socialised equally across all USDS holders, including Spark Savings vaults ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings)). Spark holds over $35M of stablecoin equity capital at Layer 1 and describes the aggregate protection as several hundred million dollars ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings)). Credora's model puts the Probability of Significant Loss at 0.39% for the ETH vault and 0.46% to 0.52% for the stablecoin vaults, rising to 1.03% for stUSDS, as of 29 June 2026 ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings/risk-architecture/credora-rating)).

Faq.question: How independent is Spark from Sky?
Faq.answer: Materially less than the separate brand suggests. Spark borrows from Sky's stablecoin reserves and operates as a two-sided capital allocator deploying that capital across DeFi, CeFi and RWAs ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/faq)), and its Q1 2026 report calls SKY the parent protocol and describes the Spark treasury as junior capital required by SKY to access the SKY credit line ([Spark Q1 2026 report](https://paragraph.com/@spark-11/spark-q1-2026-financial-report)). Spark's own governance process is a process for amending the Spark Agent artifact inside the Sky Atlas, filed in the Spark Prime section of the Sky forum and voted on Snapshot at s:sparkfi.eth, with a Spark Risk Council review that can reject a proposal before it reaches a vote ([Spark governance docs](https://docs.spark.fi/governance)). Hindenrank scores this dependency as the number one risk, noting that solvency is backstopped by Sky's $6.5B reserve and that this creates single-entity systemic risk ([Hindenrank](https://hindenrank.com/protocol/spark)).

Faq.question: Where does Spark actually make its money?
Faq.answer: Mostly from the Spark Liquidity Layer, not from SparkLend. In Q1 2026 the SLL ran $1.93B of average deployment at a 5.8% average APY for $27.62M of gross returns and $3.05M net, on a captured spread of 0.64%, while SparkLend contributed only $156k of revenue, down from $215k in Q4 ([Spark Q1 2026 report](https://paragraph.com/@spark-11/spark-q1-2026-financial-report)). Distribution rewards added $3.31M, led by sUSDS at $1.66M and stUSDS at $710k ([Spark Q1 2026 report](https://paragraph.com/@spark-11/spark-q1-2026-financial-report)). A credit analyst should therefore treat Spark primarily as a leveraged stablecoin carry book with a money market attached, not as a lending protocol whose earnings scale with borrow demand.

Faq.question: What does the SPK token actually control, and what is the supply risk?
Faq.answer: SPK is used for signalling and Snapshot voting on the Spark Agent artifact, with eligible proposers being holders of 1% of supply, 100M SPK, or nested contributors such as Phoenix Labs ([Spark governance docs](https://docs.spark.fi/governance)). Of the 10 billion genesis supply, 65% sits with Sky for a 10-year farming campaign emitting 1,625M per year in years one and two and tapering to 203.13M per year by year seven, 23% is ecosystem and 12% is team on a 12-month 25% cliff then three-year vest, and Sky retains the ability to mint additional SPK under extreme circumstances per the Sky Atlas ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/governance/spk-token)). The 17 June 2026 unlock alone was 769,050,000 SPK, about 24.1% of market capitalisation, following a 17 May 2026 unlock that preceded a 25.6% price decline within 12 days ([Crypto Daily](https://cryptodaily.co.uk/2026/06/spark-spk-unlock-yield-infrastructure)).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#spark.LongDescription: Spark is the lending and capital-allocation arm of the Sky ecosystem, formerly MakerDAO, and describes itself as a two-sided capital allocator that borrows from Sky's stablecoin reserves and deploys capital across DeFi, CeFi and RWAs ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/faq)). It has three products: Spark Savings (vaults including sUSDS), SparkLend (a USDS-centric money market), and the Spark Liquidity Layer, which provides liquidity directly into DeFi markets across networks ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/faq)). SparkLend is a fork of the Aave V3 codebase, run conservatively with a narrow collateral set, multi-oracle pricing, strict rate limits and first-loss capital ([Contango](https://medium.com/contango-xyz/contango-x-spark-3c92a9c746fc), [Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). Rates are hybrid: a variable rate driven by supply and demand within SparkLend, plus transparent rates that behave as a short-term fixed rate and change only through Sky Governance ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). Liquidation is Aave-style: below a health factor of 1 but above 0.95, up to 50% of debt can be covered; at or below 0.95, up to 100% ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)).

TypedRisks.description: Spark enabled direct holdings of USDe and sUSDe up to a total allocation of 1.1 billion USD, moving from lending market exposure to balance sheet exposure. Yield depends on perpetual funding rates that can turn negative.

TypedRisks.description: Block Analitica applied a 130 percent risk weight to direct allocation versus Morpho market exposure, giving a direct cap of about 885 million USD against a 20 percent supply threshold of roughly 1.15 billion USD. The cap is a governance judgement rather than a hard contract constraint.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Published exposure methodology and an explicit differential risk weight for direct versus market-mediated exposure
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Direct Ethena allocation as a percentage of total USDe supply, checked against the 20 percent threshold

TypedRisks.name: Fixed-maturity principal token exposure via a third-party venue
TypedRisks.description: A 200 million DAI allocation was approved to Pendle's May PT-sUSDe market via Morpho. The position combines Pendle maturity mechanics, Morpho market parameters and Ethena issuer risk in one exposure.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Allocation routed through overcollateralised Morpho markets rather than held directly, which carries a lower risk weight

TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Spark enables direct holdings of up to 1.1bn USDe and sUSDe

TypedRisks.name: Liquid staking token depeg in ETH e-mode
TypedRisks.description: SparkLend restricts ETH e-mode collateral to wstETH and rETH, which still carry redemption and secondary market depeg risk at high e-mode LTVs. A depeg inside an e-mode band produces losses faster than in a standard market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: ETH e-mode limited to two assets, plus a killswitch peg-ratio oracle that halts new borrowing
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Peg ratio of wstETH and rETH to ETH breaching the killswitch threshold

TypedRisks.name: Oracle degradation to a single feed
TypedRisks.description: SparkLend prices assets from a three-oracle median of RedStone, Chainlink and Chronicle, averaging two if one is stale and falling back to a single feed if two are stale. Single-feed fallback removes the manipulation resistance the median was designed to provide.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Three independent providers by default, with staleness detection driving the degradation path
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Number of feeds contributing to each price, alerting whenever the count drops below three

TypedRisks.name: Frozen deprecated markets trapping residual positions
TypedRisks.description: The 29 January 2026 spell froze rsETH, ezETH and tBTC on SparkLend mainnet and froze the entire Gnosis market, raising the tBTC reserve factor to 99 percent and the Gnosis reserve factor to 50 percent. Frozen reserves cannot accept new supply, so residual holders must exit into whatever liquidity remains.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Phased deprecation via governance spells rather than abrupt removal, with withdrawals and repayments left open
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Residual supplied balance in each frozen reserve and the rate at which it declines

TypedRisks.name: Forced liquidation of deprecated e-mode positions
TypedRisks.description: BTC e-mode was fully removed, executed in the June 2026 spell, with remaining positions force-liquidated on 8 June 2026. Users who did not unwind ahead of the deadline had positions closed for them.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Advance governance notice and a phased spell schedule ahead of the force-liquidation date
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Open position count in any e-mode scheduled for removal versus the announced removal date

TypedRisks.name: Compromise of the Spark Liquidity Layer relayer
TypedRisks.description: The Spark Liquidity Layer threat model explicitly assumes the RELAYER can be fully compromised, and a 1-of-2 SAFE is authorised on the ALM Controller as a hot automation wallet. A single hot key drives automated capital movement across venues and chains.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Non-custodial allocator design, a FREEZER role that can removeRelayer and removeController, and keccak256 rate-limit keys with maxAmount and slope per action
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Relayer transaction volume against the configured rate limit slope, and any action approaching maxAmount

TypedRisks.name: Rate-limit and slippage misconfiguration
TypedRisks.description: The SLL uses per-venue maxSlippage with a 0.999e18 convention where zero disables the venue, and an OTCBuffer allowing one outstanding swap at a time. A misconfigured key silently either blocks a venue or permits worse execution than intended.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Explicit rate-limit key structure with maxAmount and slope, single outstanding OTC swap constraint
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Realised execution slippage per venue versus its configured maxSlippage, and any venue with maxSlippage set to zero

TypedRisks.name: Cross-chain and bridge venue dependency
TypedRisks.description: The SLL routes capital through Circle CCTP and LayerZero across Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Unichain, Avalanche and Robinhood. A failure in any bridge or chain strands or impairs allocated capital.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Contract-level rate limits on bridging, per-venue caps, and monitoring of allocations across networks
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Bridged balance in flight per route, and any bridge attestation delay beyond the normal settlement window

TypedRisks.name: Off-chain and RWA venue exposure
TypedRisks.description: SLL venues include Maple Finance and Superstate USTB alongside on-chain protocols. These carry redemption gating, jurisdictional and issuer credit risk that on-chain rate limits cannot mitigate.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Per-venue allocation limits and rate limits, plus published dashboards at data.spark.fi and info.skyeco.com
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Redemption settlement time for each RWA venue and any change to its subscription or redemption terms

TypedRisks.name: Inherited Aave v3 codebase with custom modifications
TypedRisks.description: SparkLend is based on the Aave v3 codebase at versions 3.0.1 and 3.0.2, with a custom DAI interest rate strategy, a custom sDAI oracle and a RewardsController not wired through PoolAddressesProvider. Custom deviations from an audited base are where fork-specific bugs live.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Separate audit repositories for Core Updates, Advanced, Cap Automator, ALM Controller, XChain Helpers, XChain SSR Oracle, Gov Relay, Spark PSM, Spark Vaults V2, Savings Vault Intents, sUSDS, sDAI and stUSDS
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Divergence between the SparkLend fork and upstream Aave v3 security patches

TypedRisks.name: Loss waterfall depends on Sky-level capital
TypedRisks.description: Spark Savings losses flow through a six-layer waterfall from Spark's junior risk capital of over 35 million USD, through the Sky surplus buffer, to a SKY token backstop, and finally to equal socialisation across all USDS holders. Spark depositors ultimately share Sky ecosystem solvency risk.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Six explicit loss-absorption layers, over 35 million USD of Spark stablecoin equity capital, and a planned srUSDS senior risk capital contract
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Spark junior risk capital and Sky surplus buffer balances versus total risk-weighted allocation

TypedRisks.name: stUSDS liquidity constraints and no automatic liquidations
TypedRisks.description: Spark documents that stUSDS carries increased risk relative to other Savings vaults, including potential liquidity constraints and a lack of automatic liquidations. It lends USDS against SKY collateral, so the backstop token is also the collateral.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Explicit risk disclosure, separate vault, and redemption constraints made visible in the app
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: stUSDS redemption queue length and the SKY collateral ratio backing outstanding USDS loans

TypedRisks.name: Recovery mode halting withdrawals
TypedRisks.description: Spark can place Savings vaults into recovery mode and temporarily halt withdrawals in a potential loss event. The stated purpose is equal treatment and bank-run avoidance, but it removes exit optionality precisely when users want it.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Vaults maintain up to a 10 million USD instant liquidity buffer and an asynchronous liquidity intents mechanism for larger withdrawals
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Withdrawal intent fulfilment time relative to the normal few-minute service level

TypedRisks.name: Liquidity flight arriving from a competitor crisis
TypedRisks.description: SparkLend took 1.4 billion USD of net deposits and 350 million USD of loan growth in 48 hours as capital fled Aave after the Kelp exploit. Rapid inflow of unfamiliar borrowers concentrates new positions faster than risk parameters can be reviewed.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Contract-level rate limits on deposits, withdrawals, bridging and PSM swaps, and per-asset caps set by Sky Governance with the Cap Automator
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Deposit and loan growth per 48 hours against the Cap Automator's configured cap increase slope

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#spark.OrgIntro:
Where Spark's mandate ends and Sky's begins. This distinction matters more for Spark than for any other entity in the set, so it is set out explicitly.

- Sky owns the balance sheet. Spark borrows from Sky's stablecoin reserves and is described as the distribution layer within the SKY ecosystem, with SKY as the parent protocol; the Spark treasury acts as junior capital required by SKY to fulfil the risk-required capital needs for accessing the SKY credit line ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/faq), [Spark Q1 2026 report](https://paragraph.com/@spark-11/spark-q1-2026-financial-report)).
- Sky Governance sets SparkLend's risk parameters. Per-market supply and borrow caps are configured by Sky Governance, transparent rates change based on Sky Governance, and Sky Governance can reduce borrowing power of any asset to 0% without impacting existing borrowers ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)).
- Sky controls SPK supply and distribution. 65% of the 10 billion genesis supply sits with Sky for a 10-year farming campaign following rules set in the Sky Atlas, and Sky retains the ability to mint additional SPK under extreme circumstances ([Spark docs](https://docs.spark.fi/governance/spk-token)).
- Spark governs itself through Atlas edits, not independent sovereignty. The Spark governance process centres on updating the Spark Agent artifact in the Sky Atlas, which controls budgets, risk settings, asset onboarding, SLL integrations and new chain deployments; proposals are filed in the Spark Prime section of the Sky forum and voted on Snapshot with SPK ([Spark governance docs](https://docs.spark.fi/governance)).
- Historically the ownership was even more direct. All products created by Phoenix Labs were to belong to MakerDAO, inheriting Maker's governance system, and Phoenix Labs committed 10% of DAI-market profits to Aave DAO for the first two years as a fork licence ([Binance Square](https://www.binance.com/en/square/post/213372), [CoinDesk](https://www.coindesk.com/markets/2023/02/08/makerdao-contributors-propose-first-native-liquidity-market-focused-on-dai-stablecoin)).
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#spark.FundingNote: Spark has taken no venture equity round in the fetched sources; its funding is entirely MakerDAO and Sky treasury allocations plus its own retained earnings, with a $46.1M treasury at the end of Q1 2026 ([Spark Q1 2026 report](https://paragraph.com/@spark-11/spark-q1-2026-financial-report)).

bull.claim: Spark is profitable through a weak lending quarter: Q1 2026 gross protocol returns of $31.5M, net protocol returns of $6.91M, a net protocol surplus of $3.46M, a treasury up 5.7% quarter on quarter to $46.1M, and the first $986k of SPK buybacks initiated (Spark Q1 2026 report).

The conservative listing policy has already paid out once: in the April 2026 Kelp rsETH incident Aave V3 and V4 faced roughly $195M of potential bad debt while SparkLend was left holding $37,300 of frozen residual rsETH, having exited the asset by spell on 29 January 2026 (KuCoin).

The loss buffer is unusually deep and independently rated: six explicit loss-absorption layers up to a SKY token backstop, over $35M of Prime-level stablecoin equity capital and several hundred million dollars of aggregate protection (Spark docs), with Credora putting stablecoin vault Probability of Significant Loss at 0.46% to 0.52% and the ETH vault at 0.39% as of 29 June 2026 (Spark docs).

Scale and institutional distribution are real: $4.63B of TVL across Spark and $3.72B in SparkLend as of 26 July 2026 (DefiLlama, DefiLlama), $4.5B of distributed supply, $285M of SparkLend USDT balances making it one of the largest USDT lending venues on Ethereum, and Spark Institutional Lending at $150M deployed against a governance-approved $1B ceiling through an Anchorage tri-party structure (Spark Q1 2026 report).

bear.claim: Spark is not an independent credit: Hindenrank grades it B- with a risk score of 28/100 and names deep dependency on the Sky ecosystem as risk number one, since solvency is backstopped by Sky's $6.5B reserve and that concentrates systemic risk in a single entity (Hindenrank). S&P's first-ever stablecoin-system credit rating put Sky Protocol, the parent, at B- with a stable outlook (Steakhouse Financial).

The core lending business is shrinking, not growing: SparkLend Q1 2026 revenue of $156k was down from $215k in Q4, and the SLL's captured spread compressed from 0.83% in January to 0.41% in March against 0.70% in Q4 (Spark Q1 2026 report). Spark also initiated a wind-down of the SparkLend Gnosis Chain instance in the quarter (Spark Q1 2026 report).

Collateral concentration was loosened materially at exactly the wrong scale: Hindenrank flags the May 2026 governance decision to raise the WBTC supply cap tenfold from 3,000 to 30,000 BTC, concentrating up to roughly $2.85B of potential BTC collateral exposure, and warns that a severe BTC drawdown could trigger correlated liquidations exceeding SparkLend's isolated-pool buffers (Hindenrank).

Token supply is a persistent overhang and governance is nascent: 65% of the 10 billion SPK supply is still being emitted by Sky over ten years and Sky can mint more under extreme circumstances (Spark docs), the 17 June 2026 unlock alone was worth about 24.1% of market capitalisation (Crypto Daily), and Hindenrank flags governance capture risk during the early low-participation phase (Hindenrank).

AssetCoverage.assetStrategy:
Spark is the Sky (formerly MakerDAO) lending arm and its coverage is two different things at once. SparkLend is a deliberately short Aave v3 style collateral list: 18 reserves on Ethereum, of which only WETH, wstETH, WBTC, cbBTC, LBTC and weETH carry a non zero loan to value, while the dollar assets (USDC, USDT, USDS, PYUSD) are configured as pure borrow assets with LTV and liquidation threshold at zero and effectively unlimited caps. [The SparkLend documentation](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend) is explicit that the list is short by design, that ETH e-mode collateral is limited to wstETH and rETH, and that BTC e-mode was removed entirely. The second and larger half of Spark's asset coverage is allocation driven rather than collateral driven: the [Spark Liquidity Layer](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-liquidity-layer) moves USDS, USDC and USDT into Sky's PSM, Aave v3 and SparkLend, Spark curated Morpho vaults, Curve and Uniswap stablecoin pools, Ethena USDe and sUSDe, EtherFi weETH, Lido wstETH, Maple redemptions, Superstate USTB and OTC desks across Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Unichain, Avalanche and Robinhood Chain, all under keccak256 keyed rate limits with a max amount and a refill slope, and any unapproved venue reverts. Spark Savings adds ERC-4626 vaults (spUSDC, spUSDT, spPYUSD, spETH, spUSDG, plus Sky's sUSDS and stUSDS) whose exposure is again allocation rather than collateral, per [the Spark Savings documentation](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings). So a reader comparing Spark to Aave on collateral lists alone will badly understate its asset footprint.

SparkLend Ethereum, Pool `0xC13e21B648A5Ee794902342038FF3aDAB66BE987` and AaveOracle `0x8105f69D9C41644c6A0803fDA7D03Aa70996cFD9`, both from the [Spark address registry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sparkdotfi/spark-address-registry/master/src/SparkLend.sol). All 18 reserves are shown.

Market size context, for scale rather than parameters: the Spark app reported total market size $5.554B, TVL $3.722B and total borrows $1.832B on the Ethereum market, with wstETH at 1.025M supplied and ETH at 484.4K supplied ([Spark markets app](https://app.spark.fi/markets)).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#spark.RiskPosture: Spark's posture is deliberately conservative on the lending side and aggressive on the balance sheet side, and the two must be assessed separately. SparkLend itself is a hardened Aave v3 fork with a three-oracle median across RedStone, Chainlink and Chronicle, a killswitch peg-ratio oracle, rate-limited caps and a tight collateral set that excludes BTC e-mode entirely ([SparkLend docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). That conservatism paid off when the January 2026 deprecation spell froze rsETH three months before the Kelp exploit, leaving Spark with no direct exposure and attracting 1.4 billion USD of fleeing Aave deposits ([Sky executive vote](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sky-ecosystem/executive-votes/main/2026/executive-vote-2026-01-29-msc-pattern-and-skybase-onboarding.md), [Streetbrief](https://www.streetbrief.co/article/spark-protocol-captures-1-4b-inflow-kelp-dao-exploit-triggers-aave-liquidity-crisis-2604/)). The real risk sits in the Spark Liquidity Layer, which allocates up to 1.1 billion USD directly to Ethena's USDe and sUSDe plus 200 million DAI to Pendle PT markets ([Spark mirror post](https://mirror.xyz/0xF99d0E4E3435cc9C9868D1C6274DfaB3e2721341/LjBAybIk6-waSxwOBWp5mg_37jNvrWF_UdzqqXoEl6U)) and routes capital across CCTP, LayerZero, Maple and Superstate via a relayer whose own threat model assumes it can be fully compromised ([SLL docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-liquidity-layer)). Loss absorption is unusually deep, six layers ending in SKY token issuance and equal socialisation across USDS holders ([Spark Savings docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings)), but that final layer means Spark depositors are ultimately Sky creditors. Net posture: low protocol risk, concentrated issuer and operational risk on the treasury side, with the strongest incident record of the five.

Competitors.differences: Pendle is far larger in TVL and market share, curates most of its markets, and has its own AMM design. Spectra differentiates on fully permissionless pool creation (anyone can list any ERC-4626 vault) and a Curve/Velodrome-derived AMM and ve-tokenomics.
Competitors.name: Pendle
Competitors.positioning: The dominant yield-tokenization protocol and Spectra's primary competitor.
Competitors.similarities: Same core primitive: splits yield-bearing assets into principal (PT) and yield (YT) tokens with fixed maturities, and trades PTs on a purpose-built AMM to create fixed rates and yield speculation.

Competitors.differences: Notional achieves fixed rates through a fixed-term lending market (fCash) rather than by tokenizing and separately trading the yield of external ERC-4626 vaults; it is not a general permissionless yield-splitting layer.
Competitors.name: Notional Finance
Competitors.positioning: Fixed-rate lending/borrowing protocol competing for the fixed-income DeFi user.
Competitors.similarities: Provides fixed rates on crypto assets with defined maturities, appealing to the same fixed-income-seeking users as Spectra's PTs.

Competitors.differences: Smaller scale and less active than Spectra/Pendle; different AMM implementation and integration set.
Competitors.name: Sense Finance
Competitors.positioning: Early permissionless yield-stripping protocol with a similar PT/YT model.
Competitors.similarities: Also separates yield-bearing assets into principal and yield components ('Sense Space' AMM) and targets fixed rates and yield trading in a permissionless design very close to Spectra's.

Competitors.name: TermMax
Competitors.positioning: Fixed-rate, fixed-maturity credit with built-in leverage tokens.
Competitors.similarities: same yield-tokenisation category, competing on curator distribution.
Competitors.differences: It combines a fixed-rate order market with a built-in leverage token in the same instrument set, which most fixed-rate venues keep separate.

Competitors.name: Fira
Competitors.positioning: Bond and coupon tokens splitting loans into principal and yield legs.
Competitors.similarities: Both are yield-tokenisation venues on Ethereum.
Competitors.differences: It runs parallel fixed-rate and variable-rate vaults over the same collateral base, letting a depositor choose the rate regime rather than the market.

Components.description: Users deposit an ERC-4626 interest-bearing token (IBT) or its underlying asset and receive two tokens: a Principal Token (PT), redeemable 1:1 for the underlying at maturity, and a Yield Token (YT), which captures all future yield until maturity. This 'yield tokenization' splits a yield-bearing position into a fixed-rate component (PT) and a variable-yield component (YT), enabling fixed rates, yield speculation, and hedging.
Components.name: Principal & Yield Token (PT / YT) tokenization

Components.description: PTs trade against their underlying IBT in dedicated automated market maker pools. The price of the PT relative to the underlying implies a fixed yield-to-maturity. Spectra's pools are built on a Curve cryptoswap AMM design, letting users buy PTs at a discount (locking in a fixed rate) or provide liquidity to earn swap fees and incentives.
Components.name: AMM pools (Curve-based)

Components.description: Anyone can create a new yield-tokenization market for any ERC-4626 vault at will, without protocol-team approval. This permissionless design lets the protocol list new yield-bearing assets (from lending markets, liquid staking, and stablecoin issuers) faster than curated competitors.
Components.name: Permissionless pool creation

Components.description: SPECTRA is the ecosystem and governance token (migrated from APW). Holders can lock SPECTRA as vote-escrowed veSPECTRA to participate in weekly gauge votes directing incentive emissions, earn a share of protocol fees plus a rebase. Governance, gauge voting, and reward claims run on the Base network.
Components.name: SPECTRA token & veSPECTRA governance

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#spectra.Description: Spectra (formerly APWine) is a permissionless interest-rate derivatives protocol: any yield-bearing asset can be split into principal and yield tokens to trade fixed and variable rates.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#spectra.Differentiator: Permissionless market creation for yield tokenization: anyone can list a new PT/YT market for an interest-bearing asset.

Faq.question: How is Spectra different from Pendle?
Faq.answer: Permissionlessness and asset standard. Spectra tokenises any ERC-4626 interest bearing token through a Factory and Registry, and "anyone can create new markets at will", whereas Pendle wraps assets into its own SY standard and curates which markets appear in the UI ([Spectra dev docs](https://dev.spectra.finance/guides/tokenizing-yield), [Immunefi audit competition scope](https://immunefi.com/audit-competition/audit-comp-spectra-finance/scope/), [Pendle docs, Introduction](https://docs.pendle.finance/pendle-v2/Introduction)).

Faq.question: What happened to APWine?
Faq.answer: It became Spectra. The tokenomics documentation states plainly that "On July 10th, 2023, APWine rebranded to Spectra", and the APW token was later migrated to SPECTRA under SIP-3 with a ve(3,3) model ([Spectra tokenomics docs](https://docs.spectra.finance/tokenomics/apw), [SIP-3](https://gov.spectra.finance/t/sip-3-token-migration-and-tokenomics-upgrade/490)).

Faq.question: Has Spectra ever been exploited?
Faq.answer: Yes, once and in a contained way. On 24 July 2024 an arbitrary call vulnerability in the router allowed an attacker to drain about $73,000 in tokens approved to that contract from four individual wallets, while "the core protocol contract of Spectra remained unaffected" and the app was restored ([SolidityScan analysis](https://blog.solidityscan.com/spectra-finance-hack-analysis-2366cf9f5afc/)).

Faq.question: Who is legally behind Spectra?
Faq.answer: Perspective SAS, a French société par actions simplifiée registered with the Paris Trade and Companies Register under number 801 407 453, governed by French law with exclusive jurisdiction in the courts of Paris ([Spectra Terms of Use](https://op.app.spectra.finance/documents/spectra-terms-of-use.pdf)). That is a materially more identifiable counterparty than the offshore structures used by most peers.

Faq.question: Where is Spectra's TVL actually concentrated?
Faq.answer: Not on Ethereum. As of 26 July 2026 the largest chains are Flare at $21.29m and Hemi at $17.41m, with Ethereum only $3.77m of a $54.28m total ([DefiLlama Spectra](https://defillama.com/protocol/spectra)). The Flare weighting reflects XRP yield markets such as the stXRP pools ([Bitcoin.com News](https://news.bitcoin.com/spectra-rolls-4-88m-into-new-xrp-yield-market-as-flare-keeps-liquidity-intact/)).

Faq.question: How does the Curve relationship work?
Faq.answer: Spectra is AMM-agnostic but initially uses Curve, and the Curve DAO receives 20 percent of all swap fees in return ([Spectra risk documentation](https://docs.spectra.finance/security/risk-documentation), [Curve news](https://news.curve.finance/spectra-finance-a-curve-ecosystem-success-story/)). The April 2025 audit competition covered migrating from Cryptoswap to Curve NG and Curve Stableswap NG pools ([Immunefi audit competition](https://immunefi.com/audit-competition/audit-comp-spectra-finance/scope/)).

Faq.question: What can go wrong with a PT here?
Faq.answer: Underlying asset risk, not protocol credit risk. Spectra's own risk documentation warns that ERC-4626 IBTs "may experience a decrease in their underlying share value", in which case "the underlying backing of Principal Tokens (PTs) will decrease proportionally to maintain the protocol's solvency" ([Spectra risk documentation](https://docs.spectra.finance/security/risk-documentation)).

Incidents.title: Exploit
Incidents.description: At approximately 3:00 PM UTC on Ethereum mainnet an attacker exploited a command in Spectra's router utility contract that allowed users to enter and exit pools with a token of their choice, sweeping funds after users approved the transaction. A Discord user made false claims about YT contract problems to prompt withdrawals. Four wallets were impacted and core protocol contracts were unaffected.
Incidents.outcome: Spectra disabled the app, terminated the router contracts, paused Principal Token contracts to block exchanges at the Curve pool level, then unpaused at about 9 PM UTC and reinstated the app on 24 July. Authorities, exchanges and security teams were contacted, and Spectra sent the attacker an onchain offer to close the case if 90% of funds were returned. Attacker address 0x53635bf7b92b9512f6de0eb7450b26d5d1ad9a4c.

Incidents.title: Exploit
Incidents.description: Resolv, a major source of ERC-4626 collateral tokenised on Spectra, was exploited. A compromised SERVICE_ROLE private key held in AWS KMS combined with a completeSwap function that performed no onchain check on the ratio between deposited funds and minted tokens allowed 80 million USR to be minted from roughly 300 thousand USDC, a 266 to 1 ratio.
Incidents.outcome: USR fell below 0.025 USD at its lowest point. The attacker extracted about 11,400 ETH worth roughly 24 million USD and still held about 36 million USR worth an estimated 2 million USD. Downstream damage was amplified by a donation attack on Morpho vaults using a hardcoded 1 USD oracle for USR and wstUSR. Spectra is not named among the affected protocols in the OAK Research analysis, so direct Spectra losses are n.a.

Risks.description: Spectra tokenizes yield-bearing positions through PT/YT contracts, AMM pools, and a router. Its Code4rena audit surfaced a medium-severity finding on potential yield drainage via flash-loan exploitation of a vault-deflation attack, and another on ERC-5095 compliance; permissionless pool creation enlarges the attack surface since anyone can list arbitrary ERC-4626 vaults.

A Principal Token's fixed-rate guarantee depends on the underlying ERC-4626 vault redeeming 1:1 at maturity. If the underlying yield-bearing asset (a lending receipt, LST, or stablecoin) depegs or loses value, PT redemption value falls and holders can be under-collateralized despite holding the 'principal' leg.

Spectra is a yield layer sitting on top of external protocols (Aave, Lido, stablecoin issuers, etc.). A failure, exploit, or insolvency in any integrated underlying protocol flows directly through to the PTs/YTs minted against it, so users inherit the counterparty risk of every underlying vault they hold exposure to.

Emissions, gauge weights, and fee distribution are controlled by veSPECTRA voters, and the AMM/tokenomics were forked from Velodrome/Curve designs. Concentrated veSPECTRA holdings could steer incentives or fee parameters (e.g. changes made via SIP/SGP proposals) in ways that disadvantage ordinary LPs or PT/YT holders.

Governance, gauge voting, and reward claims were migrated to the Base network (an L2). Base sequencer downtime, reorgs, or bridge issues could disrupt voting and reward claiming, and multi-chain deployment exposes users to the liveness and security assumptions of each chain the protocol operates on.

TypedRisks.name: Peripheral router contract compromise
TypedRisks.description: On 23 July 2024 an attacker exploited a command in Spectra's routing utility contract that let users enter and exit pools with a token of their choice, sweeping funds once a user approved a transaction. The core protocol contracts were unaffected.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Router contracts were terminated, the app was disabled and Principal Token contracts paused, an incident response plan is in place
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Unusual approvals to Spectra router addresses, any new router deployment without audit
linkedAssetsUnmatched: ETH held in user wallets that approved the router

TypedRisks.name: Social engineering directing users into malicious approvals
TypedRisks.description: The July 2024 attack was amplified by a Discord user making false claims about problems with Spectra's YT contracts, prompting users to withdraw and therefore approve the malicious transaction. The attack surface was human as much as technical.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Incident response plan, direct communication channels, coordination with exchanges and security teams
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Impersonation or panic messaging in official community channels, spikes in approval transactions after such messaging

TypedRisks.name: Pause authority over Principal Token contracts
TypedRisks.description: During the July 2024 incident Spectra paused Principal Token contracts to prevent token exchanges at the Curve pool level, then unpaused them roughly six hours later. That confirms a privileged party can halt PT transfers at will.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Pause was used defensively and reversed the same day, response documented publicly
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pause events on PT contracts, duration of any pause

TypedRisks.name: Permissionless pool creation with no vetting
TypedRisks.description: Anyone can open a Spectra pool with any ERC-4626 interest bearing token, specifying only a maturity date and target APR, with no voting or human gated process. There is no screening of the yield source behind a listed market.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Documented as an explicit design choice, risk documentation instructs users to do their own research on interest bearing token issuers
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Rate of new pool creation, share of TVL in pools whose underlying has no audit or track record
linkedPartnersUnmatched: Arbitrary third party ERC-4626 vault issuers

TypedRisks.name: Counterparty risk on interest bearing token issuers
TypedRisks.description: Spectra's own risk documentation states the protocol has no control over the tokens users contribute and instructs users to research the issuers of interest bearing tokens. Spectra is a wrapper, so the credit and peg risk of the underlying passes straight through to PT holders.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Explicit disclosure in risk documentation, ERC-4626 standard interface requirement
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Solvency and peg of each underlying, collateralisation ratio of any stablecoin underlying

TypedRisks.name: Concentration in a single yield source
TypedRisks.description: Spectra has historically carried heavy exposure to Resolv wstUSR markets, and Resolv was exploited on 22 March 2026 when a compromised SERVICE_ROLE key in AWS KMS allowed 80 million USR to be minted against roughly 300 thousand USDC. USR fell below 0.025 USD at its lowest point.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Multi chain, multi asset expansion reducing dependence on any single underlying over time
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share of Spectra TVL attributable to any one underlying issuer, peg of that underlying
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: OAK Research on the Resolv USR hack

TypedRisks.name: Hardcoded oracle pricing of an underlying in downstream markets
TypedRisks.description: The Resolv incident was amplified by a donation attack against Morpho vaults that priced USR and wstUSR at a hardcoded 1 USD while the real price had collapsed. Spectra PTs written against such assets inherit the same mispricing problem wherever they are used as collateral.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Not mitigated at the Spectra layer, mitigation sits with the downstream lending market and its curator
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Oracle configuration for Spectra PT collateral in external lending markets, hardcoded versus market derived prices
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: OAK Research on the Resolv USR hack

TypedRisks.name: Negative yield reducing Principal Token backing
TypedRisks.description: Spectra documents negative yield risk: the share value of an ERC-4626 interest bearing token can fall, which reduces the assets backing the Principal Token. A PT is not principal protected if the vault behind it loses value.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Disclosed in risk documentation, users can select underlyings with lower drawdown risk
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Share price of each ERC-4626 underlying versus its issuance value, PT redemption value versus par

TypedRisks.name: AMM dependency for PT and YT pricing and exit
TypedRisks.description: Spectra is AMM agnostic but was launched on Curve, and PT exit before maturity requires trading against that pool. Spectra's own risk documentation lists AMM risk as a distinct category.
TypedRisks.mitigation: AMM agnostic architecture allowing migration to another venue, MetaVault model introducing automatic liquidity rollovers
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Pool depth and slippage per market, liquidity concentration around the equilibrium point

TypedRisks.name: Severe TVL contraction and fragmentation across chains
TypedRisks.description: Spectra V2 TVL stood at about 28.41 million USD spread across twelve chains, with Hemi at 13.1 million USD and Flare at 11.23 million USD together making up more than 85% of the total, while Ethereum held only about 966 thousand USD and Base about 588 thousand USD. Liquidity that thin makes any meaningful exit costly.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Multi chain presence capturing yield opportunities where they appear
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: TVL per chain, share of TVL on chains with limited bridging or market maker coverage

TypedRisks.name: Chain level dependency on newer networks
TypedRisks.description: The majority of Spectra TVL sits on Hemi and Flare, networks with shorter operating histories than Ethereum. A sequencer failure, reorg or bridge incident on either chain would strand the bulk of the protocol's value.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Deployment across twelve chains so no single failure removes the protocol
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Chain liveness and bridge health for Hemi and Flare, finality times

TypedRisks.name: Smart contract risk in core and MetaVault contracts
TypedRisks.description: Spectra's contracts are public and audited but new components keep being added. Audit history: Code4rena on spectra-core in March and April 2024 found 0 high, 2 medium and 11 low, Pashov Audit Group in March 2024 found 0 high, 3 medium and 15 low, and Sherlock on perspectivefi metavaults-V1 in September 2025 found 0 high, 2 medium and 9 low, all fixed.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Three independent audit engagements with no high severity findings, all issues fixed, public source code
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: New unaudited contract deployments, time between MetaVault feature releases and audit completion

TypedRisks.name: Interface risk
TypedRisks.description: Spectra lists interface risk as a distinct category in its risk documentation, meaning the frontend a user interacts with may not faithfully represent the underlying protocol state. The July 2024 incident showed how interface and approval flows can be turned against users.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Documented as a known risk, contracts remain directly accessible
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Frontend integrity checks, DNS and hosting changes for the official app
