bull.claim: Genuine growth in the Curve era: TVL rose from around $20m to $100m, a 5x increase in 12 months, with the Curve DAO taking 20 percent of swap fees as an aligned distribution partner (Curve news).

Clean audit record across three independent reviews, with 0 high-risk findings each from Code4rena (42 auditors, March to April 2024), Pashov Audit Group (March 2024) and Sherlock on MetaVaults V1 (September 2025) (Spectra audits).

Distribution into markets Pendle does not reach: Flare at $21.29m and Hemi at $17.41m are its two largest chains as of 26 July 2026, and the June 2026 stXRP roll moved $4.88m automatically into a new fixed term instrument (DefiLlama Spectra, Bitcoin.com News).
A named, EU-domiciled operator, Perspective SAS with RCS Paris 801 407 453 under French law, which is an advantage for counterparties with jurisdiction requirements (Spectra Terms of Use).

bear.claim: The economics are tiny. Annualised fees are $117,291 and annualised revenue $93,818, with cumulative revenue since inception of only $417,565 (DefiLlama Spectra).
The token market has de-rated hard: SPECTRA trades at $0.004 against an all-time high of $0.24, giving a $1.9m market cap and $2.95m FDV as of 26 July 2026 (DefiLlama Spectra).
TVL has retraced from the roughly $100m Curve reported in August 2025 to $54.28m as of 26 July 2026, and is concentrated in two long-tail chains rather than Ethereum (Curve news, DefiLlama Spectra).

Permissionless listing shifts diligence entirely to the user, and the protocol states it "does not have control over the types of tokens that users decide to contribute to its pools"; the 24 July 2024 router exploit that cost four wallets about $73,000 shows the peripheral attack surface is real (Spectra risk documentation, SolidityScan analysis).

AssetCoverage.assetStrategy: Spectra is the permissionless end of the yield tokenization spectrum. Any ERC-4626 interest-bearing token can be wrapped into a PT and YT pair with no listing gate, and the protocol runs on nine networks: Ethereum mainnet, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, BNB Chain, Avalanche, HyperEVM, Katana and Sonic, per the pool API endpoints that returned data at `https://app.spectra.finance/api/v1/{network}/pools`. Liquidity sits in Curve StableSwap-NG and twocrypto-NG pools, with a `RateAdjustmentOracle` feeding the expected PT price into the AMM so the bonding curve only has to price the deviation of the realized implied rate from the expected rate ([Spectra rate adjusted StableSwap docs](https://dev.spectra.finance/technical-reference/spectras-automated-market-makers/rate-adjusted-stableswap-pools)). The trade-off versus Pendle is stark on scale: the entire Spectra pool set returned 25 pools, and the largest, PT-yvvbUSDC on Katana, holds $380,545.80 TVL, roughly 1/130th of Pendle's largest market. The asset mix skews toward long-tail and new-chain assets (Katana vault bridge USDC and USDT, Jarvis synthetic euro, YieldNest RWA baskets, Avant avUSD on Avalanche) rather than blue chip LSDs. Spectra also formalizes negative-yield handling through a `ptRate` variable that writes down the PT's par value if the underlying IBT ever registers negative interest ([Spectra rate adjusted StableSwap docs](https://dev.spectra.finance/technical-reference/spectras-automated-market-makers/rate-adjusted-stableswap-pools)).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#spectra.RiskPosture:
Spectra is a small, permissionless protocol whose core contracts have held up well and whose risk sits almost entirely at the edges. Three independent audit engagements, Code4rena, Pashov and Sherlock, produced no high severity findings, and the one exploit it suffered in July 2024 hit a peripheral router contract and four wallets rather than the protocol itself, costing around 168 ETH and being contained within six hours. The structural exposures are different in kind. Anyone can list any ERC-4626 token as a market with no vetting, and Spectra's own documentation says it has no control over what users contribute, so the protocol's real credit quality is whatever its underlyings happen to be. That became concrete on 22 March 2026 when Resolv, a major source of Spectra collateral, was exploited for 80 million USR of unbacked mint and saw USR trade below three cents. On top of that, TVL has fallen to about 28 million USD spread thinly across twelve chains, with more than 85% sitting on Hemi and Flare rather than Ethereum. Spectra should be judged one market at a time, because the protocol offers no protection at all against a bad underlying.

Report compiled 26 July 2026. Every value above is drawn from a page fetched during the research session and linked inline. Where a figure could not be confirmed from a fetched source it is marked n.a.

Risks.description: osETH minting, Vault accounting, redemption and liquidation logic all run in permissionless smart contracts; a bug or exploit in the V3 core contracts could impair stakers or osETH holders despite multiple audits.

osETH is a collateralized position with an LTV cap (~90% mint, ~91.5% redeemable, ~92% liquidatable). If the Vault's ETH value falls relative to minted osETH, positions can be redeemed or liquidated with a 1% premium taken from the staker.

Vaults are run by independent, permissionless node operators who control validator keys and infrastructure. Poor operator performance, downtime, or malicious behavior directly affects stakers in that Vault.

Validators are subject to Ethereum (and Gnosis Chain) consensus-layer risks including slashing and penalties; the overcollateralization buffer is designed to absorb these losses but is finite and could be exceeded in an extreme slashing event.

The StakeWise DAO controls protocol parameters (LTV thresholds, approved Vaults, treasury) and the Treasury is a Gnosis Safe governed by a committee; concentrated SWISE holdings or committee action could change protocol economics.

osETH exchange-rate and position health depend on oracle-reported reward/exchange-rate data; faulty or manipulated oracle updates could misprice positions and trigger unwarranted redemptions or liquidations.

Faq.question: Is Stella still operating?
Faq.answer: No wind down notice was found, and the docs remain live, but DefiLlama shows TVL flat near $443k with a final datapoint of 10 June 2026 and zero incentives ([DefiLlama API, stella](https://api.llama.fi/protocol/stella)). The Alpha Venture DAO blog's most recent visible material dates to the May 2023 Iron Bank dispute ([Alpha Venture DAO blog](https://blog.alphaventuredao.io/)). Treat the protocol as functionally dormant with residual deposits.

Faq.question: Where did the bad debt from the 2021 exploit end up?
Faq.answer: It ended up on Cream's Iron Bank balance sheet, since the exploiter borrowed through Alpha Homora's privileged access rather than draining Alpha's own reserves ([Origin Protocol incident note](https://github.com/OriginProtocol/security/blob/master/incidents/2021-02-13-Alpha-Homora-v2.md)). Iron Bank paused Alpha Homora's lending accounts in March 2023 over roughly $32m still outstanding, and the two sides disputed the repayment terms publicly ([DL News](https://www.dlnews.com/articles/defi/defi-partners-clash-over-32m-bad-debt-iron-bank-alpha-homora/)).

Faq.question: How is the lender compensated if there is no borrow interest?
Faq.answer: Through a share of realised profit. Stella takes a cut of the net yield when a profitable position closes, and 20% of that cut becomes protocol fees accruing to ALPHA stakers ([Stella FAQ](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/additional-information/faq)). If borrowers close flat or at a loss, the lender's realised return from that position is zero.

Faq.question: What is the worst case for a lender here?
Faq.answer: Two overlapping risks. First, the 2021 precedent: a protocol level exploit that converts lender capital into a multi year negotiated claim rather than an immediate loss ([Iron Bank timeline](https://ibdotxyz.medium.com/timeline-between-iron-bank-alpha-homora-v2-e0bfe75467b8)). Second, the academic finding that in Alpha Homora 72.35% of leverage taking borrowers had a negative APY once governance token incentives are stripped out, which implies weak organic demand for the borrow side that funds lender returns ([Wang et al., Speculative Multipliers on DeFi](https://fc22.ifca.ai/preproceedings/71.pdf)).

Faq.question: Is governance live?
Faq.answer: Not as documented. Kraken's asset statement records that ALPHA stakers were to receive sALPHA for governance, which was "not live yet at the time of writing" ([Kraken UK crypto asset statement, Stella](https://assets-cms.kraken.com/files/51n36hrp/facade/400112dfaed7a751d09ea875c21aae46fdb699b9.pdf)). No Snapshot space or on chain governor for Stella was located in this session.

Faq.question: How were liquidations handled historically?
Faq.answer: Alpha Homora liquidated leveraged AMM positions when the collateral ratio breached the threshold, and the empirical record shows 270 of 10,430 analysed positions were liquidated over a nine month window, with the largest single liquidation loss at 10.63% of collateral ([Wang et al., Speculative Multipliers on DeFi](https://fc22.ifca.ai/preproceedings/71.pdf)). Arbitrage loss was a bigger tail risk in some cases, with one position losing 81.67% of collateral ([Wang et al.](https://fc22.ifca.ai/preproceedings/71.pdf)).

Faq.question: Does the ALPHA token have a claim on anything today?
Faq.answer: Documented claim is a fee stream from Stella activity, but with TVL under half a million dollars that stream is negligible ([Stella FAQ](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/additional-information/faq), [DefiLlama API, stella](https://api.llama.fi/protocol/stella)). Total supply is 1 billion with 15% to team and advisors and 36.67% to ecosystem ([Stella token distribution](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/tokenomics/token-distribution)).

Incidents.title: Exploit
Incidents.description: Alpha Homora V2 was exploited through a new pool contract that was neither publicly announced nor accessible via the UI, letting the attacker borrow from Cream v2 / Iron Bank in a flash loan attack. Debt at the time of the theft was 11,245 ETH plus 4,263,139 DAI plus 4,032,014 USDC plus 5,647,242 USDT.
Incidents.amountUsdDisplay: $32.429m owed to Iron Bank; $37m to $37.5m user losses cited
Incidents.outcome: A joint repayment agreement was struck: 20% of Alpha protocol fees to Iron Bank, collateralised by 50m ALPHA worth roughly $60m to $90m at the time. Alpha Homora V2 relaunched in May 2021 with a $100m credit limit, up to 7x leverage, and TVL reached $675m.

Incidents.title: Bad debt
Incidents.description: Repayment had stalled at roughly $5,000 per month, only about 1.5% or $500k net had been repaid, and the 50m ALPHA collateral had fallen more than 90% to around $6m. Iron Bank had asked for additional collateral on 14 February 2023.
Incidents.outcome: Iron Bank escalated to freezing accounts the following day.

Incidents.title: Governance attack
Incidents.description: Iron Bank paused Alpha Homora's lending accounts, blocking withdrawals for users who had accessed Iron Bank through the Alpha Homora front end, and stated it reserved the right to apply those funds against the debt if collateral was not topped up by 5 March.
Incidents.amountUsdDisplay: ~$41m of user funds frozen on Ethereum
Incidents.outcome: Alpha published a sequence of open letters, proposed Iron Bank return about $11m of the $41m, and demanded return of 63,000,000 ALPHA of collateral. Depositors ultimately voted to stop negotiating, accept goodwill funds and pursue legal action. Excess identified was $8,686,364.33 with $5,326,879.99 still outstanding.

Incidents.title: Liquidation cascade
Incidents.description: During the freeze, observers noted that some positions inside the platform that should have been liquidated had not been, because of the impact on fund balances.
Incidents.outcome: No loss figure was disclosed. The dispute continued.

Incidents.title: Wind-down
Incidents.description: The Iron Bank team abandoned the project and transferred multisig ownership to the Keep3r multisig at 0x0d5dc686d0a2abbfdafdfb4d0533e886517d4e83 with no notice to affected users.
Incidents.amountUsdDisplay: Funds locked over one year, value exceeding $60m
Incidents.outcome: Affected users escalated to Yearn governance seeking Keep3r's help and filed police cases. Funds remained locked as of April 2024.

Incidents.title: Wind-down
Incidents.description: Binance delisted Stella (ALPHA) alongside BSW, KMD, LEVER and LTO, citing periodic review of development activity, trading volume, network stability, community engagement and regulatory compliance.
Incidents.outcome: Spot trading suspended 4 July 2025. Coinone had already ended ALPHA trading on 30 March 2025, and KuCoin scheduled delisting with withdrawals closing 13 February 2026.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#stella.LongDescription: Stella is the rebranded continuation of Alpha Finance Lab and Alpha Venture DAO, whose flagship product Alpha Homora was DeFi's first leveraged yield farming protocol, launched in October 2020 ([Cointelegraph, May 2021](https://cointelegraph.com/news/alpha-homora-defies-market-slump-bolsters-tvl-and-token-price-on-v2-relaunch)). The rebrand to Stella was announced in May 2023, repositioning the project from a DeFi lab into a single product: leveraged strategies with 0% cost to borrow ([Stella rebrand announcement, 23 May 2023](https://medium.com/@stellaxyz_/stella-the-leveraged-strategies-protocol-with-0-cost-to-borrow-bad4f89d5cd3)). Instead of charging interest, Stella uses a Pay As You Earn model: borrowers, called leveragoors, pay nothing while a position is open, and Stella takes a cut of the net profit only when a profitable position is closed ([Stella strategy docs](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/protocol-mechanism/stella-strategy)). Of that yield cut, 20% is collected as protocol fees accruing to ALPHA stakers ([Stella FAQ](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/additional-information/faq)). The lineage carries a heavy credit history: a February 2021 exploit of roughly $37.5m drawn from Cream's Iron Bank, and a bad debt dispute that ran into 2023 ([Cream Finance post mortem](https://medium.com/cream-finance/alpha-homora-v2-exploit-post-mortem-344d277bdea6), [DL News, 2023](https://www.dlnews.com/articles/defi/defi-partners-clash-over-32m-bad-debt-iron-bank-alpha-homora/)).

Risks.description: Stella's leverage relies on 'spell'-style strategy contracts routing capital between Stella Lend and external protocols (e.g. Uniswap V3). The predecessor Alpha Homora suffered a ~$37M exploit in Feb 2021 where a faked spell contract was treated as legitimate, demonstrating the concrete danger of this composable-strategy design.

Leverage layered on top of external DeFi protocols creates protocol-to-protocol contagion. The 2021 Alpha Homora incident abused Cream Finance's Iron Bank and left ~$32M of cross-protocol bad debt, showing how a failure in one integrated protocol can cascade into Stella's positions and lenders.

Leveraged positions (initially Uniswap V3 LP positions) are volatile and subject to impermanent loss; adverse price moves can push a leveragoor's position below the required collateralization and trigger liquidation, with lenders exposed to shortfall if liquidation is not fast enough.

Valuing leveraged LP positions and triggering liquidations depends on accurate on-chain price feeds. Manipulated or lagging oracle prices could misvalue collateral or delay liquidations, a recurring attack surface for leverage/LP protocols.

The protocol and ALPHA token are steered by the Alpha Venture DAO / Stella core team, which sets supported strategies and risk parameters. Concentrated control over which strategies are whitelisted and how the PAYE fee is set concentrates decision-making risk.

TypedRisks.name: Protocol viability at near-zero TVL
TypedRisks.description: TVL stands at $442,829 on Arbitrum only, against a category of leveraged farming that requires deep liquidity to liquidate safely. The Stella analytics page shows $0.00 cumulative yields.
TypedRisks.mitigation: n.a. Protocol remains deployed and positions remain withdrawable.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Weekly TVL, cumulative yields on the analytics page, and open position count.

TypedRisks.name: Unresolved Iron Bank debt overhang
TypedRisks.description: Alpha Homora owed Iron Bank $32.429m at the time of the 2021 exploit and still owed $31.947m as of 2 March 2023, of which only about 1.5% had been repaid. As of April 2024 user funds had been locked for over a year and their value exceeded $60m.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Repayment agreement of 20% of protocol fees, collateralised by 50m ALPHA; goodwill fund created for affected depositors; police cases filed.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Any repayment transactions to Iron Bank, and the status of the Keep3r multisig holding Iron Bank.

TypedRisks.name: Collateral value collapse against a fixed debt
TypedRisks.description: The 50m ALPHA pledged to Iron Bank was worth roughly $60m to $90m at the time of the agreement and had fallen to about $6m, a decline of more than 90%. Repayment ran at roughly $5,000 per month against a $32m obligation.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Alpha proposed alternative settlement terms and demanded return of 63,000,000 ALPHA in collateral.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: ALPHA price and the market value of the pledged collateral versus outstanding debt.

TypedRisks.name: Counterparty freezing user funds unilaterally
TypedRisks.description: On 1 March 2023 Iron Bank paused Alpha Homora's lending accounts, freezing roughly $41m of user funds on Ethereum, and stated it reserved the right to use those funds to offset the debt. This is a governance action by a third party over Stella's users' assets.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Depositors voted to stop negotiating, take goodwill funds and pursue legal action; a goodwill fund was set up.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Iron Bank market pause status and multisig ownership changes.
TypedRisks.sourceLabel: Alpha open letter to Iron Bank

TypedRisks.name: Undercollateralized lending by design
TypedRisks.description: Stella deliberately enables undercollateralized loans by holding the LP token as collateral inside the contract. If that containment assumption breaks, lenders have no external claim on the borrower.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Collateral Factors are assigned per LP based on volatility and backtesting: 0.92 for Uniswap V3 and Trader Joe V2 pairs, 0.95 for Penpie LST PT positions.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Positions where Debt Ratio approaches the Collateral Factor limit, and any contract path allowing LP collateral to leave the vault.

TypedRisks.name: Discretionary leverage parameter setting
TypedRisks.description: Maximum leverage is derived from Collateral Factor and Borrow Factor which are "tailored by the Stella research team" on historical volatility, with a threshold variable normally set between 0.97 and 0.985 per strategy. This is a team judgement rather than an on-chain governed parameter.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Parameters are documented publicly per LP; extra collateral can be added by users to improve Debt Ratio.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Changes to published Collateral Factors and threshold values.

TypedRisks.name: Off-chain oracle dependency on centralised exchanges
TypedRisks.description: The Stella Trade price oracle is an off-chain mechanism that triggers the liquidation engine using a weighted median of centralised exchange prices, weighted Binance 3, Coinbase, Bybit and OKX 2 each, and Kucoin, Gate.io, MEXC and Kraken 1 each. An off-chain oracle is a trusted operator dependency, and exchange outages or wash trading feed straight into liquidation decisions.
TypedRisks.mitigation: A secondary on-chain oracle is described as a contingency in the event of primary oracle outage or failure.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Oracle uptime, deviation between the off-chain mark price and on-chain DEX prices, and exchange-specific outages.
linkedAssetsUnmatched: spot pairs supported on Stella Trade

TypedRisks.name: Liquidation on 30-day position expiry
TypedRisks.description: Positions are liquidated when the Debt Ratio exceeds its limit or when the loan expires after 30 days. Time-based forced closure is an unusual risk that can crystallise a loss for a user whose position was never unhealthy.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Expiry is disclosed in documentation and coverage of the protocol; users can add extra collateral or close early.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Count of positions approaching their 30-day expiry date.

TypedRisks.name: Lender withdrawal delay
TypedRisks.description: An intentional 2-day withdrawal delay applies on the lending side after each deposit, and adding assets during the delay restarts the countdown. Lenders cannot exit during a fast-moving stress event.
TypedRisks.mitigation: The delay is a deliberate anti-sandwich measure tied to daily yield distribution, disclosed in documentation.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Lending pool inflow timing versus stress events; ysToken transfer restrictions.

TypedRisks.name: Concentrated integration risk in a few Arbitrum venues
TypedRisks.description: Every listed strategy sits on Uniswap V3, Trader Joe V2, Camelot or Penpie, and Penpie positions carry the highest collateral factor at 0.95 despite Pendle PT maturity mechanics. A failure at any one venue affects a disproportionate share of a very small book.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Collateral factors differentiated by venue; strategies documented per LP.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Venue-level TVL and any incident at Uniswap V3, Trader Joe, Camelot, Penpie or Pendle.

TypedRisks.name: Audited-yet-exploited precedent
TypedRisks.description: The original Alpha Homora contracts were audited by OpenZeppelin, Quantstamp and PeckShield and were still exploited through a new pool contract that was neither publicly announced nor accessible via the UI. No current Stella audit report was located in sources fetched for this report.
TypedRisks.mitigation: n.a. Current audit coverage for the Stella-era Arbitrum contracts was not confirmed.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Publication of a Stella-era audit report and any bug bounty program.

TypedRisks.name: Exchange delistings and token liquidity collapse
TypedRisks.description: Binance delisted ALPHA on 4 July 2025, Coinone delisted it with trading ending 30 March 2025, and KuCoin scheduled ALPHA for delisting with withdrawals closing 13 February 2026. Delisting removes the venues where ALPHA fee accrual and collateral value are priced.
TypedRisks.mitigation: ALPHA remains tradable on decentralised exchanges and remains bridgeable to Arbitrum.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Remaining centralised exchange listings and ALPHA on-chain liquidity depth.

TypedRisks.name: Fee-based value accrual with negligible fees
TypedRisks.description: ALPHA accrues value from 20% of the yield cuts Stella takes from leveraged users, but the analytics page shows $0.00 cumulative yields and TVL is under $450,000. A token whose only claim is a fee stream that is near zero cannot fund development or the Iron Bank repayment.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Staking with a 30-day unbonding period and 72-hour claim window; fixed maximum supply of 1 billion ALPHA.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Protocol fee revenue per month versus operating cost and Iron Bank obligation.

TypedRisks.name: Legal and jurisdictional exposure from the dispute
TypedRisks.description: Depositors voted to pursue legal action against Iron Bank, Alpha threatened legal action to unmask an anonymous Iron Bank team member, and police cases were filed after the Iron Bank multisig was transferred without notice. Litigation of this kind consumes a treasury that is already fee-starved.
TypedRisks.mitigation: Coordinated depositor action and a goodwill fund; documented public record of the dispute.
TypedRisks.monitoringSignal: Court filings, police case progress, and further multisig transfers.

AssetCoverage.assetStrategy: Stella is the outlier in this set because it is largely dormant and its public disclosure effectively stops in 2024. Its model is a **zero-borrowing-interest leveraged strategy protocol on Arbitrum**: lenders deposit a single asset into either a Hyper or a Standard lend pool, and strategy users borrow that liquidity to run a leveraged position on a specific DEX or yield venue, paying the lender a share of profit rather than an interest rate. The unit of listing is therefore a **strategy** (a specific pool on a specific venue with a specific leverage cap) plus a small set of **lendable underlying assets**. Leverage limits are derived from a Collateral Factor and Borrow Factor per strategy rather than published per asset, and Stella states only that "the threshold variable is set to 0.97-0.98.5 based on each strategy" ([Stella leverage docs, page dated 2023-09-29](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/leverage)). A distinctive and rarely seen mechanic is that **every strategy position expires after 30 days from opening and becomes liquidatable at expiry regardless of health**, in addition to becoming liquidatable when the Debt Ratio exceeds 100% ([Stella liquidation docs, page dated 2024-06-28](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/liquidation)). Caps exist in two layers, since "each strategy operates with its own specific borrowing cap, in addition to the underlying asset's borrowing cap", but no numeric cap is published ([Stella lend docs](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-lend/why-stella-lend-is-unique)). Staleness is material and should be stated plainly: the supported-strategies page is dated 2023-11-08, the supported-lend-assets page is dated 2023-09-26, the Stella data API at graph.stellaxyz.io returns HTTP error code 522 and is offline, and DefiLlama reports Stella TVL at roughly $443k, Arbitrum only ([Stella supported strategies](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/supported-strategies), [Stella supported lend assets](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-lend/supported-assets), [DefiLlama Stella](https://defillama.com/protocol/stella)).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#stella.RiskPosture: Stella is best understood as a small residual protocol carrying a very large unresolved liability from a previous life. The 2021 Alpha Homora V2 exploit left $32.429m owed to Iron Bank, the pledged 50m ALPHA collateral lost more than 90% of its value, repayment ran at about $5,000 a month, and the counterparty responded by freezing roughly $41m of user funds and then walking away from the project entirely in February 2024. That history is not closed and it defines the entity. The current product has some sensible design features, published Collateral Factors of 0.92 to 0.95 per LP, a 2-day lender withdrawal delay against sandwiching, and a documented oracle contingency, but the oracle is off-chain and depends on centralised exchange prices, leverage parameters are set at the research team's discretion rather than on chain, no current audit report was located, positions carry a hard 30-day expiry liquidation, and TVL of $442,829 on Arbitrum alone is far below the liquidity depth any leveraged farming design needs to liquidate cleanly. Successive exchange delistings through 2025 and into 2026 point the same direction. Treat this as a wind-down profile rather than a going-concern leverage venue.

Faq.answer: Symbiotic is a permissionless, modular shared-security (restaking) protocol on Ethereum. It lets holders deposit collateral into vaults so that stake can be reused to secure multiple networks and services, with a three-way opt-in among depositors, operators, and networks. With Core V2 (July 2026) it repositioned as collateral markets infrastructure that lets DeFi applications share a unified collateral base.
Faq.question: What is Symbiotic?

Faq.answer: Symbiotic is fully permissionless and asset-agnostic: any developer can launch a shared-security market and any ERC-20 token can be used as collateral, rather than being restricted to ETH and ETH liquid-staking derivatives. It uses immutable core contracts and a modular vault/operator/network design where each network defines its own collateral, operator set, rewards, and slashing.
Faq.question: How is Symbiotic different from EigenLayer?

Faq.answer: As of the capture date, no native SYMB token had been publicly launched with confirmed supply and allocation. The protocol has run a points program rewarding vault deposits and delegation; token mechanics remain unannounced from a primary source, so no token facts are asserted here.

Faq.answer: Core V2, launched July 1, 2026, marks the protocol's transition from a restaking platform to collateral-markets infrastructure. It lets applications such as insurance, credit, and RWA vaults share a unified collateral base, with dynamic capital routing (idle vault capital can be deployed to lending protocols like Aave and Morpho and recalled when needed) and independent, on-chain-enforced per-vault risk management.

Risks.description: Because Symbiotic accepts any ERC-20 token as collateral, volatile or thinly-traded assets can undermine the value backing security guarantees, and rapid price drops can leave networks under-collateralized relative to the value they are protecting.

Security depends on a modular stack of vault, delegation, slashing, rewards, relay, and network contracts. Bugs in these contracts, or in the network-defined middleware/slashing logic, could lead to loss of deposited collateral despite extensive audits.

Slashing and stake accounting can depend on network-defined slash verifiers and off-chain data; a faulty or manipulated slash-verification/oracle input could trigger unjust slashing or fail to slash genuine faults.

Risk parameters, allocation limits, accepted collateral, and delegation are set by curators per vault; misconfiguration, malicious curation, or resolver/veto arbitration decisions can expose depositors to losses outside their control.

Reusing the same collateral to secure many networks simultaneously creates correlated exposure: a large slashing event or cascading failure across shared collateral could propagate losses across multiple networks and vaults at once.

Faq.answer: SNX holders stake their tokens as collateral to back a shared pool of debt. That pooled debt issues synthetic assets (synths) like the sUSD stablecoin and powers Synthetix Perps, an oracle-priced perpetual futures market. Traders get liquidity from the staker-backed pool rather than a traditional order book.
Faq.question: How does Synthetix work?

Faq.answer: sUSD is Synthetix's dollar-pegged synth. It is not fully reserve-backed like USDC; it is minted against pooled SNX (and later protocol) collateral. Because the peg relies on staker incentives rather than redeemable reserves, it can and has depegged — most notably to around $0.68 in April 2025 after the SIP-420 collateral changes.
Faq.question: What is sUSD and is it a normal stablecoin?

Faq.answer: The original V2 system and Perps V2 live on Ethereum and Optimism. Synthetix V3 (Core V3 + Perps V3), the 'Andromeda' release, deployed on Base. Synthetix later wound down its V3 perps on Arbitrum to focus on Base.

Faq.answer: Stakers carry the pooled debt of the whole system, so their obligation can grow if other traders profit. Synths depend on oracle accuracy (a false oracle price caused a large 2019 exploit), and sUSD carries depeg risk as seen in 2025. Perps traders face liquidation and funding-rate risk.
Faq.question: What are the risks of using Synthetix?

Faq.answer: SNX is the collateral and governance token. Staking SNX backs synths and perps liquidity and earns trading fees; SNX is also used in protocol governance (the Spartan Council and related councils). OrgStructure.description: Elected councils govern the protocol. The Spartan Council votes on Synthetix Improvement Proposals (SIPs) and parameter changes (SCCPs); the Treasury Council manages the treasury and funding; the Grants Council funds public-goods work.

Risks.description: Synths and perps price entirely off external oracles. A false price feed has already been exploited: in June 2019 a bad sKRW rate (~1000x) let a bot arbitrage into sETH with over $1B of notional exposure before the oracle was halted. Perps V2/V3 rely on Pyth off-chain feeds delivered by keepers, so feed manipulation, staleness, or keeper failure remains a live risk.

sUSD is not reserve-backed; it is minted against pooled SNX/protocol collateral and holds its peg through staker incentives. After SIP-420 lowered the collateral ratio and pooled the debt, the buy-back-below-peg incentive weakened and sUSD depegged ~31% to ~$0.68 in April 2025, requiring a debt jubilee and forced 420-Pool sUSD ratios to recover.

All SNX stakers share a single pooled debt: a staker's liability rises when other participants' synth positions gain value. This mutualized 'debt pool' design means concentrated winning trades, oracle errors, or a synth mispricing can inflate the debt every staker owes, a structural risk distinct from isolated-margin perp venues.

The V3 rebuild is large and novel; the iosiro V3 audit found 6 high and 11 medium-risk issues (all addressed) and attributed them partly to the size and complexity of a first-time-audited new system. The multi-contract modular architecture and ongoing SIP-driven upgrades keep contract-risk surface high.

Protocol parameters (collateral ratios, fees, market listings, debt policy) are set by elected councils via SIPs/SCCPs. Governance moved fast and materially — e.g. SIP-420's collateral change directly triggered the 2025 sUSD depeg — so governance decisions can rapidly alter risk for stakers and synth holders.

Faq.answer: TCO2 is a tokenized carbon credit (one tonne, 1:1 with a real registry credit and its attributes). BCT (Base Carbon Tonne) and NCT (Nature Carbon Tonne) are fungible 'reference' tokens backed by pools of TCO2s: BCT accepts a broad range of credits, NCT accepts only nature-based credits. Reference tokens can be redeemed for TCO2s, and only TCO2s can be retired.
Faq.question: What are BCT, NCT and TCO2?

Faq.answer: In May 2022 Verra prohibited creating tokens from already-retired credits, arguing that retirement means the environmental benefit has been consumed, so a token on top could enable double claims. Toucan had bridged roughly 22 million Verra credits (~4% of issued credits) using retirement-based bridging. Verra then opened a public consultation on a safer 'immobilized' credit model.
Faq.question: Why did Verra ban Toucan-style tokenization?

Faq.answer: Toucan publicly welcomed the decision, said its retirement-based bridge had always been a compromise, asked bridgers to pause tokenization, and committed to participate in Verra's consultation and to keep the 'Web3 ethos alive' while moving toward bi-directional/immobilized bridging.
Faq.question: How did Toucan respond to Verra's ban?

Faq.answer: Toucan's carbon infrastructure originated on Polygon and has expanded to Celo and Base, targeting low-cost, proof-of-stake networks suited to high-volume, low-value carbon transactions.
Faq.question: Which blockchains does Toucan run on?

Risks.description: Registry recognition risk. In May 2022 Verra banned Toucan-style tokenization of retired credits, invalidating the core bridging mechanism and stranding tokenized supply. Toucan's on-chain credits depend on continued acceptance by off-chain registries (Verra, Puro.earth); adverse registry or regulatory decisions can impair the product's legitimacy overnight.

Low-quality / stale credit backing. Much of the early bridged supply consisted of old (often 10+ years) low-quality credits that would not qualify in today's market, and researchers (e.g. CarbonPlan) labeled some on-chain credits 'zombies.' This undermines the real-world integrity of reference tokens like BCT.

Smart-contract and bridge risk. Toucan relies on upgradeable (UUPS proxy) Solidity contracts across the bridge, TCO2 and pool logic on Polygon/Celo/Base. Audits (byterocket) found and fixed multiple issues, but bugs, upgrade-key compromise or bridge exploits could cause loss or mis-issuance of tokens.

Concentration and demand-collapse risk. On-chain carbon demand was heavily tied to KlimaDAO's treasury mechanics; when that demand and token incentives cooled, BCT/NCT liquidity and prices fell sharply, exposing the ecosystem to reflexive, correlated deleveraging.

Centralization / evolving governance risk. Toucan is a small team-run project (not yet fully open-source at the time of the Verra events) with control over pool acceptance criteria and contract upgrades, concentrating decisions that materially affect token holders.

Faq.answer: Uniswap is an automated market maker: instead of an order book, liquidity providers deposit token pairs into pools and traders swap against those pools. Prices are set algorithmically by the pool's constant-product formula (v2) or concentrated-liquidity curve (v3/v4), and LPs earn the pool's swap fee.
Faq.question: How does Uniswap work?

Faq.answer: Introduced in v3, concentrated liquidity lets LPs allocate capital to a custom price range rather than across the whole curve, providing up to ~4000x more capital efficiency than v2 for LPs who choose ranges well, but exposing them to more active management and impermanent loss if price leaves the range.
Faq.question: What is concentrated liquidity (v3)?

Faq.answer: Hooks are contracts attached to a pool that run custom logic at points like before/after a swap or liquidity change. They enable features such as dynamic fees, on-chain limit orders, and TWAMMs. Because hooks are third-party code, the specific hook attached to a pool is itself a smart-contract risk surface.
Faq.question: What are hooks in Uniswap v4?

Faq.answer: Uniswap v4 deployed on day one (January 2025) across Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, OP Mainnet, Base, BNB Chain, Blast, World Chain, Avalanche and Zora. Uniswap Labs also runs its own L2, Unichain.
Faq.question: Which chains is Uniswap on?

Faq.answer: UNI is the governance token used to vote on the DAO treasury and protocol changes. In the 2025 'UNIfication' vote, governance approved activating protocol fees and using them to burn UNI, plus a one-time burn of 100 million UNI from the treasury.
Faq.question: What does the UNI token do and is there a fee switch?

Faq.answer: v3 pools offer LP fee tiers of 0.05%, 0.30% and 1.00% depending on the pair. Under UNIfication, v2 LP fees move from 0.30% to 0.25% with a 0.05% protocol fee, and v3 protocol fees are set at a fraction of LP fees (1/4 for smaller pools, 1/6 for larger).

Risks.description: Uniswap v4's hooks let arbitrary third-party contracts execute inside a pool's swap/liquidity lifecycle. A malicious or buggy hook can trap funds, manipulate accounting, or brick a pool, so the risk of any given v4 pool depends on the specific hook attached, not just the audited core.

Concentrated-liquidity LPs (v3/v4) who set narrow price ranges face amplified impermanent loss: when price moves outside their range their position becomes fully one-sided and stops earning fees, so poorly-chosen ranges can produce losses versus simply holding the assets.

Protocols that read Uniswap pool prices as an on-chain oracle can be manipulated. Thin or concentrated liquidity makes spot price cheaper to push, and integrators that use instantaneous pool prices rather than time-weighted averages are exposed to manipulation-driven exploits.

UNI voting power is concentrated among large holders and early venture backers, and the 2025 UNIfication vote gave governance direct control over fee activation and treasury burns. Concentrated voting means a small set of holders can steer fee economics and treasury decisions.

Uniswap Labs received an SEC Wells notice in April 2024 alleging it operated as an unregistered broker/exchange and issued an unregistered security. Although the investigation was closed with no action in Feb 2025, the legal status of front-ends, the UNI token and fee-switch value accrual remains an unsettled regulatory risk.

The push into Unichain and multi-chain v4 deployments adds L2/bridge dependency: Unichain is an OP-Stack rollup relying on its sequencer and fault-proof system, and cross-chain UniswapX intents introduce bridging and settlement risk beyond a single L1.

Risks.description: Rapid Obsolescence & Depreciation: GPUs lose value quickly (new generations every 18-24 months). If AI demand slows or better chips arrive, collateral value can crash, leading to under-collateralization.
Double Default Risk: collateral value and revenue (compute rentals) can drop simultaneously in a downturn.
Liquidation Challenges: oversupply during forced sales could tank the secondary market for used GPUs.
Concentration & Cyclical Risk: heavily tied to the AI boom; vulnerable to hype cycles (similar to dot-com vendor financing issues).
Higher Costs: often more expensive than plain corporate debt due to complexity and risk premiums.
Regulatory & Structural Risks: in TradFi, heavy capital requirements for banks. In DeFi: smart contract, governance, or custody risks (though mitigated in USD.AI).
Systemic Concerns: some compare aggressive GPU financing to pre-2008 financial engineering (hidden leverage via SPVs).

Faq.answer: Venus is governed by the Venus DAO. XVS holders stake in the XVS Vault to gain voting power and submit or vote on Venus Improvement Proposals (VIPs), which come in Normal, Fast Track, and Critical tiers with different thresholds and timelocks. OrgStructure.description: The decentralized autonomous organization that governs Venus. XVS holders stake and vote on Venus Improvement Proposals (VIPs) covering markets, risk parameters, treasury, and features. Proposing requires substantial voting power (e.g., ~300k XVS) and quorum thresholds for passage.
OrgStructure.name: Venus DAO

OrgStructure.description: The research-and-development entity that builds and maintains the Venus protocol and executes VIP-approved work; it is periodically reimbursed by the DAO (e.g., ~$1.49M for H1 2024 and ~$1.7M for H2 2024). Venus was originally created in 2020 by the Swipe team, founded by Joselito Lizarondo.
OrgStructure.name: Venus Labs

Risks.description: Venus has repeatedly suffered oracle/price-manipulation losses on low-liquidity collateral: the May 2021 XVS price spike drove $200M+ in liquidations and ~$100M bad debt, and the March 2026 THE (Thena) attack used a donation to inflate the vTHE exchange rate, leaving ~$2.15M bad debt. Thinly-traded listed assets remain an oracle attack surface.

Listing volatile or thinly-liquid long-tail assets as collateral (XVS in 2021, THE in 2026) has directly caused bad debt. Even with Isolated Pools segregating risk, aggressive collateral factors and supply caps on such assets can be gamed, socializing losses within a pool.

The March 2026 donation attack reportedly stemmed from a dismissed audit finding, and the protocol has a complex multi-component surface (Core Pool, Isolated Pools, PSM, converters, bridges, multichain governance). Contract bugs or unsafe parameter interactions can be exploited despite extensive audits.

VAI is an overcollateralized synthetic stablecoin that has historically traded off its $1 peg, requiring interventions such as a stability fee and a USDT-backed Peg Stability Module. VAI's peg depends on collateral solvency and PSM liquidity, and can drift under stress.

Concentrated XVS voting power and delegate-based governance mean a small set of large holders/delegates can steer risk parameters and emergency actions (e.g., votes to force-liquidate attacker wallets). This introduces centralization and potential misuse risk in an otherwise permissionless system.

Faq.answer: Votium is a non-custodial vote-incentive ('bribe') marketplace where protocols pay whitelisted ERC20 rewards to Convex vlCVX and Curve veCRV holders in exchange for directing Curve gauge emissions to their pool. Votium does not have a native governance token.
Faq.question: What is Votium and does it have its own token?

Faq.answer: Lock CVX as vlCVX and either delegate your Convex voting power to Votium (votium.eth) via Snapshot once — after which Votium votes for the highest-value incentives on every future round automatically — or vote yourself for whichever incentivised pools you prefer. You must be locked and delegated before a proposal starts to be eligible.
Faq.question: How do I earn incentives as a vlCVX holder?

Faq.answer: Convex/vlCVX rounds run bi-weekly, from Thursday 00:00 UTC until Tuesday 00:00 UTC, aligned with Convex gauge-vote proposals. Incentives are distributed within roughly 24-48 hours after a proposal ends via a Merkle airdrop; you can let rewards accumulate before claiming to minimise gas.
Faq.question: When do rounds run and when are rewards distributed?

Faq.answer: There are no withdrawal fees and no cost to delegate or vote (aside from gas). A maintenance fee is taken from the incentives themselves; the fee is adjustable by the multisig between 0% and a hard-capped maximum of 4%.
Faq.question: What fees does Votium charge?

Faq.answer: Votium is non-custodial — your CVX/CRV is never staked or held by Votium and you always retain custody. Your locked CVX stays on Convex's smart contracts. Residual risk comes from interacting with the delegation registry, the auction contract (buyers) and the Merkle claim contract.
Faq.question: Is my CVX or CRV at risk when I use Votium?

OrgStructure.description: Team-controlled multisig that administers all fund-affecting contract functions (fee level up to the 4% cap, fee recipient, team permissions, token whitelist, Merkle-root updates, pausing claims).
OrgStructure.name: Votium Multisig

Risks.description: Votium is described as experimental software provided 'as is'. Users interact with the auction/deposit contract, the Snapshot/Gnosis delegate registry, and the updateable Merkle airdrop distributor — any bug in these could cause loss of deposited incentives or unclaimed rewards despite an external audit (Blockian).

A team multisig controls all fund-affecting functions — fee level (up to the 4% hard cap), fee recipient, token whitelist, team permissions, and critically the Merkle root and claim pause. A compromised or malicious multisig could post an incorrect root or halt distributions. No public timelock is documented.

Incentive buyers must trust that delegated/self-directed votes are cast and counted correctly, and voters must trust that Votium computes each round's Merkle distribution honestly and in proportion to delegated vlCVX and incentive size. Distribution is computed off-chain before the root is posted.

Votium is entirely dependent on external systems it does not control: Convex (vlCVX locking and vote power), Curve (gauge weights and the ~10-day cooldown on gauge changes), and Snapshot (delegation and vote signalling). Failure, deprecation, tokenomics changes, or governance shifts in Convex or Curve directly impair Votium's usefulness and reward flow.

The core activity — paying token holders in exchange for how they vote in protocol governance ('vote buying') — sits in an unsettled legal/regulatory area for DAO governance and could attract scrutiny; participants bear this uncertainty.

Faq.answer: Yearn is a DeFi yield-aggregation protocol that pools user capital into automated vaults which move funds between yield opportunities to maximize returns while minimizing individual user effort. Faq.answer: YFI was fair-launched by Andre Cronje on July 17, 2020 with no pre-mine, no VC round, no private sale and no founder allocation. The initial 30,000 YFI were distributed entirely to users who provided liquidity to Yearn's early pools; Cronje kept zero tokens for himself. The launch became a widely-copied template for 'fair launches' in DeFi.

Faq.answer: Governance is conducted on-chain via veYFI (vote-escrowed YFI). Holders lock YFI to receive veYFI and vote on protocol upgrades, gauge weights and treasury allocation; longer locks yield more voting power and larger reward boosts.

Faq.answer: Yes. In February 2021 a flash-loan attack drained roughly $11 million from a V1 DAI vault by manipulating a Curve pool exchange rate. Yearn V2/V3 vaults were not affected by the 2023 incident.

OrgStructure.description: Created Yearn and fair-launched YFI in July 2020 with no allocation to himself. He later stepped back from day-to-day development; the protocol is maintained by a distributed set of contributors and yTeams under DAO governance.

OrgStructure.description: A community of independent contributor teams (yTeams) builds and maintains vaults and strategies, funded and directed through on-chain veYFI governance and the protocol treasury rather than a single company.

Risks.description: Vault and strategy contracts are complex and have been exploited historically (Feb 2021 V1 DAI vault ~$11M via flash loan; April 2023 legacy yUSDT misconfiguration ~$10M+). A copy-paste/config error persisting for years shows how latent bugs in legacy code can be catastrophic.

Yearn strategies deposit into and depend on underlying protocols such as Curve, Convex, Aave, Compound and Liquity. A failure, exploit, depeg or economic attack on any of those base protocols (e.g. the Curve 3CRV pool manipulation used in 2021) can propagate losses into Yearn vaults.

Some strategies rely on price/exchange-rate assumptions and pool ratios; the 2021 exploit manipulated a Curve pool exchange rate and the 2023 exploit manipulated share-price/pool-ratio calculation, both effectively pricing/oracle-adjacent manipulation vectors.

Protocol direction, gauge weights, strategy approvals and treasury allocation are controlled through veYFI vote-escrow governance; concentration of locked YFI or governance capture could steer risk parameters or strategy whitelisting against depositor interests.

Newer products wrap third-party assets whose stability Yearn does not control — e.g. yBOLD's exposure to Liquity V2 BOLD and its Stability Pools, and yCRV/yETH exposure to CRV and staked-ETH LSTs — so depeg or underperformance of the wrapped collateral flows through to holders.

Risks.description: MAX LRT vaults and LRT contracts carry share-issuance inflation-attack and reentrancy risk from external protocol interactions. An early Zokyo audit found (and resolved) a high-severity inflationary/share-allocation attack in ynETH, and upgradeable beacon-pattern contracts add upgrade-vulnerability surface despite timelocks.

Access controls, parameters, upgrades, and emergency pause are managed by core-team multisigs (Security Council), creating centralization risk. The planned transition from Security Council to veYND DAO governance introduces additional uncertainty (per LlamaRisk).

The LSDRateProvider relies on a single price feed for LST rate accuracy; LlamaRisk notes additional price sources would reduce reliance and that this dependency is vulnerable to mispricing and depeg events.

MAX LRTs and native LRTs hold liquid staking token collateral (e.g., slisBNB, various LSDs) that carries inherent depeg exposure; a depeg of underlying collateral or the LRT itself on secondary AMMs could impair redemptions at par.

Heavy dependence on third-party protocols (EigenLayer, Kernel, Karak, Binomial, Lista DAO, Curve, etc.) and on selected operators. Operator performance and third-party protocol failures directly affect yield and principal safety.

As a restaking protocol on EigenLayer (and Kernel/Karak on BNB Chain), restaked assets are subject to slashing penalties for operator/AVS misbehavior; EigenLayer's slashing (ELIP-002) makes slashing outcomes more probable, and withdrawal buffers may be insufficient under stress, forcing queues or reliance on secondary-market liquidity.

Competitors.name: Pendle Finance
Competitors.positioning: Tokenized yield: split principal and yield (PT/YT).
Competitors.similarities: same parent, adjacent product, fixed versus floating on a maturity.
Competitors.differences: The dominant yield-tokenization market: PT buyers lock a fixed rate, YT buyers go long yield, a true fixed-income primitive for DeFi, with the deepest liquidity and asset coverage in the category.

Competitors.name: Notional Finance
Competitors.positioning: Fixed-rate, fixed-term lending and borrowing.
Competitors.similarities: Both let a counterparty lock a rate.
Competitors.differences: True fixed-rate/fixed-term loans through fCash, rather than variable money-market rates, giving predictable cost of capital for borrowers and lenders.

Competitors.name: Sense Finance

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#contango.Name: Contango V2
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#contango.Tagline: One-click looping across external money markets.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#contango.Description: Contango builds looped positions by borrowing on an underlying money market and re-supplying, so a user gets levered exposure to a rate or yield spread without managing the loop. The $44,266,567 of borrowed notional against roughly $5.49m of net supplied TVL is the signature of a looping product (DefiLlama API, 26 Jul 2026).
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#contango.LongDescription: Contango builds looped positions by borrowing on an underlying money market and re-supplying, so a user gets levered exposure to a rate or yield spread without managing the loop. The $44,266,567 of borrowed notional against roughly $5.49m of net supplied TVL is the signature of a looping product (DefiLlama API, 26 Jul 2026). It aggregates looping across many external money markets rather than running its own, so it turns any third-party lending market into a one-click leverage venue. TVL roughly $5.49m; borrowed $44,266,567 as of 26 July 2026, split Ethereum $29,289,378, Arbitrum $5,252,391, Base $4,235,088, Optimism $3,245,931, Avalanche $1,131,670 (DefiLlama API). Maximum leverage: `n.a.` Yield sources: underlying money-market rate spreads on the markets it routes into. Liquidation mechanism: inherited from the underlying money market, evidenced by Contango's handling of frozen Aave rsETH markets below.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#contango.Differentiator: It aggregates looping across many external money markets rather than running its own, so it turns any third-party lending market into a one-click leverage venue.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#contango.AuditsNote: Audit reports are published in the repository at github.com/contango-xyz/core-v2/tree/main/audit, and the repo states there is no active bug bounty while audits are in place, with disclosures to security@contango.xyz (GitHub repo). Firm names and dates: `n.a.`

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#deltaprime.Name: DeltaPrime
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#deltaprime.Tagline: Undercollateralised prime accounts for leveraged farming.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#deltaprime.Description: DeltaPrime issues undercollateralised "prime accounts" that let a user borrow multiples of deposited capital and deploy the proceeds into farming strategies, which is textbook leverage farming. DefiLlama classifies it as Leveraged Farming (DefiLlama API, 26 Jul 2026).
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#deltaprime.LongDescription: DeltaPrime issues undercollateralised "prime accounts" that let a user borrow multiples of deposited capital and deploy the proceeds into farming strategies, which is textbook leverage farming. DefiLlama classifies it as Leveraged Farming (DefiLlama API, 26 Jul 2026). The borrowed capital never leaves the protocol's whitelisted strategy set, which is what allows the account to be undercollateralised. TVL $3.56m as of 26 July 2026: Avalanche $1,954,844, Arbitrum $1,608,643 (DefiLlama API). This is roughly 99% below its pre-incident scale. Maximum leverage: `n.a.` Yield sources: whitelisted Arbitrum and Avalanche farms. Liquidation mechanism: `n.a.`
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#deltaprime.Differentiator: The borrowed capital never leaves the protocol's whitelisted strategy set, which is what allows the account to be undercollateralised.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#deltaprime.AuditsNote: PeckShield audits of v1.0, v2.0 and v2.1 among others, published at github.com/DeltaPrimeLabs/deltaprime-primeloans/tree/main/audits per the DefiLlama API record. Note that these audits predate the 2024 key-compromise incidents, which were operational rather than contract-logic failures.

Incidents.title: First key-compromise exploit
Incidents.description: An attacker gained control of an admin private key and drained roughly $6m from DeltaPrime pools, the first of two operational breaches in under two months.
Incidents.outcome: Team continued operating; a second breach followed in November 2024.

Incidents.title: Second key-compromise exploit
Incidents.description: Compromised admin keys were used to drain roughly $4.75m to $4.8m across Arbitrum and Avalanche deployments.
Incidents.outcome: Post-mortem and reimbursement plan published December 2024. Audits predate the incidents, which were operational rather than contract-logic failures.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#dolomite.Tagline: Money market where collateral keeps its native rights.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#dolomite.Description: Dolomite is a variable-rate overcollateralised money market whose distinguishing feature is that collateral keeps its native rights (staking, vesting, governance) while pledged, so users borrow against assets that continue to earn. DefiLlama classifies it as Lending with $274,263,180 borrowed against $247.92m supplied (DefiLlama API, 26 Jul 2026).
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#dolomite.LongDescription: Dolomite is a variable-rate overcollateralised money market whose distinguishing feature is that collateral keeps its native rights (staking, vesting, governance) while pledged, so users borrow against assets that continue to earn. DefiLlama classifies it as Lending with $274,263,180 borrowed against $247.92m supplied (DefiLlama API, 26 Jul 2026). It supports a far wider long tail of collateral types than a pooled money market, including assets that remain productive while collateralised. Total supplied $247.92m; total borrowed $274,263,180, of which Ethereum $262,596,162, Arbitrum $8,862,277 and Berachain $2,796,205, as of 26 July 2026 (DefiLlama API). Note the borrowed figure exceeds the supplied figure in DefiLlama's accounting because supplied TVL nets out borrowed collateral. Utilisation, supply APY and borrow APY per market: `n.a.`
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#dolomite.Differentiator: Collateral keeps its native staking, vesting and governance rights while pledged.

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#euler.Name: Euler V2
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#euler.Description: Euler V2 is a modular lending kernel: anyone can deploy an isolated vault with its own oracle, LTV and interest-rate model, and link vaults into borrowable clusters. It is a money market in the strict sense, with $602,588,217 borrowed as of 26 July 2026 (DefiLlama API).
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#euler.LongDescription: Euler V2 is a modular lending kernel: anyone can deploy an isolated vault with its own oracle, LTV and interest-rate model, and link vaults into borrowable clusters. It is a money market in the strict sense, with $602,588,217 borrowed as of 26 July 2026 (DefiLlama API). Permissionless vault creation with cross-vault borrowing means Euler competes as lending infrastructure that third parties build markets on, not as a single curated market. Total supplied $325.03m; total borrowed $602,588,217, of which Ethereum $313,151,621, Plasma $110,283,049, Monad $94,690,755, Avalanche $38,330,016 and Sonic $20,821,132, as of 26 July 2026 (DefiLlama API). CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#exactly.Description: Exactly runs paired variable-rate and fixed-rate pools, where the fixed-rate side offers borrowing and lending at a rate locked to a specific maturity date. Documented at docs.exact.ly. DefiLlama classifies it as Lending (DefiLlama API, 26 Jul 2026).
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#exactly.LongDescription: Exactly runs paired variable-rate and fixed-rate pools, where the fixed-rate side offers borrowing and lending at a rate locked to a specific maturity date. It is the main fixed-rate credit venue whose liquidity sits on Base and Optimism rather than Ethereum mainnet, which matters for a Base-priority sourcing strategy. Total supplied $4.74m as of 26 July 2026: Optimism $2,680,666, Base $2,062,337, Ethereum $45. Total borrowed $845,761: Base $464,586, Optimism $330,016, Ethereum $51,158 (DefiLlama API). CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#fira.LongDescription: Fira issues Bond Tokens and Coupon Tokens against lending positions, splitting a loan into a principal claim and a yield claim with a defined term, which is yield tokenisation with maturity. CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#steakhouse-fina.Name: Steakhouse Financial
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#steakhouse-fina.Tagline: Largest risk curator in DeFi lending.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#steakhouse-fina.Description: Steakhouse is a risk curator: it underwrites collateral, sets loan-to-value parameters and allocates depositor stablecoins across overcollateralised lending markets, which is the economic core of a money market even though the matching engine belongs to Morpho and Euler. DefiLlama classifies it under "Risk Curators" per the DefiLlama API, but the product a depositor buys is a variable-rate overcollateralised lending position. It is the single most important non-Morpho credit actor on Robinhood Chain because it curates the vaults behind Robinhood Earn per Morpho's announcement.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#steakhouse-fina.LongDescription: Steakhouse is a risk curator: it underwrites collateral, sets loan-to-value parameters and allocates depositor stablecoins across overcollateralised lending markets, which is the economic core of a money market even though the matching engine belongs to Morpho and Euler. DefiLlama classifies it under "Risk Curators" per the DefiLlama API, but the product a depositor buys is a variable-rate overcollateralised lending position. It is the single most important non-Morpho credit actor on Robinhood Chain because it curates the vaults behind Robinhood Earn per Morpho's announcement. It is the largest curator in DeFi lending, curating roughly $1.5bn across 51 Morpho vaults and about 53% of Morpho's stablecoin TVL against Gauntlet's roughly $0.7bn across 63 vaults, per Steakhouse's DeFi Markets Update of 2 July 2026. Total supplied $2.402bn as of 26 July 2026 (DefiLlama API). Morpho deposits grew from $1.55bn on 1 January to $1.70bn on 1 July 2026 (Steakhouse, 14 July 2026). Bad debt: the curator reports zero bad debt across the first half of 2026, and less than $0.1 of bad debt across Q1 (Steakhouse, 15 May 2026); a third-party tracker shows $0.23 cumulative bad debt (CuratorWatch curator profile). Borrowed, utilisation, supply APY and borrow APY are not published at the curator level: `n.a.`
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#steakhouse-fina.Differentiator: Largest curator in DeFi lending, roughly $1.5bn across 51 Morpho vaults and about 53% of Morpho stablecoin TVL.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#steakhouse-fina.AuditsNote: No audits by design: Steakhouse is a risk curator and deploys no contracts of its own. Smart-contract risk sits with the venues it allocates to (Morpho, Euler, Kamino).

CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#term-finance.Tagline: Sealed-bid on-chain repo auctions with a real term structure.
CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#term-finance.Description: Term Finance runs sealed-bid, weekly, fixed-rate auctions that clear lenders and borrowers at a single rate for a defined term, issuing Term Repo Tokens that behave like zero-coupon instruments. CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#term-finance.LongDescription: Term Finance runs sealed-bid, weekly, fixed-rate auctions that clear lenders and borrowers at a single rate for a defined term, issuing Term Repo Tokens that behave like zero-coupon instruments. Rate discovery happens through a periodic sealed-bid auction rather than a continuous curve, which produces a genuine term structure rather than a spot rate with a maturity wrapper. CATEGORY#Entity|PROTOCOL#termmax.LongDescription: TermMax issues fixed-rate, fixed-maturity credit through paired Fixed Tokens and eXtra Tokens, with a Gearing Token representing the leveraged borrower side, so both lenders and borrowers lock a rate to a date. Competitors.name: Curve (crvUSD)
Competitors.positioning: Soft-liquidation CDP dollar.
Competitors.similarities: Yield Basis borrows crvUSD and is built by the same founder, so it is a demand-side complement and a competitor for the same BTC collateral.
Competitors.differences: LLAMMA soft-liquidation continuously converts collateral to crvUSD as price drops, eliminating hard liquidation cascades.
